title: No Rule on Algorithmic Rent-Setting
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on setting rents with algorithmic, revenue-management or other pricing software, and none on sharing rent or occupancy data with other landlords; no 2026 law adds one. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. New Hampshire's general antitrust law still applies: every contract, combination or conspiracy in restraint of trade is unlawful, including one that has the purpose or effect of fixing, controlling or maintaining prices, rates or fees, and the law's definition of trade covers dealings in real property. Whether using a shared pricing tool with competing landlords amounts to such an agreement is a question for case law and federal antitrust law, which this library does not cover; take advice before adopting one.

title: Application and Renewal Fees
bodyText: Before you collect any fee as part of the rental application or renewal process, tell the applicant in writing how much the fee is and whether you require a satisfactory criminal background check and credit check. If you collect the fee and then don't rent the unit to that applicant, return everything except the actual cost of the documented background check, credit check and reasonable administrative costs within 30 days of receiving the fee; keep the invoices so you can document what you kept. If you break this rule, the applicant can get back all the money they paid you as part of the application, plus court costs. The rule applies to every residential landlord, whatever the size of the property. New Hampshire sets no cap on the fee, has no rule on fees for minors or on screening applicants in order, and does not require you to run any check or forbid renting to someone who fails one. One screening rule comes from the eviction statute (others, on annulled criminal records and fair housing, are covered separately): a tenancy you ended at the expiration of a lease term of 12 months or more (or a shorter lease renewed for a total of 12 months or more) under the no-fault ground of the eviction statute is not an eviction for rental applications and tenant screening reports, so don't treat it as one. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Collection Fees on Unpaid Rent
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on charging a collection fee on past-due rent. Its debt-collection law, which bars collecting any fee incidental to a debt unless the agreement creating it expressly authorizes the fee, covers only consumer transactions, and the law's definition of a consumer transaction leaves out leases of real property. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. A few specific rules apply. If a tenant's check bounces, the bad-check statute lets you recover the check amount plus court, service and collection costs, but only after you give the notice it requires and the tenant fails to pay within 10 days. In a nonpayment eviction the tenant can stop the case by paying all rent due, other lawful charges contained in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs. And the money judgment a court awards in the eviction case itself is capped at $1,500, though you can sue separately for more. If you want to pass a collection agency's fee on to the tenant, state it in the lease; whether a court will enforce it is not settled by statute (case law, not covered here). The federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act may govern a collection agency you hire; federal law is not covered here.

title: Charging for Services You Do Not Provide
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute aimed specifically at charging a tenant a fee for a service you don't actually provide. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. New Hampshire's consumer protection act does apply to renting real estate. It makes it unlawful to represent that services have characteristics or benefits they don't have, or to advertise services with intent not to supply them as advertised, and a tenant harmed by such a practice can recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, two to three times that for a willful or knowing violation, plus attorney's fees. So charge only for services you actually provide, describe each one accurately in the lease, and stop charging when a service ends.

title: Fees and the Nonpayment Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire's eviction statute does not define rent in general, and no statute says that a fee becomes rent because your lease calls it additional rent. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. What the statutes do say: (1) A nonpayment eviction notice needs only 7 days, but it rests on neglect or refusal to pay rent due, so don't build a nonpayment notice on fees alone unless a statute treats them as rent; whether a lease's additional-rent label is enough is a question for case law, not covered here. (2) A tenant can stop a nonpayment eviction by paying, before the hearing, all rent due plus other lawful charges contained in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs, so charges you want included must be in the lease. (3) If you bill a tenant in writing for the reasonable cost of remediating a bed bug infestation the tenant caused and the tenant neither pays within 30 days of the end of remediation nor enters a repayment agreement, the statute makes that failure a ground for eviction for nonpayment of rent. (4) Where the deposit statute applies, you may deduct unpaid rent and other lawful charges due under the lease from the deposit, with an itemized list. (5) If a tenant appeals a judgment, the rent the tenant must keep paying (weekly into court in a nonpayment case; into court or to you, as the court directs, in other cases) is measured by the rent called for by the lease when you filed.

title: Passing Government Fees to Tenants
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute addresses making a tenant reimburse you for a fee a government charges you, such as a registration, inspection or certificate fee, and New Hampshire has no statewide rental registration or rental license. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. One state filing duty sits with you: if you own restricted property, file with the town or city clerk, within 30 days of becoming the owner, the name, address and telephone number of a person in New Hampshire authorized to accept service of legal papers for the property (it may be you). The municipality may charge a reasonable filing fee and may fine you up to $100 for not filing. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). One government cost does shift by statute: in a nonpayment eviction, a tenant who wants the case dismissed must pay your court filing fee and service charges along with the rent due. Cities and towns may have their own housing codes and fees; check local ordinances, which this library does not cover.

title: No Late Fee Limit
bodyText: New Hampshire sets no maximum late fee and no grace period for residential tenancies; the amount and timing are whatever the lease states. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. A statute does cap late fees for self-storage units, but it doesn't apply to homes, and manufactured housing parks have their own statute, which this library does not cover. Keep the fee a reasonable estimate of what late payment costs you, since a court may refuse to enforce a fee it sees as a penalty (case law, not covered here). Put the fee in the lease: a tenant facing a nonpayment eviction can end the case by paying, before the hearing, all rent due plus other lawful charges contained in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs.

title: No Lease-Type Parity Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule requiring the same rent or terms for a month-to-month tenancy and a fixed-term lease, and no cap on the rent difference between them. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The law still treats them differently. Unless a different contract is shown, every tenancy is a tenancy at will with rent payable on demand. A month-to-month tenant may end the tenancy on 30 days' notice and, if the notice doesn't end on a rent due date, owes rent for the whole month in which the notice expires unless the lease says otherwise. For restricted property, you may end a tenancy only for a reason the eviction statute lists; one of them is the expiration of a lease whose original term is 12 months or longer (or a shorter lease renewed to 12 months or more in total), if you gave written notice at least 60 days before the term ends that the lease won't be renewed and you file a possessory action within 6 months after it expires. For nonrestricted property, you may end a tenancy for any reason with proper written notice. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure).

title: Rent Increases Written Into the Lease
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute regulates a rent-escalation clause (a lease term that raises the rent on set dates or by a set formula), and none gives such a clause a safe harbour from the retaliation rules. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. A fixed-term lease that states the rent for each period binds both sides, so write any scheduled increase into the lease with its amount (or formula) and effective date. Keep in mind the retaliation rule: if you institute a rent increase, an eviction or a substantial change in the terms of the tenancy within 6 months after the tenant reports a code or habitability violation in good faith, files an action against you under the landlord-tenant statute, or meets with other tenants, the law presumes retaliation unless the court finds the tenant's act was primarily meant to prevent an eviction. Whether an increase already scheduled in the lease counts as one you institute after the tenant's act isn't settled by statute (case law, not covered here); keep records showing the increase was set before the tenant's complaint.

title: Rent Increase Notice
bodyText: For restricted property, a tenant's refusal to agree to a rent increase is good cause to end the tenancy only if you gave the tenant written notice of the amount of the increase and the date it takes effect at least 30 days before that date. If the tenant still refuses, you may then serve a 30-day eviction notice that states the reason with specificity. For nonrestricted property, no statute sets a rent-increase notice; you may end any tenancy with a proper written notice, so the practical route is the same written notice of the new rent, given at least 30 days ahead. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). No statute lets you raise the rent during a fixed lease term; the lease's own terms control, so a mid-term increase needs a lease clause that provides for one. Two other limits apply. If you raise the rent within 6 months after a tenant reports a code or habitability violation in good faith, files an action against you under the landlord-tenant statute, or meets with other tenants, the law presumes retaliation. And if you convert a rental building or complex of more than 10 units to condominium or similar ownership, then once the conversion notice has been served you may raise the rent only by the unit's pro rata share of increases in insurance, fuel, utility, tax, maintenance and operating costs that benefit the tenant. New Hampshire has no statewide rent cap and no price-gouging law that reaches rent. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Rent Receipts
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to give a receipt for rent, whether paid in cash or otherwise. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Giving a dated, signed receipt for every cash payment is still the safer practice, for three reasons. In a nonpayment eviction, if the tenant pays everything the statute requires before the hearing, you must file a receipt for that payment with the court and state in writing that you sent the tenant a copy; if you don't, the hearing goes ahead and the case is dismissed if the tenant proves payment. In a court petition about someone occupying your property without permission, cash rent receipts signed and dated by you are one of the listed kinds of proof that a person is a tenant, so keep your receipts consistent with who your tenants are. And receipts are your record if a tenant disputes what was paid. A security deposit has its own receipt rule, covered in the deposit clauses.

title: No Rent Reporting Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to offer tenants positive rent reporting to credit bureaus, and none limiting a rent-reporting program you choose to offer. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. One screening rule touches the subject: ending a tenancy at the expiration of a lease term of 12 months or more under the eviction statute's no-fault ground is not an eviction for rental applications and tenant screening reports, so don't report or treat it as one. If you report rent payments or debts to a consumer reporting agency, the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act applies; federal law is not covered here.

title: Rooms Tax on Short Occupancies
bodyText: New Hampshire's meals and rooms tax can reach rent for a furnished room or apartment that you offer to the public for short stays. The tax is 8.5 percent of the rent for each occupancy of a room in a hotel, and the law defines a hotel broadly, as any establishment that holds itself out to the public as offering sleeping accommodations for rent, including rooming houses, furnished room houses, boarding houses and apartments. Occupancy by a permanent resident, someone who has occupied the room for at least 185 consecutive days, is not taxed. Under the Department of Revenue Administration's rule: if a signed lease or similar document runs for 185 or more consecutive days, you need not collect the tax; if the rental period is unknown or expected to be under 185 days, you collect the tax when rent is paid; if a stay you collected tax on reaches 185 consecutive days, you refund the tax collected before the 185th day; and if an occupancy under a 185-day lease ends early, you owe the tax on the total rent paid. An ordinary lease of a dwelling for 185 days or more is therefore not taxed, but a short furnished rental can be. The operator collects the tax and pays it to the state. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Put Every Fee in the Lease
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute requires your lease to list every fee or bars a fee the lease doesn't mention. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Several rules still make listing them the only safe course. A tenant facing a nonpayment eviction can end the case by paying rent due plus the other lawful charges contained in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs, so a charge left out of the lease isn't part of that payment. Where the deposit statute applies, you may deduct from the deposit only unpaid rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, a share of real estate tax increases the lease requires the tenant to pay, and other lawful charges due under the lease. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. Before you collect an application or renewal fee you must disclose its amount in writing. And the deposit statute defines a security deposit as all money beyond the monthly rent that a tenant pays you for any purpose; whether a particular one-time fee falls inside that definition is a question for the courts (case law, not covered here), so the library treats money collected up front beyond the first month's rent as part of the security deposit and subject to its cap.

title: Recovering on a Bounced Check
bodyText: If a tenant pays you with a check that is dishonored for lack of funds or credit, because the tenant has no account, or because the tenant stopped payment without cause, New Hampshire's bad-check statute gives you a civil remedy. First give the tenant notice, in person or in writing; written notice is conclusively presumed given when mailed by certified or registered mail, return receipt requested, to the address on the check or the tenant's last known address. If the tenant doesn't pay the check amount plus your bank fees and mailing costs within 10 days of receiving the notice, you may sue for the check amount plus court costs, service costs and collection costs, in small claims court if the amount fits. If you win and the tenant doesn't pay on the day of judgment, the tenant owes you $10 more for each business day it stays unpaid, up to $500. The statute doesn't cap a returned-payment fee your lease sets; any fee should be stated in the lease. You may require certified funds after a bounced check, but you may never require payment solely by electronic funds transfer. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Government Shutdown Protection
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute gives tenants who are federal or state workers extra time to pay rent, protection from late fees or a defense to eviction during a government shutdown. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The usual rules apply: you may serve a 7-day eviction notice for nonpayment after demanding the rent, and the tenant can end a nonpayment case by paying, before the hearing, all rent due plus other lawful charges in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs (no more than 3 times in 12 months). If you win, the court may still delay the move-out, usually by no more than 60 days, with the tenant paying the weekly rent in advance. A written payment plan with an affected tenant can avoid the cost of an eviction; once a nonpayment case is filed, the parties may also file a payment agreement with the court.

title: No Subsidy Proration Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule on how to split a rent reduction between a tenant's share and a housing subsidy when part of a subsidized unit is unfit. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The general fitness rule applies to every residential tenancy: you can't win a nonpayment eviction if the unit is in substantial violation of the state's or the municipality's health and safety standards in a way that materially affects habitability, the tenant gave notice while not behind on rent, you didn't fix it within 14 days (or as fast as an emergency requires), the tenant didn't cause it, and you weren't kept from repairing. The court may then continue the case for up to a month, have the tenant pay rent into court, and, once the problem is fixed, dismiss the case and either pay you the rent paid in or pay you only the fair rental value of the unit in its defective condition, with the rest going to the tenant; if it isn't fixed in time, the tenant wins and gets back all the money paid in. For units owned, operated or subsidized by the federal government, federal law controls where it conflicts with New Hampshire's eviction statute, so follow the program's rules and your housing assistance contract for the subsidy's share.

title: Late Fees When a Subsidy Pays Part of the Rent
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute bars or limits a late fee on the part of the rent a housing subsidy pays, and New Hampshire sets no late-fee cap. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Charge any late fee only on the tenant's own share and only when that share is late. Two rules protect payments from public sources. A rent payment the tenant tenders as a written promise to pay by the state, a county or a New Hampshire municipality, or a payment by any organization that disburses federal or state funds, counts as payment by the tenant of that amount (though you need not accept a partial payment). In a nonpayment eviction it is a defense that you refused such a timely payment, or that the tenant could have tendered it if you had given the agency ordinary and reasonable verification of rental information it asked for, so answer agency requests promptly. A town may also apply welfare rent it would pay you to your overdue municipal water, sewer, electricity or tax bills, and that counts as the tenant's payment. Federal programs such as Housing Choice Vouchers have their own lease addenda and contract rules on fees, which we did not review.

title: Passing On Real Estate Tax Increases
bodyText: New Hampshire's deposit statute recognizes a lease term that makes the tenant pay all or part of any increase in real estate taxes levied against the property that becomes due and payable during the lease term. If your lease has such a term and the tenant hasn't paid the share, you may deduct it from the security deposit, with a written, itemized list that states with particularity the period the claim covers. The statute doesn't say how the share must be stated or whether you must pass on a tax abatement; state the tenant's share (for example, a percentage of the increase over a base year's tax) and the base year in the lease so the amount can be checked, and consider refunding a proportionate share of any abatement; the library's optional "Real Estate Tax Increases" clause does both. Without such a lease term, a tax increase is yours. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Interest on Unpaid Amounts
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute requires a residential lease to state an interest rate before you can charge interest on unpaid rent or damages, and none sets one specifically for leases. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Three general statutes matter. For business transactions in which interest is paid or secured, the rate is 10 percent a year unless otherwise agreed in writing; whether a residential lease is such a transaction is not stated (case law, not covered here), so if you want interest before a judgment, put the rate in the written lease. Once you sue, the court adds interest at the yearly judgment rate the state treasurer sets each December (the 26-week Treasury bill rate plus 2 points), including prejudgment interest. In an action on a debt where you made no demand before suing, interest runs from the date you filed; on other money claims it runs from the date of the writ or petition. Interest on a security deposit you hold is a separate rule.

title: Accepting Rent After a Notice or During an Eviction
bodyText: Once you have filed a nonpayment eviction, you may accept payment of the back rent without creating a new tenancy only if you tell the tenant in writing that you intend to go ahead with the eviction despite accepting the payment; you may also refuse the payment and proceed. Payments the tenant makes under a payment agreement filed with the court in a nonpayment case don't create a new tenancy either. Separately, if the tenant pays everything the pay-and-stay rule requires before the hearing (all rent due, other lawful charges in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs), a case based only on nonpayment is dismissed, up to 3 times in 12 months. New Hampshire has no statute on what happens when you accept rent after serving an eviction notice but before filing, or after a breach other than nonpayment; whether that waives the notice or the breach is a question for case law, not covered here. The safe practice is the same: whenever you accept money from a tenant you are trying to evict, give a written statement that you accept it without waiving the notice or the breach and intend to proceed. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Preset Deposit Charges
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule letting your lease fix cleaning, carpet, painting or repair charges in advance that you may then take from the security deposit. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The deposit statute ties damage deductions to the actual cost of repair: you may deduct the costs of repairing damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, and you must give the tenant a written, itemized list that describes with particularity the repair each item needs, with satisfactory evidence that the repair has been or will be done, such as receipts for materials, labor estimates, bills or invoices. You may also deduct unpaid rent, a share of real estate tax increases the lease requires the tenant to pay, and other lawful charges due under the lease that remain unpaid, itemized with the period each covers. A flat charge that doesn't reflect an actual repair cost is risky, and a lease term that waives the tenant's deposit rights is void. Deduct documented, actual costs. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older.

title: Unclaimed Deposits
bodyText: New Hampshire's deposit statute says that a deposit, plus any interest due on it, that remains unclaimed 6 months after the tenancy ends becomes your property, free and clear of the tenant's claim, unless there was fraud. It also says you aren't liable and lose no rights if you couldn't comply with the deposit rules because the tenant didn't give you a new address when the tenancy ended. Separately, New Hampshire's unclaimed property act lists security deposits and refunds among the kinds of property a holder must report to the state treasurer once they have gone unclaimed for 5 years. The statutes don't say how the two rules fit together, for example for a refund check you mailed that was never cashed. Safe practice: ask every departing tenant for a forwarding address in writing, send the refund and itemized list within 30 days to that address (or the last address you have), keep proof of mailing, and before treating unclaimed money as yours, check with the state treasurer's unclaimed property division or a lawyer. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Deposit Installment Right
bodyText: New Hampshire does not give tenants a right to pay the security deposit in installments, and does not forbid you from agreeing to installments. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. If you agree to a payment plan, put it in writing, and remember that the total deposit still can't exceed one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, and that you must give the deposit receipt (or, for a check, the written notice about listing conditions within 5 days of occupancy) when you receive a deposit. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older.

title: Last Month's Rent Is Part of the Deposit
bodyText: Where the deposit statute applies, money you collect as prepaid last month's rent is part of the security deposit, because the statute defines a deposit as all money beyond the monthly rent that the tenant pays you for any purpose. So the last month's rent and any other deposit together can't exceed one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater. If a written lease calls for rent quarterly or less often, the deposit you take in addition to the first rent payment still can't exceed one month's rent. Treat prepaid last month's rent like any deposit: give the receipt and condition notice, hold it in trust in a New Hampshire bank, savings and loan or credit union (or post the bond the statute allows), pay interest if you hold it a year or more, and account for it within 30 days after the tenancy ends. No statute stops you from applying it to the final month's rent. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Conditions on the Deposit Refund
bodyText: New Hampshire does not let you make the deposit refund depend on the tenant giving advance notice of moving out, returning keys by a deadline or any similar condition. The deposit statute requires you to return the deposit, with any interest due, within 30 days from the end of the tenancy, minus only the deductions it allows, itemized in writing; a lease term that waives these rights is void. What the statute does give you: if you can't comply because the tenant didn't tell you a new address when the tenancy ended, you aren't liable for that failure. So ask for a forwarding address in writing at move-out, but don't hold the deposit hostage to it or to a notice requirement. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Deposit After a Survivor Termination
bodyText: A tenant may end a lease or rental agreement early if the tenant or a household member was the victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the most recent 150 days (or an event within that time, together with past abuse, makes the victim fear for their safety) and the tenant gives you the written verification the statute lists, such as a protective order, a police report, a letter from an advocate, attorney or health care provider, or the court's self-certification form. Keep that verification strictly confidential. The tenant must vacate within 30 days of the notice unless you agree on another time, and owes rent only through the date of termination or the date the tenant actually vacates, whichever is later. The security deposit stays applied to the rental until all tenants have vacated, so if co-tenants remain you keep holding it; once everyone has moved out, return it under the normal deposit rules: within 30 days, with an itemized list of any deductions. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Returning the Deposit Early
bodyText: New Hampshire has no expedited security deposit procedure. Your deadline is 30 days from the end of the tenancy, and you may always return the deposit sooner. The statute lists what you may deduct (repair costs for damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, unpaid rent, a lease-required share of real estate tax increases and other lawful charges due under the lease), and it doesn't provide for a fee for processing or returning the deposit early. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Fee-in-Lieu-of-Deposit Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute authorizing or regulating a fee a tenant pays instead of a security deposit, or a deposit-replacement insurance or surety program. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Be careful: the deposit statute defines a security deposit as all money beyond the monthly rent that a tenant pays you for any purpose, and a deposit must be held in trust, capped at one month's rent or $100 (whichever is greater) and returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends, less only the deductions the statute allows. Whether a nonrefundable fee in lieu of a deposit, paid to you, falls inside that definition is not settled by statute (case law, not covered here); if it does, keeping it would break the return rules, which carry a penalty of twice the deposit. If you offer a deposit alternative, have the tenant buy it from a third party rather than paying you, make it optional, and don't let it push the money you collect beyond the cap. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older.

title: Holding Deposits Before the Lease
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on holding deposits, earnest money or other money you take to hold a unit before the lease is signed. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Two rules bear on it. Any fee collected as part of the rental application process must be disclosed in writing before you collect it, and if you don't rent to that applicant you must return everything beyond the documented cost of background and credit checks and reasonable administrative costs within 30 days. And once the applicant becomes your tenant, the deposit statute defines a security deposit as all money beyond the monthly rent that a tenant pays you for any purpose, so money you took to hold the unit, beyond the first month's rent, counts toward the deposit cap of one month's rent or $100 (whichever is greater) and the receipt, trust and return rules. Whether the deposit statute also covers money from someone who never becomes a tenant isn't stated. Safe practice: put any holding arrangement in writing, say when the money is credited to the first month's rent or the deposit, and refund it promptly if you don't rent to the person. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older.

title: Penalty for Missing the Deposit Receipt or Condition Notice
bodyText: When you receive a security deposit, give the tenant a signed receipt stating the amount and where the deposit (or the bond for it) will be held, and tell the tenant that any conditions in the unit needing repair should be noted on the receipt or given to you in writing within 5 days of occupancy. If the deposit is paid by personal check, bank check or a check from a government or nonprofit agency, no receipt is needed, but you must still give the written notice about the 5-day list. Missing these steps, or the trust-account and sale-transfer rules, is treated as a violation of New Hampshire's consumer protection act; a tenant can then sue for actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. The statute does not take away your right to deduct for damage if you miss the notice, but the tenant's list (or its absence) will be evidence of the unit's condition at move-in. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Nonrefundable Deposits
bodyText: New Hampshire has no notice procedure for a nonrefundable deposit, because the deposit statute leaves no room for one. A security deposit stays the tenant's money, held in trust, and at the end of the tenancy you must return it within 30 days minus only repair costs for damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, unpaid rent, a lease-required share of real estate tax increases and other lawful charges due under the lease, all itemized in writing. A lease can't waive that. And the deposit statute defines a security deposit as all money beyond the monthly rent that a tenant pays you for any purpose, so calling a pet deposit, cleaning deposit or key deposit nonrefundable doesn't take it outside these rules or outside the cap of one month's rent or $100 (whichever is greater). Whether a one-time fee labeled nonrefundable is a deposit isn't settled by statute (case law, not covered here); the library treats money collected up front beyond the first month's rent as deposit. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Separate Nonrefundable-Deposit Notice
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule requiring a separate written notice, when you collect a deposit, that part of it is nonrefundable. That is because no part of a New Hampshire security deposit can be made nonrefundable where the deposit statute applies: the deposit stays the tenant's money, held in trust, and must be returned within 30 days after the tenancy ends minus only the deductions the statute lists, and a lease can't waive that. Don't hand a tenant a receipt or notice calling any part of a deposit nonrefundable; the receipt the statute requires states the amount and where the deposit is held. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Security Deposit Cap
bodyText: Where the deposit statute applies, you may not demand or receive a security deposit of more than one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater. Because the deposit statute defines a security deposit as all money beyond the monthly rent that a tenant pays you for any purpose, the cap covers pet deposits, key deposits, cleaning deposits and prepaid last month's rent combined; there is no separate allowance for pets, furniture or alterations. If a written lease calls for rent quarterly or less often, the deposit you take in addition to the first rent payment still can't exceed one month's rent. You also may not raise your usual deposit for a tenant with a disability, though you may negotiate an interest-bearing escrow for restoring a disability-related modification. The statute doesn't address topping up the deposit after a rent increase; any top-up must keep the total within the cap measured against the current rent, so take advice before relying on one. Violating the cap is treated as a violation of the consumer protection act, with damages of at least $1,000. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Holding the Security Deposit
bodyText: A security deposit stays the tenant's money. Hold it in trust and don't mix it with your personal funds or treat it as your asset until you have accounted for it at the end of the tenancy. You may keep all your tenants' deposits together in a single trust account at a bank, savings and loan association or credit union organized under New Hampshire law. Instead of a trust account, you may post a bond written by a company located in New Hampshire with the clerk of the city or town where the property is, in an amount equal to all the deposits you hold on property in that city or town. The receipt you give the tenant must say where the deposit or bond is held, and on request you must tell the tenant the institution, account number, amount on deposit and interest rate, and let the tenant examine your records of the deposit. Breaking the trust, account, bond or receipt rules is treated as a violation of the consumer protection act; breaking the records-on-request rule (like the interest rule) makes you liable for twice the deposit plus interest, less proper charges. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Interest on Security Deposits
bodyText: If you hold a security deposit for one year or longer, you must pay the tenant interest on it, at the rate paid on regular savings accounts at the New Hampshire bank, savings and loan association or credit union where it is deposited, counted from the date you received it. If you pool deposits in one account, pay each tenant a proportionate share of the interest the account actually earns. A tenant may ask for the interest that has accrued every 3 years, by asking 30 days before that year's tenancy expires, and you must pay it within 15 days after that year's tenancy expires. Otherwise pay the interest with the deposit return within 30 days after the tenancy ends. On request, tell the tenant where the deposit is held, the account number, the amount and the interest rate. The statute doesn't say how interest works when you post a bond instead of using a trust account; take advice if you do. Failing to pay interest due exposes you to damages of twice the deposit plus interest, less proper charges. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Deposit Rights Cannot Be Waived
bodyText: No New Hampshire lease may waive any part of the security deposit law: the cap of one month's rent or $100 (whichever is greater), the receipt and 5-day condition-list notice, the trust and bank or bond rules, the transfer rules on sale, interest after one year, the 30-day itemized return, and the tenant's right to twice the deposit for a violation. A lease term that tries is void, so terms such as "the deposit is forfeited if Tenant leaves early", "a cleaning charge of $X will be deducted in every case" or "Tenant waives interest on the deposit" don't work. The one exception: the landlord and tenant may agree otherwise about whether a selling landlord who turns the deposit over to the buyer is released from liability for it. New Hampshire's eviction statute separately voids any lease term waiving a tenant's rights under that statute. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Deposits When the Property Is Sold
bodyText: When you sell the property (or assign your lease), turn the security deposits over to the buyer or assignee at the time you deliver the deed or assignment, or within 5 days after. The same applies to a court-appointed receiver in a foreclosure (within 5 days after the receiver qualifies) or, if there is no receiver, the purchaser at a foreclosure sale. Then notify each tenant by registered or certified mail that you have done so, with the name and address of the person now holding the deposit. If you turn over the deposit with any interest due, you are relieved of liability to the tenant for it, and the new holder becomes responsible for returning it, unless you and the tenant agreed otherwise. If you are buying, make sure you receive the deposits and interest, because you will owe their return. A new owner also takes over the landlord's rights under the eviction statute for a tenancy at will. Failing to follow the transfer rules is treated as a violation of the consumer protection act. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Penalties for Deposit Violations
bodyText: New Hampshire's deposit statute has two penalty tiers. (1) If you take more than the cap, skip the receipt or the 5-day condition-list notice, fail to hold the deposit in trust in a New Hampshire institution (or under the bond), or don't follow the transfer rules on sale, the violation is treated as an unfair or deceptive practice under the consumer protection act: the tenant can recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, two to three times that if the violation was willful or knowing, plus costs and attorney's fees. (2) If you don't pay interest due or don't return the deposit with the itemized list within 30 days, you owe the tenant twice the deposit plus any interest due, less payments already made and the charges you could properly claim for damage, unpaid rent or a lease-required real estate tax share. The statute does not take away your right to sue separately for damage beyond the deposit. You aren't liable for a failure caused by the tenant's not giving you a new address at the end of the tenancy. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Deposit Standards Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire does not require you to post or disclose the standards you use to set deposit amounts, even if you charge different tenants different deposits. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Two limits apply. Every deposit, however you label it, is capped at one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, where the deposit statute applies. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. And New Hampshire's fair housing law bars altering the terms or conditions of a rental, which includes the deposit you ask for, because of age, sex, gender identity, race, religion, color, marital status, familial status, physical or mental disability or national origin, and specifically bars raising your usual deposit for a person with a disability. (The general discrimination section doesn't apply to renting units in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer families, apart from its rule on listings; that exemption is written for the general section only, so don't rely on it for the disability rules, including the deposit rule.) Apply written, consistent criteria, such as a credit-based deposit tier, to every applicant and keep records of how you set each deposit.

title: No Separate Utility Deposit
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule for a separate utility deposit held by a landlord, and the library offers none. Where the deposit statute applies, money you hold to secure the tenant's utility payments is part of the security deposit however you label it, so it counts toward the cap of one month's rent or $100 (whichever is greater) together with any other deposit, and it is returned under the deposit rules. Utility charges the tenant owes you under the lease and hasn't paid are other lawful charges due under the lease that you may deduct, itemized. When the tenant's unit has its own electric or gas meter and the tenant is the utility's customer, the utility may take a deposit only from the tenant, not from you, and you aren't liable for the tenant's unpaid bill. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Rental Fee Transparency Law
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rental fee transparency law: no all-in or total-price rule for advertising rent, no rule that the lease state rent as one figure including mandatory fees, no required fee-disclosure page, and no automatic-renewal statute that reaches residential leases. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Two specific disclosures apply: before collecting an application or renewal fee you must disclose its amount in writing, and before a tenant signs you must disclose, to your knowledge, any tenant-paid metered utility service billed under a tariff carrying energy-efficiency or similar charges (the library has a separate clause for that). The general consumer protection act also applies to advertising and renting real estate, so advertised rent and fees must not mislead. Stating every fee in the lease is still wise, since only charges contained in the lease count toward what a tenant must pay to stop a nonpayment eviction or what you may deduct from a deposit as charges due under the lease.

title: No Rent Control
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide rent control or cap on rent increases, and no statute that either authorizes or forbids cities and towns from adopting rent control. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Municipalities may adopt housing codes and minimum housing standards, inspect dwellings and order unfit ones repaired or vacated, but the statute bars using those powers to impose additional ordinances, licenses or other restrictions on vacation or short-term rentals, and zoning may not limit occupancy of a dwelling unit to fewer than 2 people per bedroom. Rent itself is limited in only a few situations: if you convert a building or complex of more than 10 rental units to condominium or similar ownership, once the conversion notice is served you may raise rent only by the unit's pro rata share of increases in listed operating costs; for restricted property, a tenant's refusal of a rent increase is good cause to end the tenancy only after 30 days' written notice of the amount and effective date; and an increase within 6 months after a tenant's good-faith code complaint, legal action or tenant organizing is presumed retaliatory. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). Check local ordinances, which this library does not cover.

title: Disability Modifications
bodyText: Your lease may require your written consent for alterations, but New Hampshire's fair housing law makes it a civil rights violation to refuse a person with a disability permission to make reasonable modifications to the unit, at that person's expense, when the modifications may be necessary for full enjoyment of the premises. You may, where reasonable, condition permission on: the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition at the end of the tenancy (reasonable wear and tear excepted); a reasonable description of the proposed work; and reasonable assurances that the work will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required building permits. You may not raise your usual security deposit for a person with a disability, but where necessary to make sure restoration money will be there, you may negotiate, as part of the restoration agreement, payments over a reasonable period into an interest-bearing escrow account, not exceeding the restoration cost, with the interest going to the tenant. You must also make reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices and services. New Hampshire does not shift the cost of modifications to owners of larger or subsidized buildings. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Cold-Weather Vacating Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring a tenant to notify you before leaving a unit in cold weather or to keep the heat on or drain pipes when away or moving out. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Use the lease instead: the library's optional extended-absence clause asks the tenant to tell you before an absence of more than 7 days, and your utilities clause can require the tenant to keep tenant-paid heat on through the end of the tenancy. Keep in mind that the heat duty runs to you: in municipalities without their own housing code, a landlord may not let rented premises lack heating facilities that are properly installed, safely maintained and capable of heating all habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms to an average of at least 65 degrees F, and where you supply heat as part of the rent you must actually maintain that temperature. And you may not enter to check on a unit without the tenant's consent except for emergency repairs, such as a burst pipe.

title: No Common-Area Lighting Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on whether a tenant may be charged for common-area lights or other shared electricity wired to the tenant's own meter. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. If a tenant's meter serves any common area, say so in the lease before signing and state how the tenant will be compensated or credited, so the tenant isn't misled about what the tenant's bill covers. Your local housing or electrical code may address shared meters; check it, as municipal codes are not covered here.

title: Contractor Liens and Tenant Work
bodyText: New Hampshire's mechanic's lien statute gives a person who performs labor, provides professional design services or furnishes materials worth $15 or more to build or repair a building a lien on the building and on the owner's interest in the land, but only when the work is done under a contract with the owner. A person working under a contract with the owner's agent, contractor or subcontractor gets the same lien only after giving the owner written notice that it will claim one. The lien lasts 120 days after the work or materials are furnished unless secured as the statute provides. No statute addresses work a tenant orders, and none lets a lease keep your property free of liens. Whether a tenant acting under a lease that permits alterations counts as your agent, or makes the work one done under a contract with you, is a question for case law, not covered here. To reduce the risk, require your written consent for alterations, require the tenant to pay contractors and keep the property lien-free, and if you receive a contractor's lien notice, respond promptly. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Rule on Tenant Child Care Homes
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to let a tenant run a family child care home in a rental unit, and none forbidding a lease from restricting it. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. New Hampshire's zoning law does require cities and towns to allow family day care homes and group family day care homes by right wherever residential use is permitted, if the state's child care licensing rules are met, but that rule limits local zoning, not leases, and it expressly does not override private covenants. So your lease's residential-use clause decides whether a tenant may run a child care business in the unit. If you allow one, require proof of the state child care license and of liability insurance covering the business.

title: No Home Business Statute
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants a right to run a home-based business in a rental unit or limiting a lease term that restricts one. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Your lease's residential-use clause controls. Local zoning may separately limit home occupations, and state zoning law requires towns to allow licensed home child care by right, but neither changes what your lease may say. If you allow a home business, set limits in writing (no employees or customer traffic, no signs, no hazardous materials) and require the tenant to carry business liability insurance.

title: Municipal Utility Liens
bodyText: If a city or town owns the electric, gas, water or wastewater utility, its charges for service create a lien on the property served, collectible like taxes. When a tenant or anyone else other than the owner is the customer, the lien binds you only for charges the municipality told you about within 120 days after they became delinquent; a municipality can meet that by mailing you copies of the bills when it bills the tenant, so watch for them. One exception protects owners: for electric or gas service to a tenant whose unit has its own meter, the utility may take a deposit only from the tenant, you aren't liable for the tenant's unpaid bill, and the utility gets no lien on your property for it. Water and sewer have no such exception, so for those, either keep the account in your name and build the cost into the rent, or require the tenant to pay on time and show proof, and act on any delinquency notice within the 120-day window. If you fall behind on a municipal water bill, the water company must give your tenants at least 7 days' posted or mailed notice before disconnecting, and a tenant may take over the service. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Occupancy Limits
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide rule setting how many people may live in a rental unit. Local zoning may not limit the occupants of a dwelling unit to fewer than 2 per bedroom, or base occupancy on whether occupants are related, married, employed or students, though the state building and fire codes still apply. New Hampshire's fair housing law allows reasonable local, state or federal limits on the maximum number of occupants, but it bars discrimination because of familial status, so a limit stricter than those codes require (for example, one that keeps out families with children) is risky. List the tenants and permitted occupants in the lease: anyone who isn't a tenant, an authorized subtenant or an implied tenant (an occupant you and the tenant both know of and consent to without a signed lease) may not occupy the unit without your permission, and you can petition the court to remove such a person. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Acts the Law Bars Tenants From
bodyText: New Hampshire's landlord-tenant law lists what tenants may not do, whether or not the lease repeats it. No tenant, member of the tenant's household, guest or other occupant may willfully damage your property, willfully deny other tenants the quiet enjoyment of their homes, willfully engage in behavior that unreasonably and adversely affects the health or safety of other tenants, you or your agent, or willfully prevent you from making emergency repairs. A tenant may not willfully prevent necessary repairs or refuse you access, at a reasonable time after adequate notice, for other reasonable and lawful functions of owning rental property; may not refuse access for emergency repairs or, on 48 hours' written notice, for a bed bug evaluation when an adjacent unit or a unit above or below has bed bugs; and may not refuse reasonable written instructions, given at least 72 hours ahead, to prepare the unit for pest remediation. A tenant or guest who disables a smoke detector commits a crime. If a tenant violates these rules you can file a petition in court; after a hearing the court can order the violation to stop, order a person who unreasonably endangered others' health or safety to leave and stay away, and award damages and attorney's fees (the damages-and-fees remedy doesn't apply to the bed bug evaluation and pest-preparation rules, or to a good-faith petition asking the court whether your request for access was reasonable and lawful). These acts can also be grounds to end the tenancy. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Unlawful Use Voids the Lease
bodyText: New Hampshire has an old nuisance statute that reaches leases. If a tenant or occupant uses the premises, or any part of them, for lewdness, assignation, prostitution or the illegal manufacture, sale or keeping for sale of intoxicating liquor, that use annuls and voids the lease and returns the right of possession to you without any act on your part. The same statute lets the attorney general, a county attorney or any citizen sue to abate such a nuisance, and the court can enjoin everyone involved, including an owner or lessee, and close the place for up to a year; an owner who couldn't have known of the use with reasonable care can get the property released by posting a bond and abating the nuisance. Although that statute says the owner may re-enter without legal process, a later landlord-tenant statute forbids a landlord to deny a tenant access to and possession of the premises other than through proper judicial process, and the statutes don't say how the two fit together. Don't change locks or remove the tenant yourself: serve an eviction notice (substantial damage, health-or-safety behavior or a material lease breach may apply) and let the court decide. Your lease's residential-use clause should also bar illegal use. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Tenant Insurance and Your Repair Duties
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute says whether you may require renters insurance or require a tenant to make a claim on it. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. You may require renters insurance in the lease. Don't use it to shift your own duties: in municipalities without their own housing code, the minimum standards statute makes it unlawful for a landlord to keep rented premises in the conditions it lists (such as defective plumbing, leaking roofs or walls, inadequate heat or hot water, or unsafe wiring), and a tenant who gave notice can defend a nonpayment eviction if you didn't fix a substantial health-and-safety violation the tenant didn't cause. So don't make a tenant's insurance claim a condition of repairs you owe, and don't delay those repairs while a claim is pending. No lease may waive a tenant's rights under the eviction statute.

title: Tenant Duties Set by Law
bodyText: New Hampshire puts these duties on tenants whether or not the lease repeats them. A tenant must allow you access at a reasonable time, after notice adequate under the circumstances, to complete necessary repairs and for other reasonable and lawful functions of owning rental property; must allow access for emergency repairs; must allow a bed bug evaluation on 48 hours' written notice when bed bugs are reported in an adjacent unit or a unit directly above or below; and must follow reasonable written instructions, given to an adult in the household at least 72 hours ahead, to prepare for pest remediation. A tenant's refusal to let you inspect for lead hazards, after at least 48 hours' written notice for an inspection at a reasonable time, is good cause for eviction. Tenants and their households and guests must not willfully damage your property, interfere with other tenants' quiet enjoyment or endanger others' health or safety, and a tenant or guest who disables a smoke detector commits a crime. Only tenants, authorized subtenants and implied tenants may occupy without your permission. For tenancies entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2027, unless the lease says otherwise, tenants clear snow and ice from walkways, stairs and entryways meant for their exclusive use. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Submetering Rules; No Utility Shutoffs
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute regulating how a landlord submeters or rebills electricity to residential tenants; the only submetering rule found covers campgrounds. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Whatever the billing arrangement, you may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption or termination of any utility service supplied to the tenant, including water, heat, light, electricity, gas, telephone, sewer, elevator or refrigeration, whether or not you control the service, except for temporary interruptions needed while repairs are actually under way or during temporary emergencies. So you can't cut off a submetered unit's power for nonpayment; collect through the lease and, if needed, the eviction process. A tenant can petition the court over a shutoff and recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, two to three times that if willful, plus attorney's fees. If you resell utility service to tenants, ask the Public Utilities Commission whether its rules apply; utility regulation is not covered here.

title: Smoke and Carbon Monoxide Alarm Duties
bodyText: Every rental unit and multi-unit dwelling in New Hampshire must have automatic fire warning devices (smoke alarms) installed as the national fire codes the statute adopts require (NFPA 101 and NFPA 72), and carbon monoxide detection devices as NFPA 720 requires. A carbon monoxide device isn't required if the unit has no attached garage and no appliance or device that burns solid, liquid or gas fuel, but it becomes required if either is added. As the owner, you are responsible for maintaining the devices in suitable condition; the statute puts no maintenance duty on the tenant. A tenant or a tenant's guest who destroys, disconnects or otherwise disables a smoke detector in a rental dwelling, or tries to, is guilty of a misdemeanor. The state fire marshal, or the local authority the marshal appoints, enforces these rules and serves written notices of violation with a deadline to fix them, and local fire officials may be authorized to issue citations. Cities and towns may impose stricter requirements. Placement and device type follow the adopted codes, which this library does not reproduce. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Substitute Housing
bodyText: New Hampshire does not make you house a tenant elsewhere during ordinary repairs or after a fire. The exception is lead. If a lead exposure hazard you didn't suspect is found in a unit rented to a family with a child, you may temporarily relocate the family during lead hazard reduction, but only to an available replacement dwelling that is safe, sanitary and free of interior lead exposure hazards (free of any lead exposure hazard if a child's blood lead level exceeds 30 micrograms per deciliter), preferably in the same elementary school district. The tenant pays no more rent than for the original unit (you pay any difference), you pay the reasonable and actual moving costs both ways (capped at the deposit plus prepaid rent), and you must agree in writing that the family may move back as soon as the hazard is reduced. A family's refusal of a relocation that meets these terms is a ground for eviction; a tenant with a written lease who is forced to relocate may instead end the lease within 7 days. If the work will take more than 30 days under a written order from the commissioner, eviction is allowed only on further conditions, including a comparable replacement unit at comparable rent, return of the full deposit and prepaid rent before the family moves, and a written right to reoccupy. Separately, if a health officer, building official or fire chief orders a building vacated as an imminent danger, the occupants may return once the danger is removed. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Appliances You Do Not Supply
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule presuming that an appliance left in a unit is yours, and no list of appliances you must supply or may not exclude. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Say clearly in the lease which appliances you supply and which you don't. Where the municipality has no housing code of its own, the state minimum standards make it unlawful for a landlord to keep rented premises with gas line leaks or with leaks or defective pilot lights in any appliance the landlord furnishes, with water-heating equipment that isn't properly operating, or without properly installed and safely maintained heating facilities able to heat the habitable rooms to an average of 65 degrees F. Heat and hot water equipment are therefore yours to keep working even if the lease is silent, and any appliance you list as included is one you furnish. A tenant's own appliance, such as a washer the tenant brings, is the tenant's responsibility. Local housing codes may add requirements.

title: Unfit or Vacated Units
bodyText: If your city or town has adopted a housing code under the state enabling law, its housing officer or board can, after a complaint, a hearing and written findings, find a dwelling unfit for human habitation and order you to repair it or to vacate and close it (or, if repair isn't reasonable, to remove or demolish it), and the municipality can enforce the order in superior court and put its costs and any fines as a lien on the property. Separately, a health officer, building official or fire chief may order a building vacated immediately when its condition is a clear and imminent danger to life or health, post the building, mail you notice, and file the order in district court, where you or an affected tenant can ask for a hearing, which must be held within 7 days after the request; tenants may return once the danger is removed. New Hampshire has no statute that by itself stops rent from accruing while a unit is condemned or under a vacate order, and the vacate statute says such a proceeding doesn't affect the legal rights between landlord and tenant; whether rent is owed for a period the tenant can't lawfully occupy the unit is a question for case law, not covered here. A tenant can also defend a nonpayment eviction if the unit has a substantial health-and-safety violation the tenant reported and you didn't fix within 14 days. Don't collect rent for a period the unit is ordered vacated without legal advice. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Habitability Rules New Hampshire Lacks
bodyText: Several habitability rules found in other states have no New Hampshire counterpart. (1) No general repair statute: the state minimum standards (no infestations without an eradication program, sound plumbing, wiring, roofs, walls, floors, porches and stairs, water and hot water, no gas leaks, adequate heat) apply only in municipalities that haven't adopted their own housing code; elsewhere the local code governs. (2) No repair-and-deduct remedy and no general right to withhold rent outside court (one narrow exception: a tenant made to pay a penalty under the local fire-hazard regulations that the owner should have paid may deduct it, with costs, from rent): a tenant's protection is a defense to a nonpayment eviction if the tenant, while not behind on rent, gave notice of a substantial health-and-safety violation and you didn't fix it within 14 days (or as fast as an emergency requires), with rent paid into court while you repair. (3) No air-conditioning or cooling duty. (4) No statutory list of imminently dangerous conditions; local officials decide case by case whether to order a building vacated. (5) No general repair deadline, except that you must investigate a reported insect or rodent infestation within 7 days and take reasonable measures to remediate it. (6) No duty to provide substitute housing except during lead hazard work. (7) The mere presence of lead-based paint doesn't by itself breach any warranty of habitability, though owners of pre-1978 rentals must take reasonable care to prevent lead exposure. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Local codes may add requirements.

title: No Designated-Repairer Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease naming who must do repairs, and no statute giving tenants a right to make repairs themselves and deduct the cost from rent, so there is no statutory remedy for a contractor clause to limit. You may require that repair requests go to you and that only your chosen contractors work on the property. What you cannot do by lease is narrow the tenant's statutory routes: a tenant may defend a nonpayment eviction by showing that you failed to fix a serious code violation within 14 days of written notice, and may petition the district court over prohibited landlord conduct. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Disability Accommodations and Modifications
bodyText: New Hampshire's fair housing law makes it a civil rights violation to refuse reasonable accommodations in your rules, policies, practices or services when a person with a disability needs them for an equal opportunity to use and enjoy the home, or to refuse to let the tenant make reasonable modifications, at the tenant's own expense, that the tenant needs for full enjoyment of the premises.
