Where reasonable, you may make permission for a modification conditional on the tenant agreeing to restore the interior to its prior condition, reasonable wear and tear excepted, and you may ask for a reasonable description of the work and reasonable assurances that it will be done in a workmanlike manner with any required permits. You may not raise your usual security deposit for a tenant with a disability. If needed to be reasonably sure restoration money will be there, a restoration agreement may require the tenant to pay a reasonable amount, not more than the restoration cost, into an interest-bearing escrow account over a reasonable period, with the interest belonging to the tenant; because New Hampshire treats money a tenant pays you beyond the monthly rent as a security deposit subject to a cap, get advice before collecting such an escrow on top of a full deposit. No statute requires the restoration condition to appear in the lease. The state's small-landlord exemptions (an owner-occupied building of four or fewer families; rooms in the owner's home) are written for the general real estate discrimination section, not the disability section, so do not rely on them for accommodation or modification requests; federal law has its own rules. You need not rent to someone whose tenancy would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or cause substantial physical damage to others' property.

title: Renting the Same Unit Twice
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on renting the same unit or room to two tenants for the same period, and none setting a remedy when you cannot deliver possession on the start date. If it happens, the tenant who cannot move in has ordinary contract claims against you. The library's possession-delay clause sets what happens if the unit isn't ready. If a prior occupant stays on, you recover possession through the eviction process; you may not lock anyone out. Avoid signing a new lease until the current tenant has actually moved out or a firm move-out date is in writing. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Emergency Number Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule requiring you to give tenants an emergency repair number or an on-call contact. A related filing duty applies to restricted property, meaning any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property (nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure): within 30 days of becoming the owner, you must file with the town or city clerk the name, address and telephone number of a person in New Hampshire authorized to accept service of legal papers for you, and the town may fine you up to $100 for not filing. That filing is not a notice to tenants. Give tenants a number that works around the clock anyway: you may enter without consent only for emergency repairs, and if a tenant who is not behind on rent reports a serious code violation and you don't fix it within 14 days (or, in an emergency, as promptly as conditions require), the tenant can use it as a defense to a nonpayment eviction. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Employee Screening Law
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to run background checks on apartment staff, managers or maintenance workers who have access to tenants' units. Screening staff is still sensible, since your employees may enter a unit only with the tenant's consent, for emergency repairs or under a court order. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law, local ordinances and federal program rules were not.

title: Which Fire Code Applies
bodyText: New Hampshire's state fire code is the National Fire Protection Association's Life Safety Code (NFPA 101) and Fire Code (NFPA 1), both 2024 editions, as amended by the state board of fire control and ratified by the legislature; other national standards those codes refer to are included. Buildings must also meet the state building code (the 2024 International Building, Existing Building, Residential, Plumbing and Mechanical Codes, the 2018 Energy Conservation Code and the 2023 National Electrical Code, as amended). Where the two codes conflict, the one giving the greater life safety controls. Your local fire chief enforces the fire code, and towns may adopt local amendments only after state fire marshal review and only if they are not less restrictive. Every rental unit must have smoke alarms and, where there is an attached garage or a fuel-burning appliance, carbon monoxide alarms, and you as owner must keep them working. The fire code may not require sprinklers in detached one- or two-family homes used only as residences. Ask your local fire chief and building official which amendments apply to your building.

title: Codes Fixed to a Named Edition
bodyText: Some New Hampshire safety rules point to an outside standard at a specific edition, so a newer national edition does not apply until the legislature adopts it. The state fire code is the 2024 editions of NFPA 101 and NFPA 1, and the state building code is the 2024 International Building, Existing Building, Residential, Plumbing and Mechanical Codes, the 2018 Energy Conservation Code and the 2023 National Electrical Code, each as amended in New Hampshire. Construction work stays under the building code in effect when the permit application was received. Other rules name a standard without an edition: smoke and carbon monoxide alarms in rental units must follow NFPA 101, NFPA 72 and NFPA 720, and accessible design for covered multifamily buildings first occupied after March 13, 1991 can be shown by meeting ANSI A117.1. When in doubt about which edition applies to your building, ask the local building official or fire chief.

title: No Furnished Rental Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire has no special rules for furnished rentals and no higher deposit for a furnished unit. If the deposit statute covers you, any furniture or damage deposit is part of the security deposit, because it counts all money beyond the monthly rent that the tenant pays you for any purpose, and the total may not exceed one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. You may deduct for damage to your furniture beyond reasonable wear and tear, with a written itemized list and evidence of the repair or replacement cost, within 30 days after the tenancy ends. List the furniture and its condition in the lease or a signed inventory. Rooms in hotels, inns and other places rented for vacation use are outside New Hampshire's eviction chapter. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Disaster Rules for Tenancies
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute that ends a tenancy, or stops rent, when a declared disaster, fire, flood or storm makes a unit unusable. The lease decides, so use the library's fire and casualty clause. Statutory limits still apply after a disaster: you may interrupt utilities only temporarily while repairs are under way or during a temporary emergency; you may enter without the tenant's consent only to make emergency repairs; and you may not lock a tenant out or hold the tenant's belongings except through the courts. To end a tenancy of restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), you need a statutory ground, such as other good cause, which includes a legitimate business or economic reason, with 30 days' written notice. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; emergency orders, case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Only Serious Defects Count
bodyText: New Hampshire's habitability defense to a nonpayment eviction reaches only a substantial violation of the state minimum housing standards or of a local housing code that materially affects whether the unit is fit to live in. Cosmetic problems and minor malfunctions do not qualify. Even for a serious violation, the tenant must prove by clear and convincing evidence that, while not behind on rent, the tenant gave notice to the person who collects the rent, and the defense also requires that you did not fix it within 14 days of written notice, or as promptly as an emergency required; that the tenant's household or guests did not cause it; and that bad weather or the tenant's refusal of access did not prevent the repair. In older rentals, the mere presence of lead paint or another lead-based substance does not by itself breach any warranty of habitability, though lead hazards are regulated separately. Fix reported problems promptly in any case: smaller defects can still breach the lease or a local code.

title: What a Lease Can Shift
bodyText: New Hampshire's minimum housing standards are written as conditions you may not let a rental fall into, and the statute allows only one of them to be shifted by agreement: garbage or rubbish building up in common areas is not your violation if the tenant agreed in the rental agreement to be responsible for removal and you removed all garbage at the start of the tenancy. For tenancies entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2027, you and the tenant may also agree who clears snow and ice from which areas; without an agreement, the landlord of restricted property clears common areas and tenants clear areas only they use. Restricted property means any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). Nothing else in the standards (heat, water, plumbing, wiring, leaks, structure, pests) can be signed away, and a lease cannot waive the tenant's rights under the eviction chapter, including the defense based on serious code violations. You may still ask a tenant to do routine chores, and you must keep smoke and carbon monoxide alarms working yourself.

title: No Habitability Presumptions
bodyText: New Hampshire law does not presume that you breached your repair duties, or that you had notice of a problem, because a unit violates a code. A tenant raising the code-violation defense to a nonpayment eviction must prove by clear and convincing evidence that notice was given while the tenant was not behind on rent. Other presumptions can work against you, though: an eviction, rent increase or substantial change in terms within six months after a tenant's good-faith complaint to you or a code agency, a tenant lawsuit over prohibited practices, or tenant organizing is presumed retaliatory; and an eviction started within six months after you learn a child in the unit has an elevated blood lead level is presumed to be based on it. A presumption can also help you: a tenant is presumed responsible for a bed bug infestation if no bed bugs were reported in the unit or the adjacent units in the six months before and during the tenancy. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: No Required Habitability Statement
bodyText: New Hampshire does not require your lease to say that the unit is or will be fit to live in. Your duties apply whether or not the lease mentions them: the state minimum housing standards (in towns without their own housing code) or the local housing code, and the eviction statute's defense for serious code violations you fail to fix after notice. The library's landlord maintenance clause states your repair duty in general terms. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Habitability Can't Be Waived
bodyText: A New Hampshire lease cannot take away a tenant's rights under the state eviction chapter, and any such term is void. That includes the tenant's defense to a nonpayment eviction when you fail to fix a serious code violation after notice, and the retaliation defense. The state minimum housing standards (heat, water, hot water, plumbing, wiring, leaks, plaster, holes, porches and stairs, gas leaks, pests and common-area garbage) are written as conditions you may not let the rental fall into; the only one the statute lets the tenant take on by agreement is removing common-area garbage, and only if you removed all garbage when the tenancy began. From July 1, 2027, the lease may also allocate snow and ice removal for tenancies entered into or renewed on or after that date. The prohibited-practices rules (no utility shutoffs, lockouts or entry without consent except for emergency repairs) are flat prohibitions with court remedies, and no statute lets a lease set them aside. A lease may still assign ordinary upkeep and tenant-caused damage to the tenant.

title: Local Health Officers and Housing Codes
bodyText: New Hampshire has no health districts with their own rental regulations, and no rule that you give tenants a copy of health or housing regulations on request. Rental housing standards are local: each town's health officer is trained on, and may enforce, rental housing standards and health nuisances, and may get a court inspection warrant if entry is refused. A city or town may adopt its own housing code; where it hasn't, the state minimum standards apply. Tenants may complain to the health officer or code agency, and an eviction or rent increase within six months after a good-faith complaint is presumed retaliatory. Find out which code applies in each town where you rent. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; local ordinances and case law were not.

title: Heat Requirements
bodyText: In a New Hampshire town that has not adopted its own housing code, the rental must have heating facilities that are properly installed, safely maintained, in good working condition and capable of heating all habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms to an average of at least 65°F. If you supply the heat as part of the rent, you must actually keep those rooms at an average of at least 65°F. Where a town has its own housing code, that code's heat standard applies instead. No statute requires a special written agreement before the tenant pays for heat, but the lease should say clearly who pays for fuel or the heating utility; the heating equipment duty stays with you either way. You may never willfully cause heat or another utility to be interrupted, whether or not you control the account, except temporarily during repairs or emergencies. If you agreed to pay a utility and the tenant pays it to keep service on, you may not evict for nonpayment of rent up to the amount the tenant paid, if the tenant has proof.

title: Tenant Remedies Against You
bodyText: A New Hampshire tenant has several statutory remedies if you breach your duties. The tenant may petition the district court, without a filing fee, over prohibited practices such as utility shutoffs, lockouts, holding the tenant's belongings or entering without consent; the court holds a hearing within about 30 days, may issue orders (temporary ones right away if harm is immediate) and may award damages for those violations, for breach of the warranty of habitability, for breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment and for related claims. For a willful utility shutoff, lockout, unlawful entry or similar violation, the tenant recovers actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, doubled or tripled if the violation was willful or knowing, plus costs and attorney's fees; if you lock out a tenant and re-rent the unit, damages are at least $3,000; and each day a violation continues after a temporary order is a separate violation. After a tenant proves a prohibited-practice violation, you may not bring an eviction for six months except for nonpayment, a substantial lease violation or the tenant's own violation. In a nonpayment eviction, the tenant may defend on serious code violations you failed to fix after notice, may counterclaim (money judgments in the eviction case are capped at $1,500), and if the eviction was retaliatory may recover up to three months' rent.

title: Minimum Housing Standards
bodyText: In a New Hampshire city or town that has not adopted its own housing code, you may not let a rental be in any of these conditions: insect or rodent infestation (including bed bugs) without a periodic inspection and treatment program; defective plumbing or sewage backup from a faulty septic or sewer system; exposed wires or other electrical shock or fire hazards; consistent roof or wall leaks; falling plaster; substantial holes in floors, walls or ceilings; unsound porches, stairs or railings; garbage piling up in common areas because you didn't remove it or provide enough receptacles (unless the tenant agreed to handle removal and you cleared all garbage at the start); inadequate water or broken water-heating equipment; gas leaks or defective pilot lights in appliances you supply; or inadequate heat. Each day a violation continues after notice is a separate offense. Where a town has its own housing code, its agency may order you to repair, vacate and close, or demolish an unfit dwelling, enforce the order in superior court, and place a lien on the property for its costs and for unpaid code fines. A tenant may also defend a nonpayment eviction if you fail to fix a serious violation within 14 days after written notice.

title: No Statutory Right to Fix and Bill as Rent
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute letting you fix a tenant's lease violation yourself and add the cost to the rent. The one statutory exception is bed bugs: if you allege the tenant caused an infestation, you may bill the tenant in writing for the reasonable cost of remediating the tenant's own unit, and if the tenant neither pays nor enters a repayment agreement within 30 days after remediation is finished, that failure is grounds for eviction for nonpayment of rent; in that case you must prove the tenant was responsible and that you offered a reasonable repayment agreement. For other tenant-caused damage, you may recover your costs as damages or from the security deposit with an itemized list, and the lease may say the tenant pays for damage the tenant causes. To make the repair you still need the tenant's consent to enter, unless it is an emergency repair or you have a court order. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Shifting Chores to the Tenant
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule requiring a separate signed writing to give a tenant maintenance chores, and the lease itself may assign routine upkeep such as lawn care. Two duties tied to the state standards can be shifted only as the statutes allow. Removing garbage from common areas becomes the tenant's job only if the rental agreement says so and you removed all garbage when the tenancy began (the library's optional "Garbage Removal from Common Areas" clause does this). For tenancies entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2027, you and the tenant may agree who clears snow and ice from which areas; without an agreement, the landlord of restricted property clears shared areas and each tenant clears areas only that tenant uses. Restricted property means any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). You remain responsible for keeping smoke and carbon monoxide alarms working and for the other minimum housing standards, whatever the lease says.

title: Facilities You Must Supply
bodyText: Beyond keeping the unit in repair, New Hampshire law requires certain facilities. In towns without their own housing code: heating facilities able to keep habitable rooms, bathrooms and toilet rooms at an average of at least 65°F; an adequate water supply and properly working water-heating equipment; enough garbage receptacles for common areas; and no gas leaks or defective pilot lights in appliances you supply. Everywhere: smoke alarms, and carbon monoxide alarms where there is an attached garage or a fuel-burning appliance, which you as owner must keep working. If a child in the unit tests above the state blood lead standard and the state finds lead in the drinking water above the federal action level, you must notify the tenant or prospective tenant and install and maintain a certified lead-reducing filter on the kitchen faucet until the source is removed and testing confirms the water is below that level. State statutes do not require a stove or refrigerator; if you supply appliances, list them in the lease. Local housing codes may require more.

title: Promises to Repair
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule requiring you to put a promise to clean, repair or improve a unit in writing, with a completion date, before the lease is signed. Put it in writing anyway: the lease's entire-agreement clause can make an unwritten promise hard to enforce for either side, and a written promise with a date avoids disputes. Don't overstate a unit's condition or features. The state consumer protection law, whose definition of trade and commerce includes the advertising, offering for sale, sale or distribution of real property and services (how far it reaches a residential rental is a question for case law, not covered here), bars unfair or deceptive acts, a general ban that its examples (such as representing that goods or services have characteristics or benefits they do not have) don't limit, and a person harmed can recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, more if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Quiet Enjoyment
bodyText: New Hampshire law forbids you to willfully violate a tenant's right to quiet enjoyment of the tenancy or to try to get around the court eviction process. A tenant can petition the district court over a violation and recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, doubled or tripled for a willful or knowing violation, plus costs and attorney's fees, and the court may also award damages for breach of the covenant of quiet enjoyment. The duty runs both ways: since October 8, 2026, tenants, their household members, guests and other occupants may not willfully damage your property, willfully deny other tenants their quiet enjoyment, willfully behave in ways that unreasonably and adversely affect the health or safety of other tenants, you or your agent, or willfully prevent emergency repairs, and the court may order a person found to have endangered others to leave the premises immediately.

title: No Rent-Demand Bar
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute that bars you outright from demanding or collecting rent while a unit has code violations, and no rule suspending rent under a code repair order. The protection works through eviction cases instead: a tenant may defend a nonpayment eviction by proving a serious code violation you failed to fix within 14 days of written notice. The court may then continue the case for up to a month for you to fix it while the tenant pays the withheld and ongoing rent into court. If you fix it in time, the case is dismissed and the court either gives you the rent or pays you only the fair rental value of the unit in its defective condition and gives the rest to the tenant as damages; if you don't, the tenant wins and gets the money back. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Habitability Follows the Landlord
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute saying a lease, assignment, deed or mortgage cannot let someone collect rent free of the duty to keep the unit fit. The state minimum standards reach the same result another way: they bind any landlord, defined as an owner, lessor or agent who rents residential premises, so whoever rents the unit out carries the duties. When you sell, your buyer takes your eviction rights, and you must hand the security deposit (with any interest) to the buyer, assignee, receiver or foreclosure purchaser within five days and tell the tenant by registered or certified mail who now holds it. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Code Inspections
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide rental inspection or licensing program, but several officials may inspect rentals. A town that has adopted a housing code may let its agency enter premises to examine them, with the least possible inconvenience to the occupants, and get an administrative inspection warrant from a court if entry is refused; local building officials, fire officials (for buildings other than single-family homes and two-unit dwellings), health officers and the state's lead inspectors (in rented dwellings during business hours or at a time agreed with you) have similar powers. No statute lets a lease clause give an inspector the right to enter an occupied unit, and your own entry needs the tenant's prior consent except for emergency repairs or under a court order. Ask the tenant to agree to a scheduled inspection, or let the inspector use the warrant process. A tenant's refusal to let you inspect for lead hazards, after at least 48 hours' written notice and at a reasonable time, is good cause for eviction. Your city or town may have its own inspection ordinance.

title: No Repair-Cost Termination
bodyText: New Hampshire gives you no right to end a lease because a needed repair would cost too much, and your repair duties continue for the whole tenancy. To end a tenancy of restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), you need a statutory ground and 30 days' written notice stating it. Other good cause includes any legitimate business or economic reason, and a separate ground covers abating a lead exposure hazard by methods other than interim controls or encapsulation, by any method expected to take more than 30 days, or by taking the unit off the rental market. When a lease of 12 months or longer (or a shorter lease renewed to 12 months or longer) reaches the end of its term, you may also decline to renew if you give written notice at least 60 days before the term ends and file any eviction case within 6 months after the lease expires. For nonrestricted property you may end a tenancy for any reason with 30 days' written notice. Whether these grounds can end a fixed-term lease before its term runs out isn't settled by the statute, and court decisions weren't searched, so the cautious course is not to end a fixed term early on these grounds unless the lease allows it; the library's fire and casualty clause covers damage. Separately, a town's housing agency may order an unfit dwelling vacated and closed, or demolished where repair would cost too much compared with its value and the owner's ability to pay. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: No Small-Landlord Remedy Exemption
bodyText: New Hampshire has no notice or other procedure that lets a landlord with only a few units opt out of tenants' repair remedies. The code-violation defense to a nonpayment eviction applies to any residential rental other than vacation or recreational property, and the prohibited-practices rules and court petitions apply to every landlord. Size matters elsewhere: owners of nonrestricted property (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure) may end a tenancy without a listed reason; the deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older; and parts of the state fair housing law exempt owner-occupied buildings of four or fewer units. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Repair Requests and Notice
bodyText: New Hampshire ties several tenant protections to notice of a problem. For the code-violation defense to a nonpayment eviction, the tenant must prove, by clear and convincing evidence, that while not behind on rent the tenant gave notice to the person to whom rent is normally paid, and your 14 days to fix it (or prompt action in an emergency) run from your receipt of written notice. An eviction, rent increase or substantial change in terms within six months after you receive notice of a tenant's code complaint, by mail, in hand or left at your home, or from a code agency, is presumed retaliatory. You must investigate a tenant's or code authority's report of insects, bed bugs or rodents within 7 days and take reasonable steps to remediate. A lease may ask for repair requests in writing, which helps both sides prove notice, but it cannot cut back these statutory rights, and some of them (such as the infestation duty and agency reports) start from notice however it arrives. Keep a record of every request and when you received it.

title: No Lock or Security Device Law
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide rule requiring deadbolts, door viewers, window latches or other security devices, or requiring you to rekey between tenants. The one lock rule: if a tenant has a court protective order granting possession of the dwelling to the exclusion of another tenant or household member, and gives you a copy, you must replace the lock or set it to a new key at the tenant's expense on request and must not give a key to the person restrained; you are not liable for damages resulting directly from that lock change. Rekeying at turnover is still good practice, and building, fire or local housing codes may require particular hardware. Never change locks to keep a tenant out; lockouts are prohibited. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; local ordinances and case law were not.

title: No State Stove or Refrigerator Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire statutes do not require you to supply a stove or refrigerator. If you supply gas appliances, the state minimum standards (in towns without their own housing code) bar gas leaks and defective pilot lights in them, and you may not willfully cut off refrigeration or other services you supply except temporarily during repairs or emergencies. List the appliances you provide in the lease and say who repairs them. Your town's housing code may require cooking facilities, so check local rules. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; local ordinances and case law were not.

title: Code Repair Orders and Liens
bodyText: New Hampshire has no court receivership that takes over the rents of an ordinary substandard rental. Enforcement runs through local code orders. In a town with a housing code, the code agency may, after a complaint (including a petition by 10 residents) and a hearing, order you to repair the dwelling or vacate and close it, or to demolish it where repair would cost too much compared with its value and your ability to pay. If you don't comply, the agency may go to superior court, which may direct the agency itself to do the repair or demolition; the cost becomes a lien on the property, and code fines a court imposes also become a lien that may be foreclosed if unpaid. Fire officials may order hazardous conditions in buildings other than single-family homes and two-unit dwellings removed or remedied, with a copy served on the tenants. Tenants of a closed or condemned building must still be removed through lawful process. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; local ordinances and case law were not.

title: Cable and Internet Access
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on cable, satellite or internet provider access to ordinary apartment buildings or rental houses, and none barring different rent for cable subscribers. The state's cable access rules apply only to manufactured housing parks, which this library does not cover, and the shared tenant services rules bind phone service providers, not landlords. You may not willfully cause a tenant's telephone or other utility service to be interrupted, even if you don't control the account, except temporarily during repairs or emergencies. Federal rules on tenants' satellite dishes and antennas may also apply; this library has not reviewed them. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; federal law, local ordinances and case law were not.

title: Tenant Repairs by Agreement
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute setting how you and a tenant agree that the tenant will make repairs, so no separate signed writing or special form is required and the lease itself may assign routine upkeep. The agreement cannot move the state minimum housing standards off you, except that the tenant may take on common-area garbage removal in the rental agreement if you cleared all garbage at the start, and, for tenancies entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2027, the lease may allocate snow and ice removal. A lease also cannot waive the tenant's rights under the eviction chapter, including the defense for serious code violations you fail to fix. If a tenant agrees to do a specific repair in exchange for reduced rent, put the task, standard and rent terms in writing, and remember you still need the tenant's consent to enter to check the work. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; local codes and case law were not.

title: Tenant Remedies for Unmade Repairs
bodyText: New Hampshire tenants have no statutory right to make repairs and deduct the cost from rent, and no statutory rent escrow for ordinary rentals. Their repair remedies are these. In a nonpayment eviction, a tenant may defend by proving a serious code violation you failed to fix within 14 days of written notice; the court may give you up to a month to fix it while rent is paid into court, then either dismiss the case and apportion the rent (paying you only the fair rental value of the defective unit and giving the rest to the tenant as damages) or rule for the tenant. A tenant may petition the district court, without a filing fee, for orders and damages, including damages for breach of the warranty of habitability. A tenant may complain to the town's code or health officer, and an eviction, rent increase or substantial change in terms within six months afterwards is presumed retaliatory. You must investigate a reported infestation within 7 days and take reasonable steps to remediate it. A lease cannot waive the eviction-chapter defenses.

title: Splitting Shared Utility Bills
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on dividing a shared (master-metered) utility bill among tenants by formula, and none voiding a lease term that makes a tenant pay for utilities not separately metered to the unit. Electricity is the exception that matters: under the state utility rules, a building may be served through one master electric meter only where the utility's tariff bars the customer (you) from selling or otherwise passing that electricity on to others except by including it in a fixed rent. So for master-metered electricity, build the cost into the rent rather than billing tenants by usage or by a ratio. Separate meters are required in many new buildings by the state building code. For water, sewer or gas on a shared meter, no state rule was found; say clearly in the lease how any charge is figured, and get advice before billing usage-based charges. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; utility tariffs, local ordinances and case law were not.

title: Getting Notice of a Tenant's Shutoff
bodyText: If your tenant holds the electric or gas account, you can ask the utility to tell you before it shuts off the tenant's service. New Hampshire law lets an electric or gas utility notify the property owner before terminating a tenant's residential service between November 1 and April 30, if the owner (or the owner's agent) has asked to be notified. The statute doesn't require a particular form or the tenant's consent; contact each utility to make the request. The notice is optional for the utility and covers only that winter window. Knowing early helps you protect pipes and the building in cold weather; you still may not enter without the tenant's consent except for emergency repairs.

title: Utilities in Your Name
bodyText: If a utility serving your tenants is in your name and you fall behind, New Hampshire protects the tenants. A utility (other than a sewer utility) may not disconnect service that benefits known residential tenants without first giving them written notice at least 10 calendar days ahead, saying the shutoff results from a dispute with the landlord. If the meter serves only one tenant, that tenant may put the service in the tenant's own name without paying any of your past-due balance. A municipal water company must give tenants at least 7 days' notice and must keep serving a tenant who asks and agrees to pay going forward; it may still list your past-due balance on the tenant's bill and keep its lien on your property. If you agreed to provide a utility and the tenant pays it to keep service on, you may not evict for nonpayment of rent so long as the rent owed doesn't exceed what the tenant paid and the tenant has proof. You may never willfully cause a utility to be cut off. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and utility rules were searched; utility tariffs and case law were not.

title: Utility Shutoff Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire limits when electric and gas utilities may shut off residential service. The utility needs good cause (an unpaid past-due bill after demand or a tariff violation) and must give the customer at least 10 days' written notice, and the customer may ask for a conference with the utility and then with the state Department of Energy, with service continuing meanwhile. Shutoff notices for a primary residence can't be sent until the arrears pass set amounts. In the winter period, November 15 through March 31, the utility must also contact an adult at the home in person or by phone 2 to 8 business days before disconnecting, needs the department's approval if it can't reach anyone or the customer is known to be 65 or older, and won't get approval where the household has a financial hardship and has made good-faith payments. These rules don't add 30 days to the notice. As a landlord you may never willfully cause a tenant's utility to be interrupted, and if the account is in your name, tenants get their own notice and the right to take over service.

title: Submetering and Utility Billing
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring a special lease disclosure when you bill tenants for utilities through submeters or a formula, and none capping such charges or their late fees. Electricity is restricted: where a building is served by one master electric meter, the utility's tariff must bar you from passing the electricity on to tenants except by including it in a fixed rent, so usage-based electric submeter billing is not available. For water or other shared services, state in the lease exactly what is billed, how it is measured or divided, and when it is due, and charge only what the lease allows. Before the tenant signs, you must disclose in writing if, to your knowledge, a metered utility the tenant will pay is provided under a tariff carrying energy-efficiency or renewable-energy charges. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; utility tariffs, local ordinances and case law were not.

title: When a Tenant Doesn't Transfer Utilities
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule letting you cut off utilities that are still in your name because a tenant failed to transfer them, and the law forbids it: you may not willfully cause, directly or indirectly, the interruption of any utility service being supplied to a tenant, whether or not the service is under your control, except temporarily during repairs or emergencies. A tenant can recover at least $1,000 for a violation, doubled or tripled if willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. Instead, make the lease require the tenant to put specified utilities in the tenant's name by the start date, keep paying any account still in your name, and recover what you paid as a lease charge or through a court claim; a persistent refusal can be a breach of a material lease term. If you close an account in your name, the utility must give the tenants written notice at least 10 days before disconnecting service that benefits them, and a tenant whose meter serves only that tenant may take service in the tenant's own name. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and utility rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Lock Changes for Protective Orders
bodyText: If a tenant has a court protective order granting the tenant possession of the home to the exclusion of one or more other tenants or household members, the tenant may ask you to replace the lock or set it to a new key, at the tenant's expense. Once you get a copy of the order, you must do it, and you must not give new keys to the person the order restrains or excludes. You are not liable for damages that result directly from making that change. Keep the order and the fact that the tenant is a victim confidential; New Hampshire law requires victim verification you receive to be kept in strict confidence, with limited exceptions. The statute speaks to restricted property owners (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), but follow it for every rental, since a court order may also direct you.

title: Entry Disputes and Remedies
bodyText: New Hampshire sets no fixed number of hours' notice for entry. Instead, you may enter only with the tenant's prior consent, except to make emergency repairs (including evaluating or treating an infestation within 72 hours after you first learn of it) or under a court order. In turn, a tenant may not willfully prevent necessary repairs or refuse you access for other reasonable and lawful ownership functions, such as inspections or showings, at a reasonable time after notice that is adequate under the circumstances, and may not refuse access for a bed bug check after 48 hours' written notice when an adjoining unit has bed bugs. If you and a tenant disagree about access, either of you may petition the district court; a good-faith petition asking whether a requested entry is reasonable and lawful does not carry the usual penalty, and the court can order entry. Entering without consent outside those exceptions exposes you to actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, doubled or tripled if willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. A tenant's repair request is not, by statute, consent to enter at any time; confirm the visit. No statute addresses moving a tenant out temporarily for non-emergency work, so do that only by agreement.

title: Scheduled Service Visits
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule letting a lease clause authorize entry without notice for regularly scheduled services such as pest control, filter changes or smoke alarm checks. You may enter only with the tenant's prior consent, except for emergency repairs or under a court order. No statute says whether consent written into the lease in advance is enough, so don't rely on it alone: send notice of each scheduled visit and get the tenant's agreement, or agree on a written recurring schedule the tenant can change. The tenant may not willfully refuse access for reasonable ownership functions at a reasonable time after adequate notice, and may not refuse access for a bed bug check after 48 hours' written notice when an adjoining unit has bed bugs. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Smart Locks
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on smart locks, keypad or app-based entry, or the data those systems collect, in residential rentals. The general rules still apply to them: an electronic entry log or remote unlock does not change the rule that you may enter only with the tenant's prior consent, except for emergency repairs or under a court order, and disabling a tenant's code or credential to keep the tenant out is a prohibited lockout. Give the tenant a non-app way in (such as a key or keypad code) if the tenant asks, and say in the lease who controls codes and what access data you keep. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; federal law, local ordinances and case law were not.

title: Abandonment and Re-Renting
bodyText: New Hampshire lets you treat a unit as abandoned without going to court, if you follow the statute. Abandonment means all tenants have moved out with no intent to return. It is presumed if you give all tenants a written property abandonment notice, left at the unit and sent by certified mail to at least one adult tenant's last known address, stating your reasons and their right to retrieve belongings and to file a court petition, and at least two of these are true: all adult tenants told you in writing they would leave by a date that has passed; all keys were returned or left in the unit; the tenants removed all or most of their belongings and what remains doesn't fit continued use; or rent has gone unpaid for more than 91 days (provided you cooperated with any assistance agency and did not refuse its payments). The statute supplies notice wording that is deemed sufficient. A signed statement from every adult tenant that they have given up possession also works. Even then, you must store any belongings with reasonable care for 7 days, starting the day after you serve the notice, and let the tenant collect them without paying rent or storage fees. New Hampshire's statutes do not say whether you must try to re-rent to reduce what a departed tenant owes, or how long the tenant stays liable for rent; that is case law this library has not reviewed, so make reasonable efforts to re-rent and keep records.

title: Attorney's Fees
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute governs attorney's fee clauses in residential leases: the state's reciprocal-fee statute covers retail installment contracts and consumer loans, not leases. The library's default clause uses mutual prevailing-party wording. Several statutes award fees regardless of the lease. A landlord or tenant who violates the prohibited-practices rules (such as lockouts, utility shutoffs, entry without consent, or a tenant's willful damage) pays the other side's costs and reasonable attorney's fees, though some violations carry narrower remedies. If a tenant's prohibited-practices petition is frivolous or brought only to harass, the tenant pays your costs and fees. In a condominium conversion, a tenant who wins a claim recovers fees, and a frivolous tenant claim makes the tenant liable for yours. In an eviction case, the court's money judgment is capped at $1,500, though either side may sue separately for more. Whether and how a court enforces a lease fee clause is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: Converting to Condominiums
bodyText: If you convert a rental building or complex with more than 10 units to condominiums, a cooperative or similar ownership (including a conversion done in stages of 10 or fewer units), New Hampshire's conversion law applies; it does not apply to individually owned units that were rented, or to hotels, dormitories, transient or seasonal units. The conversion must be registered with the Attorney General, and before converting you must file your notices with the Attorney General at least 10 days before mailing them, then send each tenant by registered mail, return receipt requested, a notice of intent to convert no earlier than 120 days before you apply to register, and later a registration notice. The notice must tell tenants, among other things, that a tenant whose unit will not be substantially altered has an exclusive right to contract to buy it for 60 days after receiving the sale documents; that tenants have at least 270 days from the notice (or until the 60 days end, if later), or longer under an existing lease, before having to move; that elderly (65 or older) or disabled tenants get at least 18 months; and that a tenant may end the tenancy on 30 days' notice without penalty. After notice, you may evict only for listed reasons (such as nonpayment, a material lease violation after written notice and a chance to comply, damage not repaired, repeated disturbance, or the end of the notice period), and rent increases are limited to the unit's share of listed cost increases. Tenants who sign a lease after receiving written notice of the conversion don't get these protections. A tenant cannot waive these rights, and violations cost double actual damages (or at least $1,000 for trying to push tenants out before notice) plus attorney's fees.

title: Criminal Activity
bodyText: For restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), behavior by the tenant or the tenant's family that adversely affects the health or safety of other tenants, you or your representatives is a ground for eviction on 7 days' written notice; other criminal activity can support eviction as a material lease violation or other good cause on 30 days' notice. Since October 8, 2026, tenants, household members, guests and other occupants may not willfully behave in ways that unreasonably and adversely affect others' health or safety, and in a district court petition the court may order the person found responsible to leave immediately and stay away from the unit and common areas. Knowingly keeping a place used for illegal drug use or sales is unlawful, and the state fair housing law does not bar you from acting against a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance. An older statute says a tenant's use of the premises for lewdness, prostitution or illegal liquor sales voids the lease and lets the owner re-enter without legal process, but the prohibited-practices law bars lockouts except through the courts, so use the eviction or petition process rather than self-help. No statute requires you to evict for crime, sets a special fast-track eviction for drug or violent crime, or requires the lease to describe these rights.

title: Eviction Grounds and Cure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no general right for a tenant to cure a lease violation after notice. For restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), you may end a tenancy only for a listed reason: nonpayment after demand; substantial damage; failure to comply with a material lease term; behavior adversely affecting others' health or safety (or refusing temporary relocation for lead abatement); other good cause; certain lead-hazard abatement; willful failure to prepare for pest treatment after reasonable written notice and time; a cotenant who is the accused abuser after a domestic violence lease termination; or the end of a lease of 12 months or more (or a shorter lease renewed for a total of 12 months or more), with 60 days' written non-renewal notice and an eviction filed within 6 months after the lease ends. If other good cause is based on the tenant's, family's or guests' conduct, you must first give a written warning that the conduct, if repeated, will be grounds for eviction, served in hand, at the tenant's home or by certified mail. A tenant's refusal of a rent increase is good cause only after 30 days' written notice of the amount and effective date. Notices run 7 days for nonpayment, substantial damage, health-or-safety behavior and an accused-perpetrator cotenant, and 30 days for the other grounds, and a nonpayment case is dismissed if, before the hearing, the tenant pays all rent due, other lawful charges in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs, which a tenant may do up to three times in 12 months. Nonrestricted property may be ended for any reason with proper notice. Don't promise a cure period in the lease that the statute doesn't require.

title: Drug-Free Housing Addenda
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring, authorizing or limiting a drug-free or crime-free lease addendum, so one is an ordinary lease term. A violation can support eviction of restricted property as failure to comply with a material lease term, or on 7 days' notice where the behavior adversely affects others' health or safety; restricted property means any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). Knowingly keeping a place used for illegal drug use or sales is itself unlawful. Draft the addendum so it does not bar a qualifying therapeutic cannabis patient from using cannabis by ingestion or vaporization, which state law protects even where the lease bans smoking. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules this library has not reviewed. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Domestic Violence Eviction Protection
bodyText: If you own restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), you may not end a tenancy solely because a tenant or household member has been a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, once the victim gives you written verification. The tenant may raise this as a defense to an eviction for damage, a lease violation, health or safety behavior, or other good cause. You may still evict for nonpayment of rent, or on any listed ground unrelated to the abuse. If the court finds grounds to evict the accused person, it may enter judgment against that person alone and let the rest of the household stay; once that judgment is final you may bar the person from your property, and a return after written notice is trespass. Keep the verification, and the fact that someone is a victim, strictly confidential, sharing it only with the victim's written consent, where reasonably necessary in an eviction or housing-assistance hearing, or as the law requires.

title: Ending a Lease for Domestic Violence
bodyText: A New Hampshire tenant may end a lease or rental agreement if the tenant or a household member living at the unit has been a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the most recent 150 days, or if within that time an event related to past abuse causes the victim to fear for their safety, and the tenant gives you written verification (a protective order, a filed protective-order case, a police report, a statement from a police officer, victim's advocate, attorney or health care provider, or the court's signed self-certification form). The tenant must move out within 30 days after giving notice, or at another time you agree on, and owes rent only through the termination date or the date the tenant actually leaves, whichever is later. The security deposit stays in place until all tenants have moved out and is then returned under the deposit statute. The statute does not end the lease for remaining tenants. If a remaining cotenant or occupant is the accused perpetrator, you may evict that person on 7 days' notice. Keep the verification strictly confidential.

title: Domestic Violence Verification
bodyText: For New Hampshire's domestic violence eviction protection and lease-termination right, the victim may give you any one of these as written verification: proof of a valid protective order against the perpetrator; written verification that the victim has started a court case for a protective order; written verification that the abuse was reported to a law enforcement agency; written verification from a law enforcement official, victim's advocate, attorney or health care provider that the person is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking; or a signed self-certification form provided by the circuit court, which includes a sworn statement and a warning that false statements may be prosecuted. You may not demand a particular one of these. Keep whatever you receive strictly confidential, disclosing it only with the victim's written consent, where reasonably necessary in an eviction or housing-assistance hearing, or as the law requires.

title: Eminent Domain
bodyText: If a government takes your rental property by eminent domain, New Hampshire's eminent domain procedure law treats tenants for years (tenants under a lease for a term) as condemnees alongside the owner, so a tenant with a lease may have its own claim in the compensation proceeding. No state statute says the tenant's rent ends or is reduced when the property is taken, or lets the court cancel the lease; the lease decides. Add a clause stating that the lease ends on the date possession is taken, that rent is apportioned to that date, and how any award is divided between you and the tenant. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: No Environmental-Event Termination
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute letting you or a tenant end a lease because of an environmental event such as contamination, a chemical spill or mold. For restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), you may end a tenancy on 30 days' notice to abate a lead hazard by methods other than interim controls or encapsulation or expected to take more than 30 days, or to remove the unit from the rental market (never against a family when the method is interim controls or encapsulation; and where a family with a child is involved or the state has ordered lead hazard reduction, only after meeting the lead statute's conditions, including a comparable lead-safe replacement unit, return of the full deposit and prepaid rent before the family moves, and a written right to return), and a tenant who refuses suitable temporary relocation for lead abatement may be evicted on 7 days' notice (and a tenant with a written lease who is forced to relocate because of a lead hazard may end the lease as of the relocation date by written notice within 7 days of relocating); otherwise you need another listed ground such as other good cause. The lead statute's limits on evicting a family (none when the method is interim controls or encapsulation; the listed conditions after a state lead order or a withdrawal from the market) apply to nonrestricted property too. A health officer may order a building vacated when its condition is a clear and imminent danger, but that order does not itself change your rights against the tenant. If you want an environmental-event exit, write it into the lease. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Court Stays After Eviction Judgment
bodyText: Even after you win an eviction case, a New Hampshire court may delay the move-out if justice requires, judging the reasonableness and good faith of both sides. For cases decided on or after October 8, 2026, the stay may run up to 60 days after the judgment, or up to 75 days if the tenant proves that a longer stay won't cause you financial harm, damage to the premises or ongoing threats to anyone's health or safety, and that the tenant needs more time because of factors such as age, family status, disability or limited English. A tenant in default under the eviction statute (for example, by not appearing) gets no stay. During any stay, the tenant must pay you the former rent weekly in advance; if a weekly payment is missed, the writ of possession issues at once. In a nonpayment case you and the tenant may instead file a payment agreement: the tenant keeps the unit while paying arrears, rent, court costs and service fees on schedule, gives up any appeal, and if a payment is missed you file a sworn notice and the court issues the writ within 5 business days unless the tenant shows timely payment or a specific compelling cause and can pay. The agreement must contain the statute's capitalized warning paragraph.

title: The Eviction Process
bodyText: A New Hampshire eviction runs in the circuit court's district division. First serve a written eviction notice (and, for nonpayment, a demand for rent at or before the same time), stating the reason specifically; it gives 7 days for nonpayment, substantial damage, health or safety behavior or a domestic violence perpetrator, and 30 days otherwise, and a nonpayment notice must tell the tenant of the right to avoid eviction by paying. Anyone may serve it, in hand or by leaving it at the tenant's home; keep a copy and an affidavit of service. The court's forms show the required content. After the notice runs out, enter a landlord and tenant writ with the court, with proof the notice was served, before the sheriff serves it; it is returnable 7 days after service. A tenant who wants to contest must file an appearance by the return day and, for cases on or after October 8, 2026, an answer stating defenses and counterclaims within 5 days after it. The hearing is held within about 10 days after the appearance. You may claim unpaid rent, but the money judgment in the eviction is capped at $1,500 (you may sue separately for more), and the tenant's counterclaims can offset it. If you win, the writ of possession issues after the 7-day period to file a notice of intent to appeal; a tenant who appeals a nonpayment case must pay the weekly rent into court. Common defenses are retaliation, serious unrepaired code violations, payment before the hearing, and rent assistance vouchers you refused. A sheriff carries out the writ; you may never remove the tenant yourself.

title: Eviction Records and Screening
bodyText: New Hampshire has no law sealing, expunging or removing eviction case records, so there is nothing for you to object to. One rule affects screening: ending a tenancy at the end of a lease of 12 months or more under the statute's no-fault ground is not an eviction for purposes of rental applications and tenant screening reports, and the court notes in its records that the termination was no fault of the tenant. Don't treat that kind of case as an eviction when screening applicants, though you may still make other due-diligence inquiries. Information you receive verifying that a tenant is a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking must be kept strictly confidential. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; court administrative orders and case law were not.

title: Who Can Be Served With Eviction Papers
bodyText: New Hampshire does not provide for a lease naming someone to accept eviction papers on the tenant's behalf. The statute fixes service: the demand for rent and the eviction notice may be served by any person, either on the tenant personally or by leaving it at the tenant's last and usual place of abode, and you prove service with a true and attested copy and an affidavit of service (which need not be sworn). The landlord and tenant writ is entered with the court first and then served by the sheriff. A lease clause naming another person would not replace these steps, so serve the tenant directly. Separately, if you own restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), you must file with the town or city clerk the name of an in-state person who may accept legal papers in suits against you. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Faster Removal for Dangerous Conduct
bodyText: New Hampshire has no special criminal-activity eviction track, but two tools move faster than an ordinary case. First, for restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property; nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure), behavior by the tenant or family that adversely affects others' health or safety needs only 7 days' eviction notice. Second, since October 8, 2026, you may petition the district court (no filing fee) when a tenant, household member, guest or occupant willfully behaves in a way that unreasonably and adversely affects the health or safety of other tenants, you or your agent, or willfully prevents emergency repairs. The court holds a hearing within 30 days of filing or 10 days of service, whichever is later; on a showing of an immediate threat of irreparable harm it may issue temporary orders right away, and after the hearing it may order the person responsible to vacate immediately and stay away from the unit and common areas. The order runs only against the person found to have violated the rule. Remember the court process is required; you may not remove anyone yourself.

title: Good Cause to End a Tenancy
bodyText: New Hampshire requires a reason to end most residential tenancies. If you own restricted property, meaning any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property, you may end a tenancy only on a listed ground: nonpayment after demand; substantial damage; failure to comply with a material lease term; behavior adversely affecting others' health or safety; other good cause, which includes any legitimate business or economic reason; certain lead-hazard abatement; willful failure to prepare for pest treatment; a cotenant who is the accused abuser after a domestic violence lease termination; or the end of a lease whose original or renewed total term is 12 months or more, if you gave at least 60 days' written notice that it won't be renewed and you file the eviction within 6 months after it ends. Nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure; for those you may end a tenancy for any reason with proper written notice. The rule applies from the first day of the tenancy, whether month-to-month or fixed-term. For a lease shorter than 12 months, its expiration is not by itself a listed ground, so you need another one, such as other good cause, and 30 days' notice. If other good cause rests on the tenant's conduct, give a written warning first. Ending a 12-month-plus lease on non-renewal is not an eviction for tenant-screening purposes.

title: Tenants and Foreclosure
bodyText: If a rental is foreclosed, New Hampshire's eviction statute lets the purchaser at the foreclosure sale recover possession from an occupant holding without right, after a written notice to quit and the usual court process; no one may lock tenants out. A single-family house that a bank or other mortgagee takes through foreclosure becomes nonrestricted property, so it can be ended for any reason with proper notice; other foreclosed rentals stay restricted property, meaning a listed ground such as other good cause is still needed. (Nonrestricted property is a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses, a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units, or a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure; restricted property is any other residential rental.) The security deposit, with any interest due, must be turned over to a court-appointed receiver or to the foreclosure purchaser within 5 days, and the tenant told by registered or certified mail who holds it. New Hampshire statutes do not say whether a lease survives the foreclosure or require a special tenant notice, but federal law may protect bona fide tenants with longer notice or the rest of their lease; this library has not reviewed it. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; federal law and case law were not.

title: Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction
bodyText: A New Hampshire tenant sued for nonpayment can stop the case by paying, before the hearing on the merits, all rent due through the date of payment, plus other lawful charges contained in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing fee and service costs, in cash, certified check, money order, electronic transfer or other guaranteed funds (or a qualifying government or agency rent voucher). You then file a receipt with the court and send a copy to the tenant, and the case is dismissed. A tenant may use this right no more than three times in 12 months. Your demand for rent may not ask for more than the whole rent in arrears. While the case is pending, you may accept the arrears and still go forward only if you tell the tenant in writing that you intend to proceed with the eviction; otherwise accepting the money can create a new tenancy. There is no separate post-judgment redemption period, but the court may stay the move-out, and a filed payment agreement can keep the tenant in place. The eviction notice must tell the tenant of this right to pay.

title: Lease Guarantors
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on lease guarantors: none limits a guarantor's liability to the original term, requires a separate guaranty to state a maximum amount or end date, or caps what a guarantor may be asked to pay up front. A guaranty is an ordinary contract, so write it to say plainly whether it covers renewals, extensions and month-to-month holdover, and have the guarantor sign it. Be careful with money collected at the start: the deposit cap (one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater) covers all funds beyond the monthly rent that the tenant transfers to you for any purpose, and the statute does not say whether money a guarantor pays on the tenant's behalf counts, so treat it as part of the deposit. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: No Exemption Waivers in Leases
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute letting a tenant waive, in a lease, the exemptions that protect a debtor's property from collection, and the homestead right protects an owner's interest in the home the owner lives in, which a renter usually doesn't have. Household basics such as necessary clothing, beds and bedding, household furniture up to $3,500, a cook stove, heating stove and refrigerator, and some provisions and fuel are exempt from attachment and execution. Leave exemption-waiver language out of New Hampshire leases. To collect a debt from a former tenant, get a court judgment and use the court's collection process; you may not seize or hold a tenant's belongings yourself except through the courts. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Moving to Care or Senior Housing
bodyText: New Hampshire gives tenants no statutory right to end a lease early because of age, illness, disability, a tenant's death or a move to a nursing home, assisted living or senior housing. A month-to-month tenant can leave on 30 days' written notice, paying rent through the end of the month in which the notice expires unless the lease says otherwise; for a fixed term, the lease decides. If a tenant with a disability asks to be released early because of the disability, treat it as a request for a reasonable accommodation under the state fair housing law and consider it. Elderly or disabled tenants in a building being converted to condominiums have extra protections. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: No Lien on a Tenant's Belongings
bodyText: A New Hampshire residential landlord has no lien on a tenant's belongings for unpaid rent, and a lease clause creating one does not help: you may not willfully seize, hold or otherwise deny a tenant access to the tenant's property except through proper judicial process, and a tenant can recover actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, doubled or tripled if the violation was willful or knowing, plus attorney's fees. Belongings left behind after a tenant moves out must be stored with reasonable care for 7 days and released without rent or storage fees. An old statute gives a boarding or lodging house keeper a lien on a boarder's or lodger's baggage and effects for board or room rent; it is meant for boarding arrangements, not ordinary apartments, and rooms rented to transient guests for fewer than 90 days are outside the eviction chapter. Collect unpaid rent through a court judgment instead. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Your Remedies When a Tenancy Ends
bodyText: In a New Hampshire eviction case you can recover possession and court costs, and you may also claim unpaid rent on the writ. If you win on nonpayment, the court enters a money judgment at the same time, after weighing any tenant counterclaims, but the judgment in the eviction case is capped at $1,500; you may sue separately in the right court for anything above that, and for damage or other losses. Nothing in the eviction statute stops you from pursuing your ordinary legal remedies. After the tenancy ends, you may deduct from the security deposit unpaid rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, a lease-required share of real estate tax increases and other lawful charges due under the lease, with a written itemized list (and evidence of repair costs) within 30 days. If a judgment is entered for possession, you may enforce it by having the sheriff serve the writ of possession or by asking the court to hold the tenant in civil contempt.

title: Agreed Damages for Breach
bodyText: New Hampshire's statutes and rules do not address a residential lease term fixing in advance what a tenant owes for a breach (liquidated damages), and no regulation permits or bars one. The only liquidated damages in the landlord-tenant statutes are the $15 a tenant must pay, along with rent, lawful lease charges and court costs, to stop a nonpayment eviction before the hearing. Your security deposit is not a fund you may keep as liquidated damages: you may deduct only actual damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, unpaid rent, a lease-required share of real estate tax increases and other lawful charges due under the lease, with an itemized list. Whether a court enforces a lease's fixed damages amount is case law this library has not reviewed, so tie any fixed charge, such as an early-termination fee, to a reasonable estimate of your actual loss. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: No Lockouts for Late Rent
bodyText: New Hampshire does not allow lockouts for unpaid rent, even with notice or a lease clause allowing them. You may not willfully seize or hold the unit, change or disable the locks, remove doors, or otherwise deny a tenant access to the home or the tenant's belongings except through the courts, and you may not try to get around the eviction process. A locked-out tenant can petition the district court, which may order you to let the tenant back in, at once if needed, and award actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, doubled or tripled for a willful or knowing violation, plus attorney's fees; each day a violation continues after a temporary order is a separate violation, and if you re-rented the unit, damages are at least $3,000. For six months afterward you generally cannot evict that tenant except for nonpayment or a substantial lease violation. Use the nonpayment eviction process instead.

title: Minors in Eviction Cases
bodyText: New Hampshire's eviction statute and court rules say nothing specific about minors: they don't bar naming a minor as a defendant or say when a minor must be named. The eviction is brought against the lessee, occupant or other person in possession without right. In practice, name the adult tenants who signed the lease or are responsible for the tenancy; children living with them leave when the writ of possession is carried out. Because contracts with minors raise separate questions, don't rely on a minor alone as a tenant. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Nonpayment Demand and Eviction Notice
bodyText: To evict for unpaid rent in New Hampshire, you must make a demand for the rent and give a written eviction notice. The demand may be made any time after rent is due, before or together with the eviction notice, and may not ask for more than the rent actually in arrears. The eviction notice gives the tenant 7 days, must state the reason specifically, and must tell the tenant of the right to avoid eviction by paying all arrears plus $15 liquidated damages (and, once a case is filed, other lawful lease charges and your filing and service costs) before the hearing, a right the tenant may use up to three times in 12 months.
