No exact wording is required, but the notice must contain the same information as the court's demand-for-rent and eviction-notice forms, which are available from the court clerk and the judicial branch website. Anyone may serve the papers, in hand or by leaving them at the tenant's last and usual place of abode; keep a true and attested copy and an affidavit of service, which you file with the writ. A lease cannot shorten or waive the notice, and the lease itself cannot serve as the notice. A tenant may also defend by showing a qualifying government or agency rent payment was offered and refused.

title: No Rule on Notice Fees
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute addresses charging a tenant for preparing or serving a demand for rent or an eviction notice. Any person may serve those notices, so serving them need not cost much. Once you file a nonpayment case, a tenant who wants it dismissed must pay you the rent due, other lawful charges contained in the lease, $15 liquidated damages, and the filing fee and service charges you incurred in the court case, so court filing and sheriff costs are covered by statute. Whether a separate lease fee for serving a notice is a lawful lease charge is not settled by statute; the library does not offer one for New Hampshire. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Eviction Notice Can't Be Waived
bodyText: A New Hampshire lease cannot shorten or waive the eviction notice. Every residential eviction needs a written eviction notice stating the reason specifically and served in hand or at the tenant's home, with 7 days' notice for nonpayment after demand, substantial damage, behavior adversely affecting others' health or safety, or a domestic violence perpetrator remaining after a victim's lease termination, and 30 days in all other cases. Any lease or rental agreement term, written or oral, by which a tenant gives up rights under the eviction chapter is void. A lease may give the tenant more notice than the statute requires, but a lease that promises longer notice may bind you, so state the statutory periods rather than inventing new ones.

title: Nuisance Abatement
bodyText: New Hampshire's nuisance-abatement law treats a place used for lewdness, assignation, prostitution or illegal liquor sales as a nuisance. The Attorney General, a county attorney or any citizen of the state may sue to stop it, and the owner, agent and lessee can all be named; every defendant is presumed to know the place's general reputation. If the owner had five days' notice of the hearing and has neither abated the nuisance nor moved to enforce the owner's rights against the tenant, the court may close the place to any use until the case ends. An owner who could not have known of the illegal use, with reasonable care, may get the property released by paying costs and posting a bond to abate the nuisance. The same law makes a tenant's use of the premises for those purposes void the lease; act on that through the eviction court process, not by re-entering on your own. Knowingly keeping a place used for illegal drug use or sales is also unlawful. Separately, a local health officer, building official or fire chief may order a building vacated when its condition is a clear and imminent danger; that order doesn't change your rights against the tenant, and occupants may return once the danger is fixed. Respond quickly to complaints about illegal activity and document what you do. Your town may have its own nuisance ordinances.

title: No Owner Move-In Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule that your lease must reserve a right to end the tenancy so you or a relative can move in, and no special owner-move-in ground, notice or relocation payment. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The general rules decide it. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). For nonrestricted property you may end a tenancy for any reason with a written eviction notice. For restricted property, wanting the unit for yourself is not a listed ground by name, but the listed ground of other good cause includes any legitimate business or economic reason, and need not rest on anything the tenant did. Either way, give at least 30 days' written notice stating the reason with specificity, served in hand or at the tenant's home. No statute gives you a right to end a fixed-term lease early for your own use; if you want that option, state it expressly in the lease. An eviction within 6 months after a tenant's code complaint is presumed retaliatory, so keep evidence of your plans.

title: No Possession Bond
bodyText: New Hampshire has no possession bond for residential leases and no procedure letting a tenant agree in advance to a judgment for possession at the end of the term. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. To recover possession you use the eviction process: a written eviction notice, a landlord and tenant writ, and a writ of possession served by the sheriff. Do not put a confession-of-judgment or similar clause in the lease; a lease term by which a tenant gives up rights under the eviction chapter is void. The only security the eviction chapter provides comes later in the case: a tenant who raises a question of title must give the court sureties to pay rent pending the case, and a tenant who appeals must pay rent into court while the appeal is pending.

title: Rent Paid Into Court
bodyText: New Hampshire does not make a tenant pay rent into court before raising a defense in an eviction. Rent is paid into court, or to you under court order, in three situations. (1) If a tenant defends a nonpayment eviction by proving a serious code violation you failed to fix after written notice, the court may continue the case up to one month for repairs and must then have the tenant pay the withheld rent, and rent as it comes due, into court; if you fix the problem in time, the court dismisses the case and pays you either all of it or the fair rental value of the defective unit, with the rest to the tenant; if not, the tenant wins and gets the money back. (2) A tenant who appeals a nonpayment judgment must pay one week's rent into court when filing the notice of intent to appeal and then weekly; if a payment is missed, a writ of possession issues unless all rent due is paid to the clerk before the sheriff serves it. You may ask the court to release the rent during the appeal. In an appeal of any other eviction, the tenant pays rent as it comes due, into court or to you as the court directs. (3) If the court delays the move-out after judgment, the tenant pays you the weekly rent in advance, and a missed payment ends the delay. When you claim unpaid rent, the tenant's offsetting claims and counterclaims are raised in the eviction case: the court rules require them by the return day, and for cases on or after October 8, 2026 the court's notice tells tenants to file an answer stating defenses and counterclaims within 5 days after the return day. The money judgment in the eviction case is capped at $1,500 for either side, and either of you may sue separately for more. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Retaliation
bodyText: New Hampshire protects tenants who complain or organize. A tenant of residential property has a defense to eviction if you brought the eviction in retaliation for the tenant (1) reporting to you, or to a code, health or other inspection or enforcement agency, a violation (or what the tenant reasonably and in good faith believes is a violation) of the prohibited-practices law, or an unreasonable and substantial violation of a regulation or housing code; (2) filing a good-faith court petition under the prohibited-practices law or using the code-violation defense to a nonpayment eviction; or (3) meeting or gathering with other tenants for any lawful purpose. The defense is not available if the tenant owes you the equivalent of one week's rent or more. If you start an eviction, raise the rent or substantially change the terms within 6 months after you receive notice of the report (from the tenant in hand, by mail or left at your home, or from the agency), after you finish the repairs, after you learn of the tenant's petition, or after you discover the tenant organizing, retaliation is presumed unless the court finds the tenant acted mainly to prevent an eviction; the presumption can be rebutted. A tenant who proves retaliation may be awarded up to 3 months' rent. Ending a lease of 12 months or more by non-renewal notice does not take away the defense. Separately, if a tenant proves you committed a prohibited practice such as a lockout, utility shutoff or entry without consent, you may not evict that tenant for 6 months after the tenant's petition except for nonpayment, a substantial lease violation or a violation of that law, and you may take no other action in reprisal. If you rent a condominium unit and the association lawfully collects the rent from your tenant because you fell behind on assessments, you may not retaliate against the tenant for paying it. In housing for older persons and independent living retirement communities, residents also have a statutory right to be free from retaliation for making a complaint or joining a tenant association, with no 6-month limit or unpaid-rent exception; a violation is an unfair trade practice. A lease cannot waive the eviction-chapter defense. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Seasonal and Vacation Rentals
bodyText: New Hampshire treats vacation and seasonal rentals differently from ordinary tenancies. Rooms in hotels, motels, inns, tourist homes and other dwellings rented for recreational or vacation use are outside the eviction chapter, and the security deposit statute does not apply to rentals for vacation or recreational purposes. A special rule covers a unit you rent for vacation or recreation at least one month a year and also rent for residential purposes, for part or all of the off-season, to someone with no other residence. To recover that unit at the end of the off-season without a court eviction, you and the tenant must both sign a lease that states the date by which the tenant must leave and tells the tenant that if the tenant stays after the lease expires without your written permission, a law enforcement officer may remove the tenant without any judicial process. Once the lease expires, an officer shown the expired lease must remove the occupants, and you may re-rent the unit. If you have someone removed without following these rules, or misrepresent that the unit qualifies, you owe the removed tenant 3 months' rent plus costs and attorney's fees. Without such a lease, use the ordinary eviction process. Separately, the state meals and rooms tax can reach short stays; see the rooms tax row. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Servicemember Tenants
bodyText: A New Hampshire tenant may end a lease or rental agreement if the tenant is a member of the armed services reserve or national guard called to active duty, or a member of the armed services on active duty who is reassigned to a location out of state. The tenant must give notice within 7 days after receiving notice of the call to active duty or reassignment, by written notice that follows the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act. State law also extends federal servicemember civil relief to state duty: a member of the state guard, national guard or militia called by the governor to active duty for 30 days or more gets the same civil protections, rights and relief as if called to federal active duty, and a court may award attorney's fees to the winning side in a suit to enforce this. In an eviction case, if the tenant does not appear, the court will not issue a default writ of possession until you file a military affidavit. Federal law separately protects servicemembers who rent, including limits on evictions and default judgments; it was not reviewed for this row. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: After the Writ of Possession
bodyText: When you win an eviction case in New Hampshire, the court issues a writ of possession, which authorizes the sheriff to remove the tenant; you may instead ask the court to enforce the judgment through civil contempt. Never remove the tenant or the tenant's belongings yourself. The sheriff charges a fee set by statute for serving the writ. Belongings a tenant leaves behind after moving out, whether voluntarily or by eviction, must be stored by you with reasonable care for 7 days after the tenant vacated. During those 7 days the tenant may take them back without paying rent or storage fees; after that you may dispose of them without notice. If you retook the unit using the statutory abandonment notice, the 7 days start the day after you serve that notice. If you break the 7-day rule, the tenant can recover actual damages plus costs and attorney's fees. New Hampshire has no statute on inventories, warehouse storage or pets left behind after an eviction, and none giving you immunity for what happens while the writ is carried out. Leaving an animal without proper provision for its care is animal cruelty by the person who had custody of it, so if a tenant's animal is left behind, contact the tenant and your local animal control officer at once. A person who enters or stays anywhere knowing he or she has no license or privilege to be there commits criminal trespass, which the police enforce. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Application Answers and Annulled Records
bodyText: The library's application-accuracy clause makes a materially false statement in a rental application a breach of the lease. Two New Hampshire rules decide what counts as false. First, a person whose criminal record a court has annulled is treated in all respects as if never arrested, convicted or sentenced, and the annulment statute says that in an application for employment, a license or other civil right or privilege a person may be questioned about a criminal record only in terms such as "Have you ever been arrested for or convicted of a crime that has not been annulled by a court?" Word your screening questions that way, and don't treat an answer that leaves out an annulled record as false. Arrests that ended in a not-guilty finding, dismissal or no prosecution on or after January 1, 2019 are annulled automatically. Second, ending a tenancy at the end of a lease of 12 months or more under the no-fault non-renewal ground is not an eviction for rental applications and tenant screening reports, so an applicant who answers "no evictions" about such a move-out is not answering falsely. New Hampshire gives you no special statutory right to end a lease for a false application; use the lease's breach remedies. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). For restricted property, a material falsehood can support ending the tenancy as failure to comply with a material term of the lease, on 30 days' written notice stating the reason. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Late Benefit or Voucher Payments
bodyText: New Hampshire has no rule requiring a court to postpone or reopen a nonpayment eviction because a tenant's Social Security, other government benefit or rental assistance payment arrived late. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not. Several rules still protect payments from agencies. A written promise to pay rent on the tenant's behalf from the state, a county or a city or town, or a payment from an organization that disburses federal or state funds, counts as payment by the tenant of that amount, though you need not accept a partial payment. It is a defense to a nonpayment eviction that the tenant offered such a payment on time and you refused it, or could have offered it on time if you had given the agency ordinary and reasonable verification of the rental information it asked for. So answer assistance agencies' verification requests promptly. Before the hearing, the tenant can also end the case by paying all rent due plus lawful lease charges, $15 and your court costs, and after judgment the court may delay the move-out if justice requires, with weekly rent paid to you.

title: When the Law Lets a Tenant Leave Early
bodyText: New Hampshire gives tenants a few statutory ways to end a lease early, and a lease cannot take them away. (1) Servicemembers: a reserve or national guard member called to active duty, or an active-duty member reassigned out of state, may end the lease by written notice under the federal Servicemembers Civil Relief Act, given within 7 days after receiving the orders. (2) Survivors: a tenant may end the lease if the tenant or a household member was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking within the most recent 150 days (or a recent event related to past abuse makes the victim fear for their safety) and gives you a listed written verification; the tenant must move out within 30 days and owes rent only through the later of the termination date or move-out. (3) Condominium conversion: once you send the notice of intent to convert, a tenant may end the tenancy without penalty on 30 days' notice, whatever the lease says (unless the lease predates June 22, 1983). (4) A month-to-month tenant may leave on 30 days' notice, paying rent to the end of the month in which the notice expires unless the lease says otherwise. New Hampshire has no statute letting a tenant end a lease because you misrepresented the unit, because of illness, age or a move to care, or because of a fire or other casualty; for those, the lease and general contract law decide. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Tenancies at Will
bodyText: In New Hampshire every tenancy or occupancy is treated as a tenancy at will, with rent payable on demand, unless a different contract is shown. A written lease with a fixed term and a rent due date is that different contract; without one, or once a fixed term has run out and the tenant stays on paying rent, expect the tenancy to be treated as at will. A tenant at will who pays month to month may end the tenancy on 30 days' notice; if the end date in the notice is not a rent due date, the tenant owes rent for the whole month in which the notice expires, up to the next rent due date, unless the lease says otherwise. To end an at-will tenancy yourself, serve a written eviction notice, in hand or at the tenant's home, stating the reason with specificity: 30 days' notice, or 7 days for nonpayment after demand, substantial damage, behavior adversely affecting others' health or safety, or a domestic violence perpetrator remaining after a victim's lease termination. The 30-day period applies whether rent is paid weekly or monthly. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). For nonrestricted property any reason will do; for restricted property you need one of the statute's listed grounds, such as other good cause. If you sell, your buyer gets the same eviction rights you had against a tenant at will. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Tenant Bankruptcy
bodyText: New Hampshire's landlord-tenant statutes have no rule on what happens when a tenant files for bankruptcy. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and federal law were not. Federal bankruptcy law decides whether you may start or continue an eviction, collect past-due rent or enforce a lease term that ends the lease because of the bankruptcy; this library has not reviewed it. If a tenant tells you about a bankruptcy filing, pause collection and eviction steps and get advice on federal law before going further. One state rule touches insolvent tenants: under New Hampshire's voidable-transactions law, in effect from August 31, 2026, ending a lease after the debtor's default, in line with the lease and the law, is protected from some of the claims a debtor's creditors can bring to undo transfers.

title: When a Tenant Dies
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on what happens to a lease when a tenant dies. It does not end the lease or give the estate a right to end it, set up a contact-person or affidavit procedure, or say who may collect the tenant's belongings, security deposit or prepaid rent. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law and probate procedure were not. If the lease has a co-tenant, the tenancy continues for that person. Otherwise deal with the estate's personal representative (executor or administrator) on ending the tenancy, removing belongings and returning the deposit with the itemized list the deposit statute requires. The 7-day storage rule for belongings of a tenant who has vacated doesn't mention death, so don't dispose of a deceased tenant's belongings without the representative's agreement or legal advice. You may not change locks or otherwise deny access to the unit except through the courts. The library's optional emergency and death contact clause lets the tenant name someone you may contact, but that person has no legal authority over the estate unless appointed.

title: Removing Unauthorized Occupants
bodyText: New Hampshire has a fast court procedure for people living in a residential property without permission. No one who isn't a tenant, an authorized subtenant or an implied tenant may occupy residential property without the permission of the owner, landlord or agent. An implied tenant is someone living in the unit with the knowledge and consent of both the tenant and you, but without a signed lease, so a long-term guest you knew about and accepted may count. You may file a petition in the district court; there is no filing fee. If the petition is served in hand or at the home on the day the court enters it, the hearing is held within 48 hours; otherwise within 48 hours of service. An occupant who claims to be a subtenant or implied tenant must prove it, with evidence such as an unexpired lease signed by you or your agent, canceled checks or money orders, cash receipts you signed or electronic rent payments to you from the past month, or messages showing that you agreed the person may live there; utility bills, IDs or mail at the address are not enough without authorizing documentation from you. If you win, the court orders law enforcement to remove the occupants immediately and awards you actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater; you may dispose of belongings left behind without notice, and the occupants may be arrested for trespass. If the occupant sublet from your tenant in breach of a no-subletting lease, you may dispose of belongings only after 48 hours' notice and get no damages. If the court finds the person is a tenant, subtenant or implied tenant, you must use the ordinary eviction process. A petition not brought in good faith makes you liable for the occupant's actual damages or $1,000. Use the eviction process, not this procedure, for anyone you rented to. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: No Agreed Actual-Notice Method
bodyText: New Hampshire's landlord-tenant statutes don't use an "actual notice" standard that you and the tenant can meet by agreeing in the lease on an extra method such as a text message. Instead, each statute that requires a notice names how it is given, and that method must be used: the demand for rent and the eviction notice go to the tenant in hand or are left at the tenant's home; a written warning before an other-good-cause eviction based on the tenant's conduct goes the same way or by certified mail; notice that a security deposit was transferred on sale goes by registered or certified mail; a property abandonment notice is left at the unit and sent by certified mail; and notices before removing a vehicle are posted on the vehicle and the tenant's door or in a common area. Under New Hampshire's electronic transactions law, electronic records count only between parties who have agreed to deal electronically, and where another law specifies how a record must be sent, it must still be sent that way. Texts and e-mails are fine for routine messages and for notices no statute governs, if the lease provides for them, but send statutory notices by the statutory method (you may add an e-mail copy). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Claims Against the Property
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring a tenant to tell you about a foreclosure, tax lien or other claim against the property, and none requiring you or your lender to tell tenants that a foreclosure is pending; the foreclosure sale notice goes to the borrower and lienholders, not tenants. If you want a tenant to forward papers about the property, put that in the lease. One rule does reach your tenants if you rent out a condominium unit. If your condominium association has adopted the statutory rent-collection remedy in its declaration or bylaws and you are more than 60 days behind on common-expense assessments, the association may send you written notice, by first-class and certified mail, of the amount it claims and its intent to collect from rent. If you don't pay or show prior payment within 30 days, the association may direct your tenant to pay it all or part of the rent, up to the amount claimed, until the debt is paid. A tenant who pays the association is not in default on the rent to the extent of that payment, you may not retaliate against the tenant for paying, and a lease term waiving these rules is void. You may still go to court to dispute the amount. After a foreclosure, the buyer at the sale may recover possession from occupants only through the eviction process. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Automatic Renewal Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on lease clauses that renew a lease automatically, and no required reminder before a renewal or an opt-out deadline. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. So an automatic renewal clause is an ordinary lease term; state clearly how long each renewal lasts, at what rent, and how and when either side may stop it. Two rules affect renewals. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). For restricted property, the end of a lease is a ground to end the tenancy only if the original lease term, or the term as renewed, totals 12 months or more, you gave written notice at least 60 days before the end of the term that the lease won't be renewed and the tenant must leave, and you file the eviction within 6 months after the lease ends; renewals count toward the 12 months. And if a renewal raises the rent, a restricted-property tenant's refusal is good cause for eviction only if you gave written notice of the new amount and its effective date at least 30 days ahead.

title: Other Rules New Hampshire Does Not Have
bodyText: Three rules some states have do not exist in New Hampshire law. (1) No statute bans renting the same unit to two tenants for the same period or gives a special remedy when you can't deliver possession on the start date; the lease's possession-delay terms and contract law apply. (2) No statute makes your compliance with smoke or carbon monoxide alarm rules inadmissible in an injury case or limits what an insurer may do because of it; the alarm statute still requires the devices and makes you, as owner, responsible for maintaining them. (3) No statute gives you a special right to end a lease because the rental application was false; the lease's application-accuracy section makes a material falsehood a breach handled through the ordinary eviction grounds and notices. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Checked Across the Whole Code
bodyText: We searched all of New Hampshire's statutes, its 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules, not just the landlord-tenant chapters, for three things landlords ask about. (1) New Hampshire does have a fast remedy for squatters and other unauthorized occupants: a no-fee district court petition heard within about 48 hours, with removal by law enforcement and damages of at least $1,000 if you win (see the unauthorized occupants row). It is not for anyone you rented to. (2) There is no statewide duty to give a receipt for rent paid in cash. Give one anyway: cash receipts you sign are evidence of who is a tenant, and in a nonpayment case where the tenant pays everything due before the hearing, you must file a receipt with the court. (3) There is no statewide landlord registration or rental license, so registration is not a condition of filing an eviction. One general business rule can still stop you if you own through an out-of-state entity: an out-of-state limited liability company doing business in New Hampshire must register with the Secretary of State, and until it has registered and paid the fees for the period it was unregistered it may not maintain any action, an eviction included; an out-of-state corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority may not maintain a proceeding until it gets one (N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 304-C:175, 304-C:180 and 293-A:15.02). Owning property without more is not doing business, but renting it out may be; that is a case-law question (§§ 304-C:174, I(i) and 293-A:15.01(b)(9)). The one statewide filing is that an owner of restricted property must file with the town or city clerk the name of an in-state agent to accept legal papers; an out-of-state owner who doesn't file and doesn't appear can be served in a way the court presumes valid. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). Cities and towns may have their own rental ordinances, which were not searched; case law was not either.

title: Domestic Violence Citations Check
bodyText: New Hampshire has not moved or renumbered the laws its landlord-tenant protections for survivors rely on. The eviction statute's domestic violence protections and the survivor's right to end a lease define the abuse by reference to the domestic violence protective-order chapter, the sexual assault chapter and the stalking statute, and all three are current. Protective orders still issue under the domestic violence chapter, and the lock-change rule refers to a protective order from a court of competent jurisdiction granting a tenant possession, without citing a section number. The court's self-certification form for survivors is a court form, so get the current version from the court rather than citing a number. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Electronic Leases and Records
bodyText: New Hampshire's electronic transactions law lets you sign leases and keep records electronically: a signature or record can't be denied effect just because it is electronic, and an electronic record or signature satisfies a law requiring a writing or signature. But it applies only when both you and the tenant have agreed to deal electronically, which can be shown by the circumstances. A party who agreed to one electronic transaction may refuse to do later ones electronically, and a lease cannot take that right away. An electronic record you send is not enforceable against the tenant if you keep the tenant from printing or storing it, so send documents in a form the tenant can save. Where another law says how a notice must be delivered, such as an eviction notice served in hand or at the tenant's home, that method still applies, and the electronic transactions law expressly does not authorize electronic delivery of certain notices that federal law excludes. Whether signed on paper or electronically, give each tenant a copy of the signed lease within 30 days after everyone signs; failing to do so is a violation-level offense. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law and federal law were not.

title: No Pre-Suit Resolution Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute that lets, or forbids, a lease requiring you and the tenant to try to resolve a dispute informally, or by mediation, before going to court. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The district court offers mediation in some civil cases, but it is voluntary for both sides. If your lease includes an informal-resolution step, keep it optional for the tenant and don't make it a condition of the statutory processes: an eviction notice and possessory action, a tenant's or landlord's court petition over prohibited practices such as lockouts or entry without consent, the 30-day return of the security deposit, or a tenant's habitability or retaliation defenses. A lease term by which a tenant gives up rights under the eviction chapter is void, and the deposit statute's rights can't be waived either. A simple clause asking both sides to contact each other in writing about problems before taking other steps, without delaying any legal deadline, is safe.

title: Blank Spaces in the Lease
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring every blank in a residential lease to be filled in, and none treating a blank as a breach. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Fill in or strike every blank before signing anyway, because you must give the tenant a copy of the signed lease within 30 days, and the lease's terms, such as the rent, due date, deposit, other charges and any parking or storage assignment, are what a court looks to: a nonpayment tenant can stop an eviction by paying rent plus other lawful charges contained in the lease, and you may deduct from the deposit only lawful charges due under the lease.

title: Copy of the Signed Lease
bodyText: In New Hampshire, once everyone has signed a written lease, you must deliver a copy to the tenant within 30 days. Failing to do so is a violation, a non-criminal offense. The statute doesn't say that a missing copy keeps you from enforcing the lease, but give the copy promptly and keep proof that you did; if the tenant agreed to deal electronically, a copy the tenant can print or save is enough. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law was not.

title: No Initials Requirement
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute requires a tenant to initial a particular lease term for it to bind the tenant; the signatures on the lease are enough as far as the statutes go. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Initials can't rescue a term the law forbids: a lease term by which a tenant gives up rights under the eviction chapter is void, and so is a waiver of the security deposit rules. For example, a month-to-month tenant may leave on 30 days' notice, so a term demanding longer notice from the tenant risks being treated as such a waiver. Having the tenant initial an unusual but lawful term is still good evidence that the tenant saw it.

title: Lease Length and Recording
bodyText: New Hampshire sets no maximum length for a residential lease and has no statute requiring a residential lease to be in writing. Length still matters in three ways. (1) A lease for more than 7 years from when it is made is not valid against anyone other than you and your heirs, such as a buyer or lender, unless it is acknowledged and recorded at the registry of deeds; between you and the tenant it still binds. (2) Without a written lease or other contract showing a different arrangement, a tenancy is at will, with rent payable on demand. (3) Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). For restricted property, the end of the lease is a ground to end the tenancy only if the original term, or the term as renewed, totals 12 months or more, and you give 60 days' written notice and file within 6 months after the end. A written lease may call for rent quarterly or less often, but the deposit taken on top of the first rent payment still can't exceed one month's rent. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: In-State Agent for Legal Papers
bodyText: If you own restricted property in New Hampshire, you must file a statement with the town or city clerk where the property is, within 30 days after becoming the owner, giving the name, address and telephone number of a person in New Hampshire authorized to accept service of legal papers in any legal proceeding against you about the property. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). If you live in New Hampshire, the agent may be you; if you live out of state, it must be someone in the state. The town may charge a reasonable filing fee and may fine you up to $100 for not filing. If you live out of state, don't file and don't appear in a case, service of legal papers through the New Hampshire Secretary of State, with a copy mailed to you, is presumed lawful, including in code-enforcement cases. The filing is with the clerk, not in the lease, and New Hampshire doesn't bar you from suing a tenant if you haven't filed it. Two general rules reach out-of-state owners whatever kind of property they own. Any nonresident who owns real property in New Hampshire can be sued here on claims arising from it, with the papers left with the Secretary of State and a copy sent to you by registered mail (N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. § 510:4, I-II). And if you own through an out-of-state limited liability company doing business here, it must register with the Secretary of State, naming a registered agent, and until it has registered and paid the fees for the unregistered period it may not maintain any action, an eviction included; while unregistered it is deemed to have appointed the Secretary of State as its agent for legal papers. An out-of-state corporation transacting business here without a certificate of authority likewise may not maintain a proceeding (N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 304-C:175, 304-C:180, 304-C:182 and 293-A:15.02). Owning property without more is not doing business; whether renting it out is, is a case-law question. New Hampshire doesn't require an out-of-state owner to hire a broker or property manager; the real estate licensing law doesn't apply to an owner, or the owner's regular employees, dealing with the owner's own property. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: How Notices Must Be Delivered
bodyText: In New Hampshire, a demand for rent and an eviction notice may be served by anyone, not only a sheriff, either by handing it to the tenant or by leaving it at the tenant's last and usual place of abode. Keep a true and attested copy and sign an affidavit of service (it need not be sworn); you must file them with the court when you enter the eviction case. Your notice must contain the same information as the court's demand and eviction notice forms. The landlord and tenant writ itself is served by the sheriff. Other statutory notices have their own methods: a written warning before an other-good-cause eviction based on the tenant's conduct goes in hand, at the home or by certified mail; notice that you transferred the security deposit on a sale goes by registered or certified mail; a property abandonment notice is left at the unit and sent by certified mail to at least one adult tenant; and notices before removing a vehicle are posted on the vehicle and the tenant's door (or a common area if you don't know whose it is). E-mail and other electronic notices work only if both of you have agreed to deal electronically, the tenant can withdraw from electronic dealings at any time, and the message must be one the tenant can print or save; they never replace a method a statute specifies, so use the library's optional e-mail clause only for routine and non-statutory notices. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Extra Terms in Move-Out Notices
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on a move-out notice form you ask a tenant to sign, and no required warning if the form adds terms the lease doesn't contain. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Keep any such form to what the tenant's notice needs: a tenant may end a tenancy by written notice in the same manner as you, and a month-to-month tenant may do so on 30 days' notice, paying rent through the end of the month in which the notice expires unless the lease says otherwise. Don't use the form to get the tenant to give up rights: a term waiving rights under the eviction chapter is void, and so is any agreement to deposit deductions the deposit statute doesn't allow or a waiver of the 30-day itemized return. Put any genuine new agreement, such as an agreed move-out date or a cash-for-keys arrangement, in a separate signed document.

title: Where New Hampshire Lets Your Lease Decide
bodyText: Several New Hampshire rules depend on what the lease says, and a silent lease gets the statutory default. (1) Without a lease or other contract showing otherwise, a tenancy is at will and rent is payable on demand. (2) A month-to-month tenant who gives notice ending mid-month owes rent through the end of that month unless the lease says otherwise. (3) To stop a nonpayment eviction the tenant pays rent plus other lawful charges contained in the lease, and you may deduct from the deposit only unpaid charges due under the lease; list every fee. (4) You may deduct a share of real estate tax increases from the deposit only if the lease requires the tenant to pay it. (5) A written lease may call for rent quarterly or less often, but the deposit still can't exceed one month's rent. (6) You may remove, after the statutory notices, a vehicle parked or stored in a way the lease prohibits; spell out the parking rules. (7) In towns without their own housing code, removing garbage from common areas becomes the tenant's job only if the rental agreement says so and you cleared all garbage when the tenancy began. (8) A subtenant has rights only if you authorized subletting, and a no-subletting clause affects how a court treats an unauthorized occupant. (9) A tenant may not let a medical cannabis patient smoke if the lease or your policies applying to all tenants bar smoking, though vaporizing and ingesting can't be barred that way. (10) For tenancies covered by the new snow and ice statute, effective July 1, 2027, you and the tenant may agree who clears which areas; otherwise the statute's defaults apply. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: No Plain-Language Lease Law
bodyText: New Hampshire has no plain-language or readability law for residential leases, no readability test, and no required statement listing the rights a tenant gives up under the lease. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. What limits a New Hampshire lease instead is the void-waiver rules: any lease term by which a tenant waives rights under the eviction chapter is void, as is any waiver of the security deposit statute. Write the lease clearly anyway: the state consumer protection act applies to renting real estate and bars unfair or deceptive acts, and terms a tenant can't understand invite disputes.

title: Rules That Depend on Size
bodyText: Several New Hampshire rules turn on how many units you own or how big the building is, and each uses its own test, so check them separately. (1) Eviction grounds: "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). The count is of single-family houses you own at any one time, so other kinds of rental property don't count against the three-house limit. For nonrestricted property you may end a tenancy for any reason with proper notice; restricted property needs a listed ground. (2) Security deposits: the deposit statute doesn't apply to a person who rents out a single-family residence and owns no other rental property of any kind, or who rents units in an owner-occupied building of 5 units or fewer, except for any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. Both conditions in the first test must be met; owning one other rental of any type brings you under the statute. (3) Fair housing: the general real estate discrimination section does not reach rentals in an owner-occupied building of no more than 4 families or rooms in the owner's home, but those exemptions are written for that section only, not the disability section, and advertising rules still apply. (4) Service animals: the state service animal law covers housing except a single-family home whose occupants rent out no more than one room. (5) Condominium conversion protections apply only to buildings or complexes of more than 10 units. (6) Accessible design rules apply to new buildings of 4 or more units (all units if there is an elevator, otherwise ground-floor units). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: What New Hampshire's Tenancy Laws Cover
bodyText: New Hampshire's eviction chapter covers ordinary residential tenancies but not: rooms in rooming or boarding houses rented to transient guests for fewer than 90 consecutive days; rooms in hotels, motels, inns, tourist homes and other dwellings rented for recreational or vacation use; dormitories, nursing homes, hospitals, licensed or certified facilities, convents and group homes; your own single-family home, if it is your primary residence and the occupant has no lease; rentals where you share a kitchen or bathroom with the occupant (a separate shared-facilities chapter applies); qualifying seasonal units under a separate chapter; fraternal student housing; and live-in caregivers hired to care for or assist a person with disabilities (the person with disabilities or a guardian may remove one without court process only under a written agreement allowing it, on at least 72 hours' written notice, and, if the agreement pays the caregiver beyond free housing, after paying any money due for services). Within the eviction chapter, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure); the grounds needed to end a tenancy depend on which you own. The prohibited-practices rules (no lockouts, utility shutoffs or entry without consent, the 7-day rule for belongings, application-fee and payment-method rules) apply to every landlord renting residential premises. The security deposit rules exempt a person renting a single-family residence who owns no other rental property and a person renting units in an owner-occupied building of 5 units or fewer, except units occupied by someone 60 or older, and don't apply to vacation or recreational rentals. The state minimum housing standards apply only in towns that haven't adopted their own housing code. In federally owned, operated or subsidized housing, federal rules that conflict with the eviction chapter control. Manufactured housing parks have their own chapter, which this library does not cover. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Forms and Prescribed Wording
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statutory lease form; the prescribed wording is in side documents. (1) The district court publishes forms for a demand for rent and an eviction notice; you need not use them, but a valid demand or notice must include the same information they ask for. (2) The court's landlord and tenant writ carries a notice to the tenant that the court supplies. (3) The statute sets out a property abandonment notice, in at least 12-point type, that is deemed sufficient if you use it; it must be signed and must state your reasons, the tenant's right to retrieve belongings within 7 days and the right to file a court petition. (4) A payment agreement filed in a nonpayment case must end with a separate, conspicuous paragraph in which the tenant acknowledges that missed payments can lead to eviction without a hearing and that the tenant gives up the right to appeal; the statute gives the exact words. (5) The circuit court provides a self-certification form that a survivor of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking may use as verification. (6) In a rooming house, a guest who asks to move rooms must make the request in writing in the words the statute gives. (7) Court clerks supply petition forms for prohibited-practices cases. Get the current versions from the New Hampshire Judicial Branch. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Tenant Portals
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on tenant portals as such, but two rules limit how you use one. First, you may not require a tenant or applicant to pay anything due under a lease, renewal or extension solely by electronic funds transfer, including automatic recurring transfers; you must allow at least one non-electronic way to pay, such as a check or money order. A portal can be one option, not the only one. Second, New Hampshire's electronic transactions law applies only when both you and the tenant have agreed to deal electronically, a tenant who agreed may refuse further electronic transactions, and a lease can't take that right away; a document the tenant can't print or save is not enforceable against the tenant. So you may offer a portal for payments, repair requests and signatures, but a lease term making it the only way to sign or receive documents won't bind a tenant who declines. Notices that a statute requires to be delivered a certain way, such as eviction notices, must still go that way. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Tenant Records and Personal Data
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to give a tenant a rent ledger or payment history, though your records are your best proof in a nonpayment case. Three records rules do apply. (1) If you hold a security deposit covered by the deposit statute, you must, on request, tell the tenant the name of the bank, savings and loan or credit union where it is held, the account number, the amount on deposit and the interest rate, and let the tenant examine your records for the deposit. (2) Written verification a tenant gives you about domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, including the fact that someone is a victim, must be kept strictly confidential and disclosed only with the victim's written consent, as reasonably necessary in an eviction or housing assistance hearing, or as the law requires. (3) If you collect an application fee and don't rent to the applicant, you may keep only documented background-check, credit-check and reasonable administrative costs, so keep the receipts. For personal data: if you do business in New Hampshire and hold an applicant's or tenant's name together with a Social Security number, driver's license or other government ID number, or a financial account or card number with its access code, in electronic form, and that data is breached, you must promptly decide whether misuse is likely and, if it is or you can't tell, notify the affected people as soon as possible, notify the Attorney General's office, and, if more than 1,000 people are affected, notify the national credit reporting agencies. A person harmed by a violation can recover actual damages, doubled or tripled if willful, plus attorney's fees. No New Hampshire statute found requires a written information security program, but limiting and securing what you keep reduces the risk. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Changing Terms Other Than Rent
bodyText: New Hampshire's only statutory notice for changing a tenancy's terms is for rent: for restricted property, a tenant's refusal to accept a rent increase is good cause for eviction only if you gave written notice of the amount and effective date at least 30 days before it takes effect. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). No statute sets a notice period for changing other terms of a month-to-month tenancy, such as fees, rules, parking or utilities, or for raising a fee the lease already lists, and none says a change must be made by ending the tenancy and offering a new one. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not. Practical limits: during a fixed-term lease you can change terms only as the lease allows or with the tenant's signed agreement. For a month-to-month tenancy, give at least 30 days' written notice of any change, the same as a rent increase. For restricted property, a tenant's refusal of a non-rent change is not a listed ground by name; you would need another ground, such as other good cause based on a legitimate business or economic reason, with a 30-day eviction notice. And any substantial change in the terms of the tenancy within 6 months after a tenant reported a code violation, filed a petition or organized with other tenants is presumed retaliatory.

title: No Sunsetting Tenant Laws
bodyText: As of October 10, 2026, none of New Hampshire's landlord-tenant statutes, including the eviction chapter, the prohibited-practices and security deposit rules and the seasonal-rental chapter, carries a repeal or expiration date. The dated changes run the other way. Eviction procedure changes took effect October 8, 2026: tenants must file an answer stating defenses and counterclaims within 5 days after the return day, post-judgment stays are limited to 60 days (75 in some cases), and the tenant access and conduct rules were reworded. A new statute on snow and ice removal in leases takes effect July 1, 2027. Plan for current rules to stay in force until the legislature changes them, and check each year's new laws, since New Hampshire amends this area often. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched.

title: No Lease Translation Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to translate a lease or notices into the tenant's language, even if you advertised or negotiated in another language, and no minimum type size for leases. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Two related rules: the statutory property abandonment notice is deemed sufficient in at least 12-point type, and the court's notice that comes with an eviction writ is printed in at least 12-point type. In an eviction, a tenant's limited English proficiency is one of the factors that can justify a longer delay of the move-out after judgment (up to 75 days instead of 60). Fair housing law bars discrimination based on national origin, so if you offer translations, offer them evenly; federal language-access rules for subsidized housing were not reviewed.

title: Notices That Must Be in Writing
bodyText: Many New Hampshire landlord notices must be in writing, and a lease can't downgrade them to verbal notice, because lease terms waiving rights under the eviction chapter or the deposit statute are void. In writing: every eviction notice; the demand for rent may be served the same way; the warning required before an other-good-cause eviction based on the tenant's conduct; notice of a rent increase (30 days ahead) for restricted property; notice, at least 60 days before a 12-month-plus lease ends, that it won't be renewed; notice during a pending nonpayment case that you'll go forward despite accepting back rent; a bill for bed bug remediation you say the tenant caused; 48 hours' notice before entering to check for bed bugs, and pest-treatment preparation instructions at least 72 hours ahead; notices before removing a vehicle; the property abandonment notice; the deposit receipt and the notice to list needed repairs within 5 days of move-in; notice that you transferred the deposit on a sale; the itemized list of deposit deductions; and disclosure of any application or renewal fee before collecting it. A tenant's notice ending the tenancy must also be written. Notice before entering for repairs or other ownership functions need only be adequate under the circumstances, and you still need the tenant's consent except for emergency repairs or a court order; written notice is the easiest to prove. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Service Animals Under State Law
bodyText: New Hampshire has its own service animal law, separate from fair housing law, and it reaches rental housing. A service animal under that law is a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability, including a physical, sensory, psychiatric, intellectual or other mental disability; other species are not service animals under it, and providing emotional support, comfort or companionship, or deterring crime, does not count as work or tasks. A service animal may accompany its handler into any housing accommodation, subject only to conditions that apply to everyone. Housing accommodation means any property used as a home, except a single-family residence whose occupants rent out no more than one room. It is a misdemeanor to prohibit, hinder or interfere with a handler who otherwise follows the rules that apply to people without disabilities. A handler may register a service dog with the town free of charge and get a state tag, but the law says the tag may not be used to verify that an animal is a service animal for any purpose, so don't demand one. Requests for other assistance animals, such as emotional support animals, fall outside the state service animal law; treat them as requests for a reasonable accommodation in your pet rules under the fair housing law, which also lets you refuse a tenancy that would be a direct threat to others' health or safety or cause substantial physical damage to others' property. Federal fair housing rules and guidance on assistance animals apply too and were not reviewed here. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Pet Fact Sheet Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire does not require you to give a tenant with a dog or cat a state fact sheet about pets and eviction, or any other pet disclosure with the lease. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. State your pet rules in the lease instead, including what happens to a pet if the tenant moves out or is evicted, and remember that any pet deposit counts toward the security deposit cap.

title: Pets in Public Elderly Housing
bodyText: New Hampshire gives tenants a say on pets in one kind of housing: public housing financed by the state or federal government to house people 60 or older, other than nursing homes and high-rise apartment buildings. If 10 percent of the tenants of a project petition, the tenants vote by simple majority on whether to allow companion animals (dogs, cats, caged birds and aquarium fish); at least 6 months must pass between votes, and a later vote can't remove animals already allowed. If pets are allowed, the tenants adopt reasonable rules with input from management; a tenant who wants a pet may be required to post a damage deposit of up to 1.5 times the monthly rent; and the tenant must give management a signed agreement with a caretaker (not another tenant) who will take the animal if the tenant can't, which management may carry out if the animal is neglected or abused, plus a veterinarian's certificate of good health and spaying or neutering for cats and dogs. Each apartment may have only one companion animal, apart from birds and aquarium fish. Complaints about a pet are handled like other tenant complaints. This rule does not apply to private rental housing, where your lease's pet terms govern, subject to the security deposit cap and the service animal and disability accommodation rules. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Penalty for Refusing a Service Animal
bodyText: In New Hampshire, refusing a service animal can be a crime. The state service animal law lets a service animal (a dog individually trained to do work or perform tasks for a person with a disability) accompany its handler into any housing accommodation, subject only to conditions that apply to everyone, and makes it unlawful to directly or indirectly prohibit, hinder or interfere with a handler who otherwise follows the rules that apply to people without disabilities. Any violation is a misdemeanor, and harming a service animal carries further penalties. The only housing excluded is a single-family residence whose occupants rent out no more than one room. Don't enforce no-pet rules, pet fees, breed or size limits against a service animal; a refusal can also lead to a fair housing complaint. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Misrepresenting a Service Animal
bodyText: New Hampshire makes it a misdemeanor to misrepresent an animal as a service animal. It is unlawful to fit an animal with a collar, leash, vest, sign or harness of the type that represents it as a service animal, or with a state service animal tag, or to request such a tag, if the animal is not in fact a service animal; and it is unlawful to impersonate a person with a disability to receive service dog accommodations or accessories. These rules are not limited to public places, so they apply to housing. Still, don't make accusations or demand a tag: the state tag may not be used to verify that an animal is a service animal, and refusing a real service animal is itself a misdemeanor. If you doubt a request, follow the fair housing accommodation process and get advice. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No EV Charging Right
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants a right to install or use an electric vehicle charger at a rental property, and none requiring you to provide charging. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Whether a tenant may install a charger, and who pays for the equipment and electricity, is up to your lease or a separate written agreement. If you agree, put in writing who installs it (with any required permits), who owns it, how electricity is billed and what happens when the tenancy ends.

title: EV Chargers When the Tenancy Ends
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on what happens to a tenant-installed electric vehicle charger when the tenancy ends, because it has no statutory charging right. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. If you allow a charger, agree in writing whether the tenant removes it and restores the area or leaves it in place, and who owns it. Any money the tenant pays you toward restoration beyond the monthly rent is part of the security deposit and subject to the deposit cap.

title: No EV Charging Conditions Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute setting the conditions a landlord may impose on a tenant's electric vehicle charger, such as insurance, licensed installation or metering. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. You may set reasonable conditions in a written agreement; electrical work remains subject to the state building code and local permits.

title: No Shared-Area EV Charging Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on electric vehicle chargers in shared parking areas of rental property, such as reserved spaces, sharing or cost allocation among tenants. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. If you provide shared charging, state the rules and charges in the lease or parking rules; a vehicle parked in a way the lease prohibits may be removed only after the statutory notices.

title: Parking Rules in the Lease
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on how parking or towing rules must be delivered to tenants, what heading they need, whether you may change them during the lease, or what vehicle information you may ask for. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Put your parking rules in the lease or a signed addendum anyway, because one of the grounds for removing a tenant's vehicle is that it is parked or stored in a way the lease prohibits, and even then you must give a first written notice at least 7 days before removal and a final notice 24 to 48 hours before. If you tow from a parking lot or garage, the vehicle owner can be charged for removal and storage only if a conspicuous posted notice says illegally parked vehicles will be towed at the owner's expense. Change rules during a fixed-term lease only as the lease allows.

title: Tenant Storage Spaces
bodyText: A storage space you rent to a tenant for the tenant's exclusive use is part of the tenant's premises under New Hampshire's prohibited-practices law, which defines premises as the part of your property the tenant is entitled to use exclusively for living or storage. So the apartment rules apply to it: you may not enter it without the tenant's prior consent except for emergency repairs or under a court order; you may not seize, hold or deny the tenant access to belongings in it except through the courts; and after the tenant moves out you must keep what's left with reasonable care for 7 days, letting the tenant collect it without rent or storage fees, before disposing of it. New Hampshire's self-service storage law, with its own entry, lien and sale rules, covers property designed and used for renting individual storage spaces; it says nothing about storage that comes with a home, so don't rely on its procedures for a tenant's locker or storage unit. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Removing and Towing Vehicles
bodyText: Two New Hampshire laws govern removing vehicles from rental property. (1) A tenant's vehicle, motorcycle, trailer, ATV or other property may be removed at its owner's expense only in three situations, each with its own notice. If it blocks vehicle access to a common driveway, fire lane, parking area or travel lane, or blocks a dumpster, make reasonable efforts to notify the tenant who owns it if you know who that is; no notice is needed if there is an immediate threat to anyone's health or safety. If it is leaking fluids that damage the parking surface or create an environmental hazard, give written notice at least 48 hours before removal, placed on the item and on the tenant's door (or, if you don't know whose it is, in a conspicuous spot in a common area of each building). If it is in a posted no-parking area, unregistered or inoperable, or parked or stored in a way the lease prohibits, give a first written notice at least 7 days before removal and a final notice 24 to 48 hours before, placed the same way. Once you remove property under these rules, you may not evict the tenant for failing to remove it, unless it caused substantial damage or injured someone. Removing a tenant's vehicle any other way is a prohibited practice that can cost you actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, plus attorney's fees. (2) For a vehicle parked without permission or apparently abandoned, the owner or person in lawful possession of private property may have it removed in a reasonable manner, notifying a peace officer as soon as reasonably possible, or may ask a peace officer to have it removed. In a single-family rental the tenant may be the person in lawful possession of the driveway. A vehicle towed from a parking lot or garage can be charged for removal and storage only if a conspicuous posted notice says illegally parked vehicles are towed at the owner's expense. Leaving a vehicle on someone else's property without permission for more than 24 hours is a violation. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Unbundled Parking Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire does not require you to rent parking separately from the unit, and it doesn't regulate how you price a separate parking space. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. If you charge for parking apart from rent, list the charge in the lease: a tenant facing a nonpayment eviction can stop it by paying rent plus other lawful charges contained in the lease, and only charges due under the lease can come out of the security deposit. On the zoning side, a city or town may not require more than one residential parking space per unit, and from September 13, 2026 may not require that space to be in a garage.

title: Cannabis in Rentals
bodyText: New Hampshire allows cannabis only for registered therapeutic use; adult recreational cannabis is not legal (possessing three-quarters of an ounce or less is a violation, a non-criminal offense, and larger amounts are crimes). For a registered qualifying patient, the law says that on leased property the patient may use cannabis with the permission of the tenant in possession. Your lease or rental policies may bar smoking, and if they bar smoking for all tenants at the property, the tenant may not let a patient smoke cannabis there. But the tenant may let a patient use cannabis by ingestion or by vaporization (inhaling without burning it) even where the lease prohibits smoking, so a lease term banning all cannabis use or all vaping can't be enforced against that use. The therapeutic program does not allow patients or caregivers to grow cannabis, so you may prohibit cultivation. New Hampshire has no statute barring you from refusing to rent to a registered patient or protecting a cardholder's tenancy as such, and no statute requires anyone in lawful possession of property to let a guest or visitor use cannabis there. Federally assisted housing has its own federal rules, not reviewed here. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Disaster Guest Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute letting a tenant house people displaced by a fire, storm or other disaster despite the lease's guest or occupancy limits, and none limiting what you may charge or require when they stay. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Your lease's guest and occupancy terms apply. If a tenant asks to take in displaced family or friends, give a written temporary consent with an end date. Remember that someone who lives in the unit with both your and the tenant's knowledge and consent, without a signed lease, can become an implied tenant, so the end date and the written terms matter. The state's relocation assistance law for displaced persons covers people displaced by government acquisition of property, not private disasters.

title: Grills and the Fire Code
bodyText: New Hampshire's state fire code is the national Fire Code (NFPA 1) and Life Safety Code (NFPA 101), 2024 editions, as amended. Those national codes may limit open-flame cooking devices such as charcoal and gas grills on balconies and near buildings, especially multi-unit buildings, but their text wasn't reviewed here, and the state fire marshal's fire code rules add no grill provision, so ask your local fire chief what applies to your building. By state statute, an electric grill certified by a nationally recognized testing laboratory, such as UL, is not an open-flame cooking device under the state fire code, in any dwelling including apartment buildings. Your lease may still be stricter than the fire code; the library's fire safety clause bars all grills on porches and balconies and within 15 feet of a building, and you may keep that rule or allow listed electric grills. Cities and towns may adopt fire ordinances that are no less restrictive than the state code. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched.

title: No Firearms Lease Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute that bars, or expressly permits, lease terms restricting firearms in a private rental, and none protecting firearms kept in vehicles in a rental's parking area. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The state's firearm preemption law stops cities and towns from regulating firearms by ordinance; it doesn't address private leases. Any firearm rule in your lease is an ordinary lease term; apply it evenly. Separate laws still apply, such as limits on discharging firearms in the compact part of a town and court protective orders that can require a person to give up firearms. Federally assisted housing may have its own rules, not reviewed here.

title: Guests and Implied Tenants
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute limiting how long a tenant's guests may stay, so your lease's guest terms control. One rule makes those terms important: a person who lives in the unit with the knowledge and consent of both the tenant and you, but without a signed lease, is an implied tenant. An implied tenant can't be removed through the fast court procedure for unauthorized occupants and must instead be evicted through the ordinary eviction process, and texts or e-mails showing you agreed the person could live there can prove the status. So if a guest overstays, act promptly and in writing: tell the tenant the guest must leave or apply to be added, and don't accept rent from or otherwise approve the guest's living there unless you mean to. Tenants also answer for their guests: substantial damage by a tenant's guests is a ground to end a restricted-property tenancy, and guests may not willfully damage your property, deny other tenants quiet enjoyment, or engage in behavior that unreasonably and adversely affects others' health or safety. A guest who is a person with a disability may bring a service dog into the housing. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: No Guest Rights Statute
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants' guests, caregivers or service providers a right of access to a building, barring guest fees, or making guest rules unwaivable. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not. Your lease's guest terms govern, subject to two specific rules: a person with a disability who uses a service dog may bring it into any housing, including when visiting a tenant, and fair housing law bars rules that discriminate against protected groups, including a tenant's visitors because of their race, disability or other protected status. Keep guest rules reasonable, written and evenly applied.

title: No Police Cooperation or Crime-Free Statute
