bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you, as a landlord, to join a crime-free housing program, to answer police or child-protection investigators' requests for information about tenants or give them access to units, or to refrain from acting on a tenant's calls for police or emergency help. But New Hampshire's reporting duties bind every person, you and your staff included. Anyone having reason to suspect that a child has been abused or neglected must report it immediately, by telephone or otherwise, to the Department of Health and Human Services (N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 169-C:29 and 169-C:30). Anyone suspecting or believing in good faith that a vulnerable adult has been abused, neglected or exploited, or is living in hazardous conditions, must report it immediately to the department, or after hours to the local police or the county sheriff (§ 161-F:46). Knowingly failing to make either report is a misdemeanor (§§ 169-C:39 and 161-F:50). And anyone who finds the body of a person whose death may have resulted from a crime, suicide, an accident, an overdose or another circumstance the medical examiner law lists, as when a tenant is found dead in a unit, must immediately notify the medical examiner and the county attorney (§§ 611-B:11, II and 611-B:12). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Respond to warrants, subpoenas and court orders as the law requires, and get advice before sharing tenant information informally; a tenant's domestic violence verification must be kept confidential except as the tenant consents, as reasonably necessary in an eviction or housing assistance hearing, or as the law requires. Don't treat a survivor's calls for help as a lease violation: you may not end a restricted-property tenancy solely because a tenant or household member was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, if the victim gives you the required verification. In an eviction based on a tenant's behavior, your records of other tenants' complaints can be admitted as evidence if made at or near the time and kept in the ordinary way. Some cities and towns run their own programs or ordinances, which were not searched.

title: No Candidate Access Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to let political candidates, campaign workers or voter-registration volunteers into an apartment building to reach tenants' doors, and no duty to set aside an area for campaign literature. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. Whether outsiders may canvass in locked hallways and other common areas is up to your building rules, applied evenly; tenants may invite whomever they like to their own units, subject to the lease's guest terms. New Hampshire's election law says political advertising may not be placed on private property without the owner's consent and may be removed only by the owner, people the owner authorizes or police; the statute doesn't say whether a tenant counts as the owner of the unit, so address tenant yard and window signs in the lease. Tenants are protected from retaliation for meeting or gathering with other tenants for any lawful purpose.

title: No Air Conditioner Right
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants a right to install a window or portable air conditioner, and none requiring a lease to say whether you restrict them or setting a maximum indoor temperature. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. The state minimum housing standards (in towns without their own housing code) address heat, not cooling. If you restrict or require approval for window units, say so in the lease and state who is responsible for safe installation and any damage; a tenant with a disability may ask for a reasonable accommodation or modification, which fair housing law requires you to consider.

title: Plug-In Solar
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants a right to install a plug-in (balcony) solar panel or other solar device at a rental, and no statute voiding lease or covenant restrictions on solar. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not. A new law changes the utility side from January 1, 2027: a customer may use one plug-in solar system with an inverter output of up to 1,200 watts, certified by a nationally recognized testing laboratory and installed and used according to the state building code and the manufacturer's instructions, and the utility may not require approval, an interconnection review or agreement, fees or extra equipment for it. That law limits the utility, not you; the tenant still needs whatever permission your lease requires, and the utility is not liable for damage the system causes. If you allow plug-in solar, set conditions in writing (certified equipment, placement, removal at move-out, responsibility for damage); the state's consumer information on these systems warns that unlisted or improperly connected systems may affect homeowners or renters insurance. State zoning law discourages towns from unreasonably limiting solar, and solar access easements can be recorded, but neither governs leases.

title: No Recycling Notice Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to tell tenants where or how to recycle, or to provide recycling at a rental. Recycling is handled locally: a town may adopt bylaws governing the separation and collection of refuse, may require residents to use designated bags, containers or stickers, may fine violations, and may bill its solid waste fees, including recycling fees, to the owner of the property where the waste originates, with a lien on the property. If your lease makes the tenant pay those charges, say so. Under the state's minimum housing standards (which apply where the town has no housing code of its own), you may not let garbage build up in common areas because you failed to remove it or to provide enough receptacles, unless the tenant agreed in the lease to handle removal and you removed all garbage at the start of the tenancy. Describe the trash and recycling arrangements in your rules and check your town's bylaws. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Religious and Cultural Displays
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants a right to put religious or cultural items, such as a mezuzah, on a door frame or elsewhere at the unit, and none letting a landlord ban them. New Hampshire's fair housing law does make it unlawful to change the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental, or the facilities or services you provide, because of religion (among other protected classes), so a display rule must apply the same way to everyone and must not single out religious items; its exemptions include a rental in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units and rooms in your own home. In housing for older persons and independent living retirement communities covered by New Hampshire's senior citizens bill of rights, residents also have the right to exercise civil and religious liberties and to treat the decorating of their personal space as private. A neutral rule on what may be attached to doors or common areas, applied evenly, is the safer course. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: House Rules and Changing Them
bodyText: New Hampshire has no general statute on house rules. A rule binds a tenant as part of the lease, so attach your rules to the lease and say whether and how you may change them. What a rule breach lets you do depends on the property. You may end a tenancy of nonrestricted property for any reason with proper written notice. For restricted property you need a listed ground, such as the tenant's failure to comply with a material term of the lease, or other good cause; if other good cause is based on the tenant's or household's conduct, you must first give a written warning that the conduct would be grounds for eviction. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). No statute says when you may add or change rules during a tenancy, but the law presumes retaliation if you start an eviction, raise the rent or substantially alter the terms of the tenancy within 6 months after you learn of a tenant's code complaint, finish repairs on it, learn the tenant has sued you under the prohibited-practices law, or discover the tenant meeting or organizing with other tenants (unless the court finds the tenant acted mainly to prevent an eviction); the retaliation defense isn't available to a tenant who owes a week's rent or more. Get the tenant's written agreement to any significant change. In housing for older persons and independent living retirement communities covered by New Hampshire's senior citizens bill of rights, management must give each resident a copy of the rules, apply them uniformly, avoid unreasonable, arbitrary or capricious rules, give 30 days' written notice before changing a rule (except changes needed to protect health or safety), allow 10 days to correct a rule violation, and give 90 days' written notice before raising fees; a violation is an unfair or deceptive practice. In a condominium, everyone entitled to occupy a unit must follow the condominium's instruments, so give tenants the association's rules. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Indoor Smoking Law and Rentals
bodyText: New Hampshire's Indoor Smoking Act reaches rental housing only in limited ways. Public housing and subsidized housing are treated as publicly owned buildings, and any enclosed place where 4 or more people work for pay is a workplace. In those places smoking may be allowed only in effectively segregated, posted smoking-permitted areas that the person in charge designates, and is banned outright where it can't be effectively segregated; the person in charge may make the whole building non-smoking and must have a written smoking policy. Resident rooms in public housing are exempt. The Act doesn't name the common hallways of privately owned apartment buildings, so whether a hallway where building staff work counts as a workplace depends on the facts. "Smoking" under the Act includes electronic devices designed to produce the effect of smoking. In a private rental your lease controls: you may ban smoking for all tenants, but a tenant may let a qualifying therapeutic cannabis patient use cannabis by ingestion or vaporization even where the lease bans smoking. No New Hampshire statute addresses smoke drifting between units or a tenant's waiver of claims about it, so a waiver clause has no statutory support either way. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Snow and Ice Removal
bodyText: For tenancies entered into or renewed on or after July 1, 2027, New Hampshire's eviction statute lets you and the tenant agree who will clear snow and ice from, and keep safe access to, specific areas of the property; it can be you, the tenant, or a split. If you haven't agreed otherwise, the landlord of restricted property clears and keeps safe the on-site common areas used by tenants of more than one unit, such as driveways, walkways, stairs and entryways, and the tenants clear the walkways, stairs and entryways meant for their unit's exclusive use. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). For nonrestricted property the statute sets no default for shared areas, so allocate them in the lease. Areas owned, maintained or governed by a condominium, cooperative, homeowners' association or similar entity stay under that entity's documents. Tenancies entered into before July 1, 2027 and not renewed since aren't covered, and their lease controls. Separately, if your premises are maintained by a state-certified commercial salt applicator, you follow the state's published winter-maintenance best practices and you keep the required written records for 3 years, the law limits your liability for hazards caused solely by snow or ice, absent gross negligence or reckless disregard. Spell out snow duties in the lease.

title: Flags and Signs
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving tenants a right to display flags, political signs or banners at a rental, and none limiting a landlord's rules on them, so your lease and rules control. In a condominium, the unit owners' association may not prohibit a unit owner's outdoor display of the United States flag in a manner consistent with the United States flag code and the state flag law, though it may adopt reasonable rules on the flag's size and how it is displayed; the statute speaks of unit owners and doesn't mention tenants. The election law bars placing political advertising on private property without the owner's consent and bars removing political advertising from private property except by the owner, someone the owner authorizes, or a law enforcement officer removing improper advertising; it doesn't say how that applies between a landlord and a tenant, so state your sign rule in the lease. Any display rule must be applied evenly; New Hampshire's fair housing law bars altering rental terms or privileges because of a protected class. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Security Cameras and Video Doorbells
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute addresses tenant-installed security cameras or video doorbells, or your right to allow or bar them; your lease's alterations and common-area rules control. Two criminal laws apply to landlords and tenants alike. It is a crime to install or use, without the consent of the people entitled to privacy there, a device that observes, photographs or records images or sounds in a private place (which includes the inside of a person's home), or a device outside a private place that picks up images, location, movement or sounds from inside it that wouldn't ordinarily be audible, visible or comprehensible outside. And intercepting or recording a conversation without the consent of all parties is generally a crime, so devices that record audio are risky in shared hallways and entrances. Never aim a camera into another unit. If you allow tenant cameras or doorbells, require that they view only the tenant's own entrance or space, keep audio recording off, and be installed without damage. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Waterbeds
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on waterbeds or other liquid-filled furniture in rentals, so your lease may bar them or allow them on conditions such as your written consent, renter's insurance and payment for any damage. Any extra deposit you take for a waterbed counts toward the security deposit cap: every payment from the tenant above the monthly rent, for any purpose, is a security deposit, and the total may not exceed one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Association Documents and Tenants
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring a lease of a condominium or homeowners' association unit to disclose the association's obligations or to give the tenant the association's documents. The condominium act does bind your tenants: everyone entitled to occupy a condominium unit must comply with the act and with the condominium instruments (declaration, bylaws and rules), and the association can sue over noncompliance for money due, damages or an injunction, with the winning side recovering costs and attorney's fees. If the association has adopted the act's rent-collection provision, it can also direct your tenants to pay their rent to it when you fall more than 60 days behind on common charges (see "Condominium Rent Collection"). Give tenants the association's rules and require them in the lease to follow them. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Bed Bug History and Duties
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to disclose a unit's bed bug history to a prospective or current tenant, and no required treatment timeline notice. Bed bug duties do apply once there is a report: you must investigate a tenant's report (or a municipal health or housing authority's) within 7 days and take reasonable measures to remediate; you bear the reasonable cost of remediation unless the tenant was responsible, in which case you may bill the tenant in writing for remediating the tenant's own unit, offer a reasonable repayment agreement, and treat nonpayment 30 days after remediation as nonpayment of rent. In a court case over those costs you must prove the tenant was responsible, but the tenant is presumed responsible if there were no bed bug reports for the unit or the adjacent units above, below or beside it (or by earlier tenants of a single-family home) in the 6 months before and throughout the tenancy. Where your town has no housing code of its own, you may not let a unit be infested with bed bugs unless you run a periodic inspection and remediation program, and towns may adopt their own bed bug rules. Because past reports affect that presumption, keep records of every report and treatment. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Certificate of Occupancy Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to give a tenant, or attach to the lease, a certificate of occupancy or to disclose whether the unit has one. Whether a certificate of occupancy is needed for new construction, a conversion or a change of use is a building-code question for your local building official. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Defective Drywall Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to disclose defective or corrosive drywall to a tenant. If a wall defect makes the unit unsafe, the state's minimum housing standards (which apply where the town has no housing code of its own) still require you to repair conditions such as substantial holes in walls or ceilings and wiring that creates a danger of shock or fire. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Flood Disclosure for Leases
bodyText: New Hampshire requires no flood disclosure to a tenant. The flood notices in New Hampshire law apply to sales: a seller must give a buyer a written notice about flood risk and flood insurance before signing a purchase and sale contract, and for a one-to-four-family dwelling must disclose whether the property is in a federally designated flood hazard zone. Separately, an insurer issuing a residential tenant (renter's) policy that doesn't cover flood must tell the policyholder so at issue and renewal. If you know the unit is in a flood hazard zone or has flooded, telling the applicant in writing is good practice, and suggest renter's flood coverage. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Foreclosure Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring you to tell a prospective or current tenant that the property is in foreclosure or that a mortgage is in default. What the statutes do require when ownership changes: within 5 days of the deed, assignment or a receiver's qualification, a landlord holding a security deposit must turn it over to the new owner, assignee, foreclosure receiver or foreclosure-sale purchaser, and notify the tenant by registered or certified mail of who now holds it. A foreclosure-sale purchaser may recover possession only through written notice to quit and the court process (see "Tenants and Foreclosure"). The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Good-Cause Coverage Notice
bodyText: New Hampshire has a good-cause rule but no notice telling tenants whether it covers them. For restricted property you may end a tenancy only for a listed ground (such as nonpayment, substantial damage, a material lease breach, behavior affecting others' health or safety, other good cause, or the expiration of a lease of 12 months or more after 60 days' written notice of non-renewal), while nonrestricted property may be ended for any reason with proper written notice. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). No statute requires a lease or notice stating which category applies, but every eviction notice must state the specific reason. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Environmental Contamination Disclosures
bodyText: New Hampshire has no general duty to disclose environmental contamination to tenants, but four specific rules apply. Methamphetamine production: see "Methamphetamine Production Disclosure." Asbestos disposal sites: if the property includes an asbestos disposal site, you must tell anyone who uses or occupies it or is likely to disturb asbestos there, such as a tenant, about the presence of asbestos waste (including its location and depth of cover, to the extent known) and the need to comply with the asbestos law and any activity and use restrictions. Activity and use restrictions: where a state-approved cleanup relies on an activity and use restriction recorded for the property, the restriction must be incorporated, in full or by reference, into every lease, occupancy agreement or other instrument giving a right to use the property, so attach it or refer to it in the lease. Lead in drinking water: if the state tests the unit's water after a child's elevated blood lead result and finds lead above the federal action level, you must notify the tenant or prospective tenant and install and maintain a certified filter on the kitchen faucet until the source is removed and the water tests below that level. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Condominium Rent Collection
bodyText: If you rent out a condominium unit and fall behind on the common expenses the unit owners' association assessed, the association may be able to collect your tenant's rent. This remedy is available only if the association adopted it into its declaration or bylaws by a majority vote of those attending an annual meeting. After you are 60 days late, the association must first send you written notice by both first class and certified mail stating the exact amount it claims and its intent to collect from rent; you then have 30 days to pay, including collection costs, or prove you already paid. If you don't, the association may direct your tenant to pay it all or part of the rent (up to the amount claimed or the full rent, whichever is less) until what you owe, plus later charges, is paid; you may still go to court over the amount. You may not retaliate against a tenant who pays the association, the tenant isn't in default to the extent of those payments, and any lease clause waiving these rules is void. Everyone entitled to occupy a unit must also follow the condominium act and the condominium's declaration, bylaws and rules, and the association can sue over violations, with the winner recovering costs and attorney's fees. New Hampshire's statutes don't set association lease-approval fees, cap association rental restrictions or tenant-information demands, or address an association's power to approve leases. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Disclosing Lead Orders and Other Code Orders
bodyText: One New Hampshire rule requires disclosure of an outstanding order: if the state has issued an order of lead hazard reduction for the dwelling or unit, you must disclose the order in writing before you lease or rent it, and you must give an occupant who asks a copy of the order within 10 business days. Lead orders are also recorded at the registry of deeds and bind later owners, and a unit withdrawn from the rental market under an order may not be rented again until its lead hazards are reduced. No New Hampshire statute or rule requires you to disclose other code-inspection orders or condemnation to a prospective tenant. If a municipal official orders a building vacated as a clear and imminent danger, the official must tell the owner and all occupants, post a notice at each entrance (removing it is a misdemeanor) and mail written notice to the owner and known lessees; anyone who has received notice and fails to comply commits a misdemeanor, and displaced occupants may return once the danger is removed or the order is set aside. Never rent a unit that is under an order to vacate. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Landlord Insurance Mandate
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring residential landlords to carry liability insurance, and no state rental registration tied to insurance. Carrying liability coverage is still prudent, and your lease may require tenants to carry renter's insurance. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Lead Poisoning Prevention Law
bodyText: Beyond the federal lead disclosure and pamphlet for pre-1978 housing (see the Lead-Based Paint Disclosure clause), New Hampshire's lead poisoning law sets these rules for rental owners. You may not apply paint containing more than 0.06 percent lead in a dwelling. Owners of pre-1978 rental housing must take reasonable care to prevent exposure to, and the creation of, lead hazards; the mere presence of lead paint is not negligence or a breach of the warranty of habitability by itself, and a tenant's disturbance of lead-painted surfaces is admissible evidence. You may not evict because a child in the household has tested positive for lead; an eviction you start within 6 months after notice of a child's elevated blood lead level (from the state, the child's doctor, or a parent who gives you a copy of the test before the eviction notice expires) is presumed to be for that reason, and if the court agrees it will deny the eviction and award damages. A tenant's refusal to let you inspect for lead hazards is good cause for eviction if you give at least 48 hours' prior written notice and inspect at a reasonable time. If the state orders lead hazard reduction, the order sets a deadline (for an occupied unit no more than 90 days unless extended), is recorded and binds later owners, and no child or pregnant woman may be present during work that releases lead. You may temporarily relocate the family to a safe, sanitary unit without interior lead hazards at no higher rent to them, paying reasonable moving costs; if the work will take more than 30 days and isn't interim controls or encapsulation, you may end the tenancy on 30 days' notice only if you meet the statute's conditions, including offering a comparable unit at comparable rent, returning the deposit and prepaid rent before the family leaves, and agreeing in writing to let them move back. Refusing a suitable temporary relocation is grounds for eviction. A tenant with a written lease who must relocate may end the lease by written notice within 7 days of moving. A unit withdrawn from the rental market under an order may not be rented again until its hazards are reduced; re-renting costs $1,000 per family plus fees and other penalties. Pre-1978 buildings converted to rental use after July 1, 2024 need a lead-safety certification first (see "Lead-Safe Certification for Converted Units"), and state notice duties are in "State Lead Notices."

title: Lead-Safe Certification for Converted Units
bodyText: After July 1, 2024, a rental unit created in a building erected before January 1, 1978, by converting space from a use other than residential rental housing, needs a certification of lead safety under New Hampshire's lead poisoning law before it may be used as a residential rental. The state's lead rules provide for a "certificate of lead safe" issued by a licensed risk assessor after a risk assessment or clearance inspection finds no lead-based paint or lead exposure hazards (paint, dust and soil as applicable); it stays in effect as long as no lead exposure hazards are present, encapsulants and enclosures stay intact and in-place management records are kept, and one based on interim controls lasts one year. The state reviews certificates, may inspect to validate them, and may invalidate one if hazards remain. Where the state approves interim controls under a lead order, you must submit a certificate of compliance from a licensed risk assessor every year. No New Hampshire rule requires attaching a certificate to the lease, but keep a copy to show tenants and inspectors.

title: State Lead Notices
bodyText: New Hampshire has no state lead pamphlet, form or certificate you must give every tenant at lease signing or renewal; the general pre-signing lead disclosure is the federal one. State notices apply in these situations. If the state has issued an order of lead hazard reduction for the property, disclose the order in writing before you lease or rent, and give an occupant who asks a copy of the order within 10 business days. Before lead hazard reduction work, give every affected occupant written notice at least 5 days ahead with the scheduled dates and hours, the work sites, the alternative entrance or exit, and a copy of the occupant protection plan. Before relocated or new occupants move back in after the work, give them the known information and records about lead-based substances and hazards, written notice of any remaining hazards and planned work, and, where an order was issued, copies of the risk assessment, work scope and certificate of lead safe for their unit. If the state finds lead in a unit's drinking water above the federal action level after a child's test, notify the tenant or prospective tenant and install a certified faucet filter. The state itself sends its inspection findings and any order to the occupants. Treat a renewal of a lease for a unit under an order as a new lease and disclose the order again.

title: Methamphetamine Production Disclosure
bodyText: If methamphetamine has been produced on a property, then from that time until the Department of Environmental Services (or a licensed environmental or hazardous substances removal specialist) determines the property meets the state's remediation cleanup standards, you must, before signing a lease or rental agreement, disclose in writing to the lessee or occupant whether, to your knowledge, methamphetamine production has occurred on the property, and if it has, include a statement informing them. The determination that a property meets cleanup standards is public information available from the department. New Hampshire's statutes don't require an owner to report a suspected meth lab to police, don't bar occupancy of a contaminated unit, and set no separate penalty for failing to disclose. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Military or Airport Zone Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to disclose that a rental is near a military installation or airport, or in a noise or accident-potential zone. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Mold Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to disclose mold to a tenant or prospective tenant, and no indoor mold standard for rentals. Anyone who performs residential mold assessment (inspection, sampling or a remediation protocol) for pay must hold a national third-party mold assessment certification. Where your town has no housing code of its own, the state's minimum housing standards bar letting the roof or walls leak consistently or leaving defective plumbing, conditions that cause mold, and towns may adopt their own housing codes. Fix moisture problems promptly and document what you did. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Ordnance or Demolition Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to tell a prospective tenant about a former military ordnance site nearby or a demolition permit you have applied for. Shared meters are handled differently: where a building is served by a master electric meter, the utility's tariff must bar you from passing the electricity on to tenants except by including it in a fixed rent, so usage-based billing of a shared electric meter isn't allowed (see "Submetering and Utility Billing"); and before signing you must disclose in writing any tenant-paid metered utility service that, to your knowledge, carries energy-efficiency or renewable-energy tariff charges. For a shared water or gas meter, state in the lease exactly how charges are divided. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Owner and Manager Identity
bodyText: New Hampshire doesn't require you to give tenants your name and address, or a manager's, at the start of a tenancy, and no statute bars an eviction because you didn't. Related duties: if you own restricted property, you must file with the town or city clerk, within 30 days of becoming the owner, the name, address and telephone number of a person in New Hampshire authorized to accept legal papers for the property (it may be you); if an out-of-state owner hasn't filed and doesn't appear in a case, the law presumes service on that owner was adequate. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). The security deposit receipt must say where the deposit is held, and on request you must give the tenant the name of the bank or credit union, the account number, the amount on deposit and the interest rate. If you sell or transfer the property, tell the tenant by registered or certified mail the name and address of whoever then holds the deposit. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. Put your name (or your manager's) and an address for notices in the lease. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Pesticide Application Notices
bodyText: New Hampshire's pesticide rules require notice when a commercial applicator treats turf (lawns and similar areas) at a multifamily dwelling. The applicator must give written notice at least 72 hours, but no more than 2 weeks, before the application to the management, owners or official spokesperson; must give its written notice before treatment, at least annually, to the people living at the property when the client doesn't live there; and must either post signs at common entryways (such as main entrances, mailboxes, road intersections and the treated area) or give prior written notice to all inhabitants. The written notice names the contact person and firm, the pesticides by common chemical name, the form and method of application, the schedule, the area treated, and the right to request advance notice of each application date; signs stay up at least 48 hours. No statute requires advance notice to tenants of indoor pest treatment, but a tenant must follow your or the pest control operator's reasonable written preparation instructions only if they were given to an adult in the household at least 72 hours before remediation, and you need the tenant's consent to enter except for emergency repairs (including evaluating or treating an infestation within 72 hours after you first learn of it) or under a court order. When you hire an applicator, confirm these notices go out.

title: No Well Test Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to test a private well serving a rental or to give tenants well test results. The water-supply disclosures in New Hampshire law apply to sales: a seller must tell the buyer about the private water supply (its type, location, malfunctions and the date and any problems of the most recent test) and give the state's radon, arsenic, lead, PFAS and flood notice. For rentals, where your town has no housing code of its own, the minimum housing standards bar an inadequate water supply, and if the state tests a unit's water after a child's elevated blood lead level and finds lead above the federal action level, you must notify the tenant or prospective tenant and install and maintain a certified kitchen-faucet filter. Testing well water before each tenancy and sharing the results is good practice. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Radon Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire requires no radon disclosure to tenants and no radon testing of rentals, and its radon notice doesn't depend on floor level. The state's radon notice (with arsenic, lead, PFAS and flood) is given by a seller to a buyer before a purchase and sale contract. The state health department investigates indoor air quality complaints and, on request, inspects buildings and dwellings for radon and recommends how to abate it; anyone who designs or installs an airborne radon mitigation system must hold a current national certification. No New Hampshire statute or rule found requires radon-resistant construction, though the building codes the state adopts by reference weren't searched. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Required Disclosures at a Glance
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide lease form, first-page summary or notice of rent-law coverage that every lease must carry. What it does require, when it applies: a signed security deposit receipt stating the amount and where it is held, with notice that the tenant may list conditions needing repair within 5 days of occupancy (the 5-day notice is required even when no receipt is needed because the tenant paid by check); written disclosure of any rental application or renewal fee and of any criminal background or credit check requirement before you collect the fee; written disclosure before signing of any tenant-paid utility service carrying energy-efficiency or renewable-energy tariff charges; written disclosure before signing of known methamphetamine production that hasn't been certified as cleaned up; written disclosure of any state order of lead hazard reduction before leasing; disclosure to a tenant of an asbestos disposal site on the property; incorporation of any recorded environmental activity and use restriction into the lease; and a copy of the signed lease delivered to the tenant within 30 days after all parties sign. Senior housing covered by the senior citizens bill of rights must also give each resident a copy of that bill of rights at lease signing and each renewal, and federal lead disclosure applies to pre-1978 housing. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older.

title: Code Variances and Tenants
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to give tenants, or attach to the lease, a housing or health code variance in effect for the property. One related notice applies to lead work: before anyone (including an owner) asks the state for a variance from the lead poisoning law or rules, they must give all residents and others affected a copy of the request and tell them of their right to contact the department with questions or concerns. Fire code orders for hazardous conditions in buildings other than single-family homes and two-unit dwellings must be served on the tenant or occupant as well as the owner, and fire chiefs must explain the fire code variance process when reviewing plans and issuing violation notices. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Sex Offender Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire doesn't require you to tell tenants or applicants about registered sex offenders living nearby, or require a lease statement about the registry. The state keeps a public list of registered offenders whose offenses involved a child or who must register for more than one offense, available on the Department of Safety's website (searchable by zip code or radius) and from local police; police may also notify the community. You may point tenants to that public list. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Lease Font or Placement Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire sets no font size, type size or first-page placement for a residential lease or any lease disclosure, and has no single-family occupancy notice. The only type-size rules in its landlord-tenant statutes are for other documents: the property abandonment notice form is deemed sufficient if printed in at least 12-point type, and the court's notice accompanying an eviction writ must be in at least 12-point type. Use a readable type size anyway. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Shoreline Access Disclosure
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring a lease of shoreline property to include a notice about public access along the shore. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Source-of-Income Protection
bodyText: New Hampshire's fair housing law doesn't list source of income, or receipt of a housing voucher or other rental assistance, as a protected class. State law therefore doesn't require you to accept Housing Choice Vouchers or other assistance, to sign a program's lease addendum, or to agree to its inspection, and has no lease-statement rule on the subject. The protected classes are age, sex, gender identity, race, religion, color, marital status, familial status, physical or mental disability and national origin, and the law also declares a right to housing without discrimination based on sexual orientation. Apply any income or assistance policy the same way to every applicant. Federally assisted properties and local ordinances may carry their own rules, which this library doesn't cover. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Fire Sprinklers
bodyText: New Hampshire requires no lease disclosure about whether a rental has fire sprinklers. The state fire code and its rules may not require automatic fire suppression or sprinkler systems in detached one- or two-family dwellings used only as residences, and cities and towns may not adopt rules more stringent than the state fire code on residential sprinkler systems. Other buildings follow the sprinkler provisions of the state fire code and building code (see "Which Fire Code Applies"); whether an existing apartment building must be retrofitted depends on those codes, which this library doesn't reproduce, so ask your local fire chief. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Deaths and Crimes at the Property
bodyText: New Hampshire's statute on a property's history applies to sales: an owner or agent need not tell a buyer that the property was the site of a homicide, other felony or suicide unless the buyer asks and the owner or agent knows, and disclosing on request creates no liability. No statute addresses what you must tell a prospective tenant about deaths, crimes or similar events at a rental. Don't misrepresent the property's history if an applicant asks; New Hampshire's consumer protection act bars unfair or deceptive acts in trade, which includes dealings in real property. Evicting a tenant solely because the tenant has, or is regarded as having, AIDS is a civil rights violation. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Tenant Rights Statements
bodyText: New Hampshire has no state statement of tenant rights that every landlord must give tenants, and no rule barring a case until one is given. The exception is senior housing covered by New Hampshire's senior citizens bill of rights (housing for older persons that provides on-site personal assistance or supportive services beyond service coordination, and independent living retirement communities that furnish housing and services to people 55 or older under contract; condominiums, manufactured housing parks, continuing care retirement communities and licensed health facilities are excluded): management must give each resident a copy of the senior citizens bill of rights at initial lease signing and at each renewal, and must post the bill of rights, its complaint procedure (with the name, address and phone number of the person who receives complaints), and a notice that violations are unfair or deceptive practices that residents may report to the Attorney General's consumer protection and antitrust bureau. A violation is an unfair or deceptive act under the consumer protection act. In an eviction, the court's own notice to the tenant goes with the writ; you don't prepare it. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Rent-Cap or Coverage Notice
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide rent cap and no law requiring a lease notice about rent limits, just-cause coverage or a tenant's right to buy. Restricted property may be ended only for listed grounds (see "No Good-Cause Coverage Notice"), and a restricted-property tenant's refusal of a rent increase is good cause only if you gave written notice of the amount and effective date at least 30 days before the increase took effect. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). Tenants get purchase rights in one landlord situation: converting a rental building or complex of more than 10 units to condominium, cooperative or similar ownership, where the conversion law requires notices, gives tenants an exclusive right to buy their unit for 60 days and limits evictions and rent increases (see "Converting to Condominiums"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Truth-in-Renting Notice
bodyText: New Hampshire has no truth-in-renting law: no statute requires your lease to carry a notice that it must comply with state law, a warning about unenforceable clauses, or a state statement of landlord and tenant rights. Unenforceable clauses are still a risk: a lease provision by which a tenant waives rights under New Hampshire's eviction statute is void, as is a waiver of the security deposit rights. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Accessory Dwelling Units
bodyText: Every New Hampshire municipality with zoning must allow one accessory dwelling unit (ADU), attached or detached, as a matter of right in all districts that allow single-family homes, without extra lot-size, setback, frontage, design or similar requirements beyond those for a single-family home; if the zoning ordinance says nothing about ADUs, one is a permitted use. State law doesn't restrict renting an ADU, and a municipality may not require a family relationship between the occupants of the ADU and the main home, limit an ADU to one bedroom, or deny it a separate electrical panel and service. A municipality may, however, require the owner to live in one of the two units (without dictating which) and to show it is the owner's principal residence, may cap the ADU's living space (not below 750 square feet; 950 unless the town allows more), may require up to one extra parking space if it requires parking for the main home, and may bar ADUs with attached townhouses or on rented land; selling the ADU separately as a condominium is barred unless the municipality allows it. Structures existing on or before July 1, 2025, such as detached garages, may be converted to ADUs even if they don't meet current setback or lot-coverage rules, though the town may require you to show the structure is a protected preexisting nonconforming structure or had an earlier zoning approval or exemption. New Hampshire has no statute limiting the rental of homes in single-family zones beyond this optional owner-occupancy rule. Check your town's ordinance before renting an ADU or the main house; if the town requires owner occupancy, moving out of both units could put the property out of compliance.

title: Alarm Tampering Charges
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute sets or limits a fee for removing, disconnecting or tampering with a smoke or carbon monoxide alarm. A tenant or a tenant's guest who destroys, disconnects or otherwise disables a smoke detector in a rental dwelling, or tries to, is guilty of a misdemeanor, and you as owner remain responsible for keeping the smoke and carbon monoxide devices in suitable condition. Your lease may make the tenant pay the reasonable cost of repairing or replacing a device the tenant disabled; tie the charge to your actual cost rather than a flat penalty. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Asbestos in Rentals
bodyText: New Hampshire has no asbestos disclosure for ordinary leases, but its asbestos management law reaches rentals in two ways. The Department of Environmental Services identifies and orders abatement of regulated asbestos-containing material in rental dwellings that exceeds the state's exposure standards. And if the property includes an asbestos disposal site, you must tell anyone who uses or occupies it or is likely to disturb asbestos there, such as a tenant, about the asbestos waste (its location and depth of cover, to the extent known) and the need to comply with the asbestos law and any activity and use restrictions. The state licenses asbestos abatement contractors; use one for any work that may disturb asbestos. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Balcony Inspection Mandate
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring periodic engineering inspections of balconies, decks, porches or exterior stairs at rentals. Where your town has no housing code of its own, the minimum housing standards bar porches, stairs or railings that aren't structurally sound. State fire officials and local fire chiefs may inspect buildings other than single-family homes and two-unit dwellings and order hazardous conditions fixed, and a copy of the order is served on the tenant or occupant. Inspect elevated structures yourself regularly. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Confession-of-Judgment Clauses
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute authorizes or specifically bans a confession-of-judgment (cognovit or warrant-of-attorney) clause in a residential lease. In an eviction case, a tenant may confess judgment in court, and the court may still delay the writ of possession; in a nonpayment case the parties may instead file an agreement that the writ won't issue if the tenant follows a payment schedule (which waives the tenant's appeal). But a lease provision by which a tenant gives up rights under New Hampshire's eviction statute, such as written notice and a court hearing, is void, so don't put a confession-of-judgment clause in the lease. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Consumer Protection Act
bodyText: New Hampshire's Consumer Protection Act makes unfair or deceptive acts or practices in trade or commerce unlawful, and trade and commerce include dealings in real property, so it can reach how you advertise and manage rentals. Its list of examples doesn't mention leases, blank spaces at signing or copies at signing (a separate statute requires you to deliver a copy of a signed written lease within 30 days). Several landlord-tenant laws plug into the Act: violating the prohibited-practices statute (such as lockouts, utility shutoffs or entry without consent) triggers the Act's private remedies, with exceptions; failing to give a proper deposit receipt, to hold deposits in trust as required, or to transfer them on sale is deemed a violation of the Act; and so is violating the senior citizens bill of rights. A person injured by a violation recovers actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, two to three times that amount for a willful or knowing violation, plus costs and attorney's fees, and any attempted waiver of those damages is void. The Act doesn't cover transactions entered into more than 3 years before the person knew or should have known of the conduct.

title: Domestic Violence Confidentiality
bodyText: Written verification a tenant or household member gives you to show they are a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking (for New Hampshire's eviction protection or early lease termination), including the fact that the person is a victim, must be kept in strict confidence. You may disclose it only if the victim requests or consents in writing, if it is relevant and reasonably necessary in an eviction proceeding or a hearing on termination of housing assistance, or if other law requires it. Keep these documents separate from the general tenant file and limit who can see them. Victims may also enroll in the Attorney General's address confidentiality program, which gives them a designated substitute address that state and local agencies must accept; that rule binds agencies, but honor a participant's request to use the designated address for mail.

title: Calls for Police or Emergency Help
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute specifically protects a tenant's right to call police or emergency services or bars lease penalties or evictions based on such calls. Related protections apply: you may not end a restricted-property tenancy solely because a tenant or household member was a victim of domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking, where the victim gives written verification (a report to a law enforcement agency is one form); and a tenant's good-faith report of a code violation to an inspection or enforcement authority triggers the retaliation defense and presumption. Here, "restricted property" (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property) and "nonrestricted property" (a single-family house whose owner owns no more than three single-family houses; a unit in an owner-occupied building of four or fewer units; a single-family house a bank or other mortgagee took through foreclosure). Don't treat a call for help as a lease violation. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Eviction Penalty Statute
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute specifically voids a lease clause that imposes a penalty because you served an eviction notice or filed an eviction case. The statutes do limit what an eviction can cost the tenant: in a nonpayment case the tenant can have the case dismissed by paying, before the hearing, all rent owed, other lawful charges in the lease, $15 in liquidated damages and your filing and service costs (no more than 3 times in 12 months); any money judgment in the eviction case is capped at $1,500, with larger amounts left to a separate case; and a lease provision waiving the tenant's rights under the eviction statute is void. Charge only actual, lawful costs, not a penalty for using the court process. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Liability Disclaimers in Leases
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute specifically voids a lease clause excusing you from liability for your own negligence or requiring the tenant to indemnify you. Specific waivers are void by statute: of a tenant's rights under the eviction statute, of security deposit rights, of a condominium tenant's protections when paying rent to the association, of condominium-conversion rights, and of damages under the Consumer Protection Act. Lease language also doesn't shield you from the statutory damages for lockouts, utility shutoffs and other prohibited practices. Whether a court enforces a broad exculpatory clause is case law this library hasn't reviewed; prefer clauses that don't disclaim your own negligence. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Fair Housing Basics
bodyText: New Hampshire's fair housing law makes it unlawful, because of age, sex, gender identity, race, religion, color, marital status, familial status (children under 18 living with a parent or custodian), physical or mental disability or national origin, to refuse to rent or negotiate, to change the terms, conditions or privileges of a rental or its facilities or services, or to falsely say a unit isn't available for inspection or rent. Its advertising ban covers notices, statements, ads and signs indicating a preference based on race, color, religion, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, sexual orientation or national origin, and the law separately declares a right to housing without discrimination based on sexual orientation. It is also a violation to coerce, intimidate, threaten or interfere with anyone exercising these rights, to evict a tenant solely because the tenant has or is regarded as having AIDS, or to put a race, color, religion or national origin restriction in a lease or deed (such provisions are void). Disability rules on accommodations and modifications are in "Disability Accommodations and Modifications." Exemptions: a building of four or fewer units where you live in one (this exemption covers the advertising ban under state law, but not the listing provision); renting rooms in your own home; reasonable occupancy limits; religious organizations' noncommercial housing; conduct toward a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance; and familial status in qualifying housing for older persons. Federal fair housing law may apply where the state exemptions do, and isn't covered here. A person may file with the Commission for Human Rights and, after 180 days (or sooner with its consent) and within 3 years, sue in superior court, where either side may have a jury; after a probable-cause finding the landlord may remove the case to superior court. The state constitution's equality guarantee binds the state, not private landlords, and no statute makes a landlord's sexual harassment of a tenant a separate crime.

title: Foreign Principal Leasing Ban
bodyText: Since June 27, 2025, New Hampshire law bars a "foreign principal" from acquiring any ownership or controlling interest in real property in the state, and from leasing or otherwise contracting to occupy or control any real property, or letting another foreign principal or agent do so. A foreign principal is the government or any government official of China, Russia, Iran, Syria or North Korea (including their agencies and ruling parties); a company or other entity organized under their laws or with its principal place of business there; or an individual who is an employee or agent of one of those countries. There is no exception for short leases. The law puts responsibility for compliance solely on the foreign principal and says real estate and closing agents have no duty to screen; acquiring property in violation is a felony, and the state may seek forfeiture. The restriction doesn't reach other noncitizens, and New Hampshire law lets an alien resident take, hold and convey real estate like a citizen. Don't knowingly lease to a foreign principal.

title: Passing Government Fines to Tenants
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute bars, or specifically allows, passing a government fine (such as a code or ordinance fine imposed on you) on to a tenant. Your lease may make the tenant pay fines that result from the tenant's own violations, as the association-compliance clause does for association fines, but a lease charge for a fine caused by a condition you are responsible for (for example a minimum-housing-standards violation) has no statutory basis, and a lease can't make a tenant waive rights under the eviction statute. Town solid waste and recycling fees may be billed to the property owner, so say in the lease if the tenant reimburses them. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Immigration Status
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute bars or requires asking rental applicants about immigration or citizenship status, protects tenants from immigration-related threats, or makes it unlawful to rent to someone who is unlawfully present. New Hampshire's fair housing law does bar discrimination because of national origin in renting, setting terms and advertising, so apply any identity or status verification the same way to every applicant. Federal law isn't covered here. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Jury Trial Waivers
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute addresses a lease clause waiving the right to a jury trial. The state constitution guarantees a jury trial in controversies concerning property and suits between persons, except where another practice is and has been customary and except where the value in controversy is $1,500 or less and no title to real estate is involved. Eviction (possessory) cases are brought in the district court; whether a jury right applies there, and whether a lease jury waiver is enforceable, are questions of case law this library hasn't reviewed, so a jury waiver clause adds little. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Key-Control Mandate
bodyText: New Hampshire doesn't require apartment owners, at any size, to adopt a key-control policy, keep a key log or run background checks on employees who can enter units. A condominium's bylaws may require employees of the managing agent or association to pass a background check before employment, at the agent's or association's cost. A written key-control practice (logged keys, restricted master keys, rekeying between tenants) is still sensible, and remember that entering a unit without the tenant's consent is allowed only for emergency repairs or under a court order. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Penalty for Using Void Terms
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute penalizing a landlord for knowingly putting a prohibited term in a residential lease; prohibited terms are simply void (waivers of rights under the eviction statute, of security deposit rights, of condominium rent-collection and condominium-conversion protections, and of Consumer Protection Act damages). One exception: inserting into a written instrument relating to real property a provision that restricts its conveyance, occupancy or lease based on race, color, religion or national origin, or honoring such a provision, is itself a civil rights violation. Acting on a void clause (for example, locking out a tenant or keeping a deposit contrary to the statute) carries the remedies for that conduct. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Lease Form and Copies
bodyText: New Hampshire has no list of terms every residential lease must contain and doesn't require a written lease: every tenancy is at will, with rent payable on demand, unless a different agreement is shown. If you use a written lease, you must deliver a copy to the tenant within 30 days after all parties sign it (failing to do so is a violation), and a lease for more than 7 years binds third parties only if it, or a notice of lease, is acknowledged and recorded. Specific content applies when relevant: the security deposit receipt and 5-day condition notice, application and renewal fee disclosures, utility tariff, methamphetamine, lead-order and asbestos disposal site disclosures, recorded activity and use restrictions, and at least one non-electronic way to pay (see "Required Disclosures at a Glance"). Put every fee and rule you intend to enforce in the lease, and give the tenant a signed copy at signing.

title: No Plain-Language Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring residential leases to be written in plain language or meet a readability standard. Write the lease clearly anyway: unclear terms invite disputes, and a material lease term you rely on to end a restricted-property tenancy should be one the tenant can understand. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Pools at Rental Properties
bodyText: A pool, spa or similar facility at an apartment complex or condominium complex is regulated by New Hampshire's public bathing rules unless it serves 3 or fewer living units and is used only by their residents and guests. A covered pool's construction and design need prior approval from the Department of Environmental Services, a pool operated for residents or members generally must be registered with the department, the department may sample the water at the owner's cost, and its rules set safety and water-quality standards this library doesn't reproduce. A pool serving 3 or fewer units (for example, at a single-family rental) is outside these rules; local building codes may still require barriers. New Hampshire has no lease notice requirement for pools. Check with the department before opening a pool to tenants.

title: Terms a Lease Cannot Contain
bodyText: New Hampshire has no single list of banned lease terms; the bans are spread across several statutes. A lease may not: make the tenant waive rights under the eviction statute (such as the grounds and notice for ending a tenancy, the right to stop a nonpayment case by paying, and the retaliation and habitability defenses); waive security deposit rights, or take a deposit above one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, for a covered landlord; require payment solely by electronic funds transfer; waive a condominium tenant's protections when paying rent to the association or a tenant's condominium-conversion rights; waive damages under the Consumer Protection Act; or restrict occupancy or leasing based on race, color, religion or national origin. Lease language also can't authorize lockouts, utility shutoffs, seizing belongings, entry without consent other than for emergency repairs or with a court order, or disposing of a vacating tenant's belongings within 7 days or charging for their storage; and a smoking ban can't stop a tenant from letting a qualifying therapeutic cannabis patient use cannabis by ingestion or vaporization. Offending provisions are void individually, not the whole lease. New Hampshire has no statute specifically on confession-of-judgment, exculpatory or indemnity clauses, home-warranty charges or repair fees (confession-of-judgment and exculpatory clauses have separate rows), and no money penalty for using a void term, though acting on one triggers the remedies for that conduct. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older.

title: Questions About Protected Traits
bodyText: New Hampshire's fair housing law has no separate ban on asking applicants about, or keeping records of, protected characteristics. But it bars making or publishing any statement, notice or ad about a rental that indicates a preference, limitation or discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, marital status, familial status, disability, sexual orientation or national origin, and asking about those traits can be evidence of discrimination. Inquiry into or use of an arrest record is permitted when another state or federal law authorizes it. Under the criminal-record annulment law, a person may be asked about criminal history only in terms such as "Have you ever been arrested for or convicted of a crime that has not been annulled by a court?" in applications for employment, licenses or other civil rights or privileges; the law doesn't say whether a rental application is covered, so use that wording. Ask only what you need to screen. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Sex Offender Residency Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide law restricting where registered sex offenders may live, requiring you to check the registry, or making it a crime to rent to two registered offenders who live together. Registered offenders must report their residence addresses to law enforcement, and the state publishes a public list of certain offenders. Local ordinances weren't searched. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: New Hampshire's Money Limits at a Glance
bodyText: New Hampshire's money limits for residential rentals: Security deposit: no more than one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, counting every payment above the monthly rent, with interest if you hold it a year or more, and double the deposit plus interest if you violate the return or interest rules. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. Application and renewal fees: no cap, but you must disclose the fee first and, if you don't rent to the applicant, refund everything beyond actual documented screening and reasonable administrative costs within 30 days. Late fees, returned-payment fees and rent: no statutory cap or rent control. Stopping a nonpayment eviction: the tenant pays all rent owed, other lawful lease charges, $15 in liquidated damages and your filing and service costs (no more than 3 times in 12 months). Money judgment in an eviction case: limited to $1,500, with more recoverable in a separate case. Statutory damages: under the Consumer Protection Act, actual damages or $1,000, whichever is greater, up to triple for willful violations, plus fees, which apply to most prohibited practices; at least $3,000 for an unlawful lockout where you have re-rented the unit; and actual damages or $1,000 for an unauthorized occupant petition in your favor (or against you if not brought in good faith).

title: No Radiator Cover Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring radiator covers, on request or otherwise, and no lease rider about them. Where your town has no housing code of its own, the minimum housing standards require heating facilities that are properly installed, safely maintained and in good working condition. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Tenant Information and Privacy
bodyText: New Hampshire has no general statute barring a landlord from sharing tenant information. Specific rules apply: domestic violence, sexual assault or stalking verification (and the fact that someone is a victim) must be kept in strict confidence; if you keep tenants' names with Social Security numbers, driver's license or other government ID numbers, or financial account numbers with access codes in electronic form and that data is breached, you must assess the risk and, if misuse has occurred or is reasonably likely (or can't be ruled out), notify the affected people and the Attorney General; and the state privacy law applies to businesses that, in a year, control or process the personal data of at least 35,000 consumers (or 10,000 if more than 25 percent of gross revenue comes from selling personal data). Share tenant information only with the tenant's written consent or where needed for the tenancy or required by law. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Tenant Organizing
bodyText: It is a defense to an eviction that you brought it in retaliation for a tenant's meeting or gathering with other tenants for any lawful purpose, and the law presumes retaliation if you start an eviction, raise the rent or substantially change the terms of the tenancy within 6 months after discovering that activity (unless the court finds the tenant organized mainly to prevent an eviction). The defense isn't available to a tenant who owes a week's rent or more. In senior housing covered by New Hampshire's senior citizens bill of rights (housing for older persons that provides on-site personal assistance or supportive services beyond service coordination, and independent living retirement communities that furnish housing and services to people 55 or older under contract; condominiums, manufactured housing parks, continuing care retirement communities and licensed health facilities are excluded), residents also have the right to organize and meet, to engage in concerted activities, and to be free from retaliation for complaining or joining a tenant association. Don't restrict lawful tenant meetings or penalize tenants for organizing.

title: Tenant Screening Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire regulates tenant screening in a few specific ways. Before collecting any rental application or renewal fee, disclose in writing the fee and any requirement for a satisfactory criminal background and credit check; if you don't rent to that applicant, return everything beyond the actual documented check costs and reasonable administrative costs within 30 days. You aren't required to run checks, and you may rent to someone who doesn't pass. A no-fault termination at the end of a lease of 12 months or more (or a shorter lease renewed for a total of 12 months or more) isn't an eviction for rental applications and screening reports, though you may still make other due-diligence inquiries. Under the annulment law an annulled arrest or conviction is treated as if it never happened, and applications for employment, licenses or other civil rights or privileges may ask about a criminal record only in terms such as "Have you ever been arrested for or convicted of a crime that has not been annulled by a court?"; word criminal-history questions that way. Fair housing law applies to screening, though it doesn't protect a person convicted of illegally manufacturing or distributing a controlled substance, and allows arrest-record inquiries only where other law authorizes them.
