New Hampshire has no conditional-offer rule, look-back period, minimum-income limit, or negligence shield for renting to people with records. Federal credit-reporting rules aren't covered here.

title: Unconscionable Lease Terms
bodyText: New Hampshire's unconscionability statutes are in its Uniform Commercial Code and cover contracts for the sale of goods and leases of goods, letting a court refuse to enforce an unconscionable contract or clause, enforce the rest without it, or limit it. No statute applies unconscionability to residential leases of real property, and no statute declares any lease clause immune from it. Whether a court will refuse an unconscionable residential lease term is case law this library hasn't reviewed; specific statutory bans are in "Terms a Lease Cannot Contain." New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Veteran Landlord Incentive
bodyText: New Hampshire has no program or tax credit that pays landlords for renting to veterans, and veteran status isn't a protected class in its fair housing law. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Water Heater Temperature Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring you to set a water heater to a maximum temperature before a new tenant moves in. Where your town has no housing code of its own, the minimum housing standards require that any equipment available to heat water operate properly. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Window Guard Requirement
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule requiring window guards or window stops in rentals where children live, and no window-guard lease notice. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Utility Allowances and Overage Charges
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute governs a utility allowance (you pay a utility up to a monthly amount and the tenant reimburses the excess) for an ordinary residential rental (New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law, utility tariffs and local ordinances were not). For water, sewer or similar services a lease may set one up as a contract term, and an overage the lease makes the tenant owe is a charge you may deduct from a security deposit if unpaid. Electricity is different: under the state's utility rules, electricity delivered through a master meter generally may be passed on to tenants only by including it in a fixed rent, and where individual metering is required the utility meters and bills each unit, so don't bill tenants for metered electric use. Gas master-meter systems need state approval. Whatever you agree, you may not cut off or interrupt a utility the tenant receives, and if you fail to pay a utility you agreed to provide, a tenant who pays it to keep service on can't be evicted for the rent used that way.

title: Who May Represent an LLC or Corporation Landlord in Eviction Court
bodyText: If your rental is owned by a limited liability company, corporation or partnership with 5 or fewer members, a member or employee of good character who isn't a lawyer may represent it in the circuit court in eviction and other landlord-tenant matters under New Hampshire's eviction statute, but only with the entity's written authorization, and a new written authorization is needed for each appearance. Larger entities need a lawyer. The court's rules add their own conditions for any non-lawyer representative: before appearing, the representative must file a document authorizing them to appear in that case and a written statement disclosing past criminal convictions (other than annulled ones), past findings that they violated court orders or conduct rules, and prior cases in which they represented others.

title: Children in the Household
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute requires a lease to address occupancy by children. Familial status (one or more children under 18 living with a parent or legal custodian, or with the custodian's designee who has written permission) is protected under the state fair housing law, so you may not refuse to rent, or set different terms, because a household includes children. Reasonable local, state or federal limits on the maximum number of occupants still apply (see "Occupancy Limits"), and housing for older persons that meets the law's definition is exempt from the familial-status rules. A unit in an owner-occupied building with housing for no more than 4 families, and rooms in a private home where the owner or a family member lives, are exempt from the general ban on discrimination in rentals, though not from the disability rules (see "Fair Housing Basics"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Sprinkler Retrofit Duty
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute requires a residential landlord to install or retrofit fire sprinklers in an existing rental. The state fire code and its rules may not require automatic fire suppression or sprinkler systems in detached one- or two-family dwellings used only as residences, the smoke-alarm rules may not require a sprinkler system in a one- or two-family dwelling unit that otherwise meets them, and cities and towns may not adopt rules more stringent than the state fire code on residential sprinkler systems. Whether another building needs sprinklers depends on the state fire code and building code (see "Which Fire Code Applies"), which this library doesn't reproduce; ask your local fire chief. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Landlord Registration
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statewide landlord registration, rental license or registration-before-occupancy requirement. The only statewide filing aimed at landlords is for owners of restricted property (any residential rental that isn't nonrestricted property): within 30 days after becoming the owner, file a statement with the town or city clerk naming a person in New Hampshire authorized to accept legal papers about the property (see "In-State Agent for Legal Papers"). The town may charge a reasonable filing fee and may fine you up to $100 for not filing. General business filings can apply too. If you rent as a sole proprietor under a name other than your own, or as a partnership, you must register the trade name with the Secretary of State and renew it every 5 years; failing to is a violation for an individual and a misdemeanor for anyone else (N.H. Rev. Stat. Ann. §§ 349:1, I, 349:5, 349:8 and 349:9). And an out-of-state limited liability company or corporation doing business here must register with the Secretary of State or obtain a certificate of authority, and cannot maintain an eviction until it does (see "In-State Agent for Legal Papers"). Some cities and towns may have their own rental registration or inspection programs, which this library doesn't cover; check locally. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Lease Type-Size Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire sets no minimum type size for a residential lease, and no rule penalizes small print in a lease. Its 12-point rules reach only other documents: the property abandonment notice form is deemed sufficient in at least 12-point type, and the court's notice that accompanies an eviction writ must be in at least 12-point type. Use a readable size anyway. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Rights a Lease Cannot Waive
bodyText: New Hampshire has no single statute listing every tenant right a lease cannot waive; the bans are in several statutes, and each makes the waiver void: any of the tenant's rights under the eviction chapter (such as the grounds and notice for ending a tenancy, the right to stop a nonpayment case by paying, and the retaliation and habitability defenses); the tenant's security deposit rights, except that you and the tenant may agree on what happens to your liability for the deposit when you sell or assign; a condominium tenant's protections when paying rent to the owners' association; a tenant's rights in a condominium conversion; and the right to damages under the Consumer Protection Act. Leave such terms out (see "Terms a Lease Cannot Contain"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Property-Tax Rent Statement
bodyText: New Hampshire doesn't require you to give tenants a statement of the property-tax portion of their rent. The only property-tax rule in its landlord-tenant statutes is about deposits: if your lease makes the tenant pay all or part of a real estate tax increase during the lease term and the tenant hasn't paid it, you may deduct that share from the security deposit with a written itemized list stating the period the claim covers (see "Passing On Real Estate Tax Increases"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Paying to Keep the Tenancy
bodyText: In New Hampshire a tenant sued for nonpayment can end the case by paying, before the hearing, all rent due plus the other lawful charges in the lease, $15 liquidated damages and your filing and service costs, no more than three times in 12 months (see "Paying to Stop a Nonpayment Eviction"). There is no right to redeem after judgment, but three other routes can keep a tenant in place: during the case you may accept the arrears and still proceed only if you tell the tenant in writing that you intend to; after judgment in a nonpayment case you and the tenant may file an agreement that the writ won't issue if the tenant follows a payment schedule (which waives the tenant's appeal); and the court may delay the move-out on condition that the tenant pays weekly rent. A tenant who appeals a nonpayment judgment must pay the rent into court weekly. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Selling the Property or Changing Managers
bodyText: When you sell a New Hampshire rental, the buyer of a property occupied by a tenant at will takes over your rights under the eviction statute, and security deposits must be turned over to the buyer at the deed or within 5 days after, with notice to each tenant by registered or certified mail of who now holds the deposit (see "Deposits When the Property Is Sold"). A foreclosure purchaser may recover possession only through the court process (see "Tenants and Foreclosure"). New Hampshire has no general rule requiring notice to tenants of a new owner or manager, an estoppel certificate or a release of the selling landlord's other duties; tell tenants in writing where to pay rent and whom to contact, and a buyer of restricted property must file its own in-state agent statement within 30 days of becoming the owner (see "In-State Agent for Legal Papers"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Self-Help Evictions
bodyText: New Hampshire bars self-help eviction. You may not try to get around the court eviction process, willfully interrupt a utility service the tenant receives (except temporarily during actual repairs or emergencies), or willfully seize, hold or otherwise deny the tenant access to the unit or the tenant's belongings other than through proper judicial process. A lease clause allowing it would waive the tenant's rights under the eviction statute and be void. A tenant can petition the court for an order and damages (see "No Lockouts for Late Rent"). An older statute says certain unlawful uses of the premises let the owner re-enter without legal process, but the statutes don't say how it fits with the later ban, so use the courts (see "Unlawful Use Voids the Lease"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Leasing in Single-Family Zones
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute limits renting out homes in single-family zones. The only related state rule is about accessory dwelling units: a city or town may require the owner of a single-family home with an accessory dwelling unit to live in one of the two units, though it may not say which one. Local zoning may add other limits, which this library doesn't cover; check locally (see "Accessory Dwelling Units"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Written Leases and Long Terms
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute found requires a residential lease to be in writing; whether the general rule for contracts for the sale of land reaches leases is a question of case law this library hasn't reviewed. A lease for more than 7 years is not valid against anyone other than you and your heirs, such as a later buyer or lender, unless it is acknowledged and recorded. Without a written lease or other contract showing a different arrangement, a tenancy is at will. Put every lease in writing anyway (see "Lease Length and Recording"). New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; case law was not.

title: Voucher Inspections
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute addresses refusing a voucher or other subsidized tenancy because of the program's inspection, or a subsidized tenant's refusal of an inspection. Source of income isn't a protected class under the state fair housing law, so state law doesn't require you to join a voucher program or accept its inspection (see "No Source-of-Income Protection"). Apply any policy the same way to every applicant. Federal program rules and local ordinances may apply and aren't covered here. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: No Exemption Notice
bodyText: New Hampshire doesn't require you to tell tenants that a rental is exempt from rent limits, eviction-cause rules or a tenant purchase right. The state has no rent cap; its split between restricted and nonrestricted property decides whether you need a listed ground to end a tenancy, but no notice of which applies is required (see "No Rent-Cap or Coverage Notice" and "No Good-Cause Coverage Notice"). The only tenant purchase right arises when a building of more than 10 units is converted to condominium or similar ownership (see "Converting to Condominiums"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Casualty and Re-Renting Rights a Lease Can Change
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute giving a residential tenant a right to end the lease or stop paying rent after a fire or other casualty, and no statute requiring you to try to re-rent after a tenant leaves early, so there is no statutory casualty or re-renting right that a lease must preserve or could waive. A lease may therefore allocate what happens after a casualty (see "Fire or Casualty Damage"), but it still can't waive the tenant's rights under the eviction statute, such as the notice and grounds needed to end a tenancy, or the tenant's security deposit rights. Whether a court would excuse rent for a destroyed unit or reduce a departed tenant's liability because you didn't try to re-rent is case law this library hasn't reviewed (see "Abandonment and Re-Renting"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and court rules were searched; case law was not.

title: Move-In Condition List and Move-Out Deductions
bodyText: New Hampshire doesn't require a joint move-in or move-out inspection. Where the deposit statute applies, when you receive a deposit you must tell the tenant that any conditions in the unit needing repair or correction should be noted on the receipt or given to you in writing within 5 days of occupancy; if the deposit is paid by check and no receipt is required, you must still give that written notice (see "Security Deposit Receipt and Condition List" and "Existing Condition of Property"). Failing to comply is treated as a violation of the consumer protection act. At the end of the tenancy, any deduction for damage beyond reasonable wear and tear needs a written, itemized list stating the repair needed and satisfactory evidence that it has been or will be done (see "Return of Security Deposit"). Keep dated photos at move-in and move-out. The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Electric Submetering
bodyText: New Hampshire has no electric submetering disclosure because its utility rules generally don't let you resell electricity to tenants by usage. Where a building is served through one master electric meter, the utility's tariff must bar the customer from passing on the electricity except by including it in a fixed rent, and where individual metering isn't required, meters you install yourself may not be used to bill for electricity use. So include master-metered electricity in the rent, or have the utility meter and bill each unit. Separately, before the tenant signs, you must disclose in writing if, to your knowledge, a metered utility the tenant will pay is provided under a tariff carrying energy-efficiency or renewable-energy charges (see "Energy Improvement Utility Charges Disclosure" and "Submetering and Utility Billing"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; utility tariffs, case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Energy-Efficiency Charges on a Utility Bill
bodyText: New Hampshire's version of a meter conservation charge disclosure is its energy-improvement tariff rule. Before the tenant signs, you must disclose in writing if, to your knowledge, a metered utility service the tenant may have to pay for is provided under a utility tariff with unamortized or ongoing charges for energy-efficiency or renewable-energy improvements; the disclosure should include, if known, the remaining term and amount of the charges and any estimates or documentation of energy or fuel savings. Use the "Energy Improvement Utility Charges Disclosure" clause and give it to the tenant before signing. New Hampshire has no other rule on conservation charges billed to tenants. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; utility tariffs, case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Pet Deposits, Fees and Pet Rent
bodyText: Where New Hampshire's deposit statute applies, a pet deposit or one-time pet fee is part of the security deposit, because the statute treats all money beyond the monthly rent that a tenant pays you for any purpose as a security deposit. It counts toward the cap of one month's rent or $100, whichever is greater, is held in trust and is returned under the deposit rules, so a nonrefundable pet fee isn't allowed (see "Security Deposit Cap" and "No Nonrefundable Deposits"). No statute addresses monthly pet rent; if you charge it, state it in the lease as part of the monthly rent. One special rule: in state- or federally financed public housing for older people that votes to allow companion animals, a pet owner may be required to post a damage deposit of up to 1.5 times the monthly rent (see "Pets in Public Elderly Housing"). The deposit statute doesn't apply to a person renting a single-family home who owns no other rental property, or renting units in an owner-occupied building of five units or fewer, except any unit occupied by someone 60 or older. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Renters Insurance Rules
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute or rule regulating whether you may require renters insurance, setting minimum coverage, governing coverage you buy for a tenant who doesn't carry it, capping related fees, or requiring an insurance or flood notice. You may require renters insurance in the lease (see "Tenant's Property & Renter's Insurance"), but don't use it to shift repairs you owe under the state minimum housing standards (see "Tenant Insurance and Your Repair Duties"). New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, constitution, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Property Managers Need a Real Estate License
bodyText: If you pay someone else to rent out or manage your property, New Hampshire's real estate licensing law applies to that person. The law treats as a real estate broker anyone who, acting for another for a commission or other compensation, rents or leases real estate, offers or negotiates rentals, lists property for lease, advertises or holds themselves out as being in the rental business, helps find prospective tenants, or collects or offers to collect rent, and it is unlawful to act as a broker or salesperson without a license. So a leasing agent or property manager you pay to find tenants, negotiate leases or collect rent must hold a New Hampshire real estate license, as a broker or as a salesperson licensed under a broker. The law does not apply to you as the owner, to your own regular employees dealing with your property, to someone acting for you under a power of attorney, to a lawyer doing legal work, or to a receiver, trustee, executor, guardian or similar fiduciary acting in that role. A person who wasn't licensed when offering the service can't sue in a New Hampshire court for a fee or commission for it, and the real estate commission may fine unlicensed practice up to $10,000 per offense, or the amount the person gained if that is greater, and seek an injunction. Check a manager's license with the New Hampshire real estate commission before you hire. New Hampshire's statutes and 2026 laws were searched; the commission's rules and case law were not.

title: Dog Bites and Dog Licenses
bodyText: New Hampshire's dog statute makes the person who owns, keeps or possesses a dog liable for damage the dog causes to another person or to that person's property, including livestock and other domestic animals, unless the injured person was trespassing or committing another wrong at the time; a parent or guardian is liable if the owner or keeper is a minor. The statute doesn't mention landlords, and whether a landlord who allows a tenant's dog can be treated as its keeper or possessor is a question of case law, not covered here. Every owner or keeper of a dog 4 months old or older must license it each year with the clerk of the town or city where it is kept and keep the town's tag on its collar; failing to do so carries a $25 forfeiture. A dog may be found a nuisance or menace if, among other things, it barks for sustained periods of more than half an hour, or at night, so as to disturb the peace and quiet of the neighborhood, chases people who aren't on its owner's or keeper's premises, or bites people (from January 1, 2027, when not on the owner's property), and a dog whose owner or keeper fails to abate a nuisance after an order may be taken into custody. Because that question isn't settled, take the cautious course if you allow dogs: ask for proof of the town license, require renter's insurance that covers pet liability (the library's pet insurance clause, which doesn't apply to assistance animals), and keep the right to revoke approval of a dog that becomes a nuisance or safety concern. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Renting a Room in Your Own Home
bodyText: If you rent out a room with its own sleeping area in a place where the occupant shares a significant part of the home with you, such as the kitchen, dining area, bathroom or bathing area, without a rented right to use that space alone, New Hampshire treats it as a shared facility under its own chapter, and the eviction chapter doesn't apply. Rentals to transient guests for fewer than 90 days, hotel and vacation rooms, and rooms in dormitories, nursing homes, hospitals, group homes, jails and emergency shelters are not shared facilities. A shared-facility tenancy is at will, with rent payable as agreed, unless a written contract says otherwise, and a verbal agreement is allowed. To end it, give the occupant written notice, handed to the occupant or attached to the main entrance of the occupant's own area: 30 days for any reason, without stating one; 7 days for nonpayment of rent; or 72 hours for damage to the premises, behavior by the occupant or a guest that adversely affects the health or safety of the other occupants or you, or a material breach of the rental agreement. These notices replace the court eviction process: the occupant has no possessory rights in any part of the facility, you may take possession of the occupant's area at the end of the notice period, and you may ask law enforcement for help. The occupant may leave on 30 days' written notice, or as a written agreement provides. Store belongings an occupant leaves behind with reasonable care for 3 days after the occupant vacates; after that you may dispose of them without notice. You may set the amount of any security deposit; if it is more than 30 days' rent, give a written receipt saying where it will be kept and when it will be returned, and if there is no written agreement, return it within 20 days after the occupant leaves. The general deposit statute is written for rental units with their own living, sleeping, kitchen and bathroom facilities. If you break the shared-facility rules, the occupant may petition the court for the same remedies tenants have against lockouts and other prohibited practices, but not the lockout remedies if you followed the notice rules. New Hampshire's statutes, 2026 laws, court rules and administrative rules were searched; case law and local ordinances were not.

title: Arbitration Clauses in New Hampshire Leases
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute deals specifically with arbitration clauses in residential leases. The general arbitration statute makes a written provision to arbitrate later disputes arising out of the contract valid, irrevocable and enforceable, except on grounds that would undo any contract, and it excludes only employer-employee agreements (RSA 542:1). A lease cannot waive a tenant's rights under the eviction chapter, deposit rights, or Consumer Protection Act damages (RSA 540:28; 540-A:8, III; 358-A:10, I). Such a term is void, but no statute penalizes you for including it. Tenants may also petition the district court over lockouts, utility shutoffs and similar violations (RSA 540-A:4, II). The library offers an optional clause, `arbitration-agreement`. It covers money claims only. Possession, small claims, security-deposit, injury, emergency and government-agency matters stay out. Every remedy and the right to a lawyer are kept, you pay the arbitration fees above a court filing fee, the tenant has 30 days to opt out, and both of you initial it separately. Parts of it rest on federal arbitration law, so a court here could still refuse to enforce it. If one did, the dispute would simply go to court. New Hampshire case law was not reviewed.

title: Checks Marked 'Paid in Full'
bodyText: New Hampshire follows the Uniform Commercial Code rule on checks marked 'paid in full' (RSA 382-A:3-311). If a tenant, or anyone else you have a claim against, gives you a check or other payment instrument for less than you claim, with a conspicuous statement, on the check or in a writing with it, that it is offered in full satisfaction of the claim, then cashing it settles your whole claim, the unpaid balance included. This applies only when the payment was offered in good faith and the amount was not yet fixed or was subject to a genuine (bona fide) dispute, so writing 'paid in full' on a short check for rent nobody disputes does not by itself settle the rent owed. Writing 'under protest' or 'without prejudice' when you endorse the check does not save the balance: the rule on reserving your rights does not apply to an accord and satisfaction (RSA 382-A:1-308(b)). There are two ways out. If you are an organization (for example an LLC) and, within a reasonable time before the check, sent the tenant a conspicuous statement that communications about disputed debts, including checks offered in full satisfaction, must go to a named person, office or place, the claim is not settled if the check or the writing with it was not received there. And whether or not you are an organization, the claim is not settled if you offer to repay the amount of the check within 90 days after it is paid; an organization that sent the statement just described cannot use this second way out. Neither way out works if you, or your agent responsible for the disputed debt, knew within a reasonable time before the check was collected that it was offered in full satisfaction. The cautious course: don't cash a check for less than you claim that is marked as payment in full of a disputed amount; return it, and if one is cashed by mistake, offer the money back within 90 days.

title: Duty of Good Faith
bodyText: New Hampshire's landlord-tenant statutes impose no general duty of good faith of the kind in the Uniform Residential Landlord and Tenant Act (RSA chs. 540, 540-A and 540-B searched); good faith appears only in specific rules. Courts in many states read a covenant of good faith and fair dealing into every contract, a lease included; whether and how New Hampshire's courts do is case law this library has not reviewed, so act as if the duty applies. In practice: give notices, enter, handle the deposit, enforce lease terms and end a tenancy honestly and for the purpose the law or the lease gives you the right, not as a pretext.

title: Animals Left in a Rental
bodyText: New Hampshire's statutes give a landlord no special right to enter a unit to check on or remove a tenant's animal, and no procedure for taking custody of an animal a tenant leaves behind. Entry follows the general rule: you may enter only with the tenant's prior consent, to make emergency repairs, or under a court order (RSA 540-A:3, IV and V-d). The property-left-behind rule requires you to store a vacating tenant's personal property with reasonable care for 7 days, and it does not mention animals (RSA 540-A:3, VII). Abandoning an animal without adequate provision for its care, sustenance or shelter is cruelty, a crime for the person who had the animal in his or her possession or custody (RSA 644:8, I and III(e)). No statute says that a landlord who feeds or shelters an abandoned pet becomes its owner or keeper, but the cruelty law reaches anyone with an animal in his or her possession or custody, so once you take an animal in, give it proper care. An officer charging a person with cruelty may confiscate the animals (RSA 644:8, IV(a)(1)). Cautious course: ask tenants in writing for an emergency contact who can care for their animals; if you believe an animal is left without care and you cannot reach the tenant or the contact, call the local animal control officer or police rather than entering yourself, and if you do end up holding an animal, hand it to animal control or a shelter promptly and keep a written record.

title: No Carpet Cleaning Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute on carpet cleaning at move-out: nothing lets you require professional cleaning as a matter of law, nothing conditions such a requirement on the carpets having been professionally cleaned before the tenancy, and there is no age or depreciation test for carpet or paint. The deposit rule is general: you may deduct the cost of repairing damage to the premises, excluding reasonable wear and tear, and you must give the tenant a written, itemized list describing each repair with particularity and satisfactory evidence, such as receipts or estimates, that the repair has been or will be done (RSA 540-A:7, I). You may also deduct other lawful charges due under the lease that remain unpaid, itemized (RSA 540-A:7, II). Cautious course: charge for carpet cleaning only where the carpet is dirtier or more damaged than ordinary use would leave it, document its condition at move-in and move-out with photos, and keep the cleaning invoice to attach to the itemized list. A lease term requiring professional cleaning regardless of condition risks being treated as a charge for reasonable wear and tear; case law this library has not reviewed.

title: Recording a New Hampshire Lease Is Optional
bodyText: New Hampshire has no lease registry and does not require you to record an ordinary residential lease. Recording matters only for a long lease: a lease for more than 7 years from when it is made is not valid against anyone but you and your heirs, such as a later buyer or lender, unless it is acknowledged and recorded at the registry of deeds (RSA 477:7). Between you and the tenant an unrecorded lease still binds. Instead of recording the whole lease, you may record a notice of lease signed and acknowledged by all parties that gives the parties' names and addresses, the date the lease was signed, the description of the premises as it appears in the lease, the term, and the start date and any extension or renewal rights (RSA 477:7-a, I). Nothing in New Hampshire's eviction or tenant-protection chapters turns on whether a lease was recorded. Consider recording a notice of lease when the term, counting renewal options, runs past 7 years or when the tenant has a purchase option it needs protected against a future owner.

title: Time Limit to Sue for Rent or Damages: Three Years
bodyText: New Hampshire's landlord-tenant chapters set no special deadline for suing a former tenant, so the general limitation statute applies. Personal actions, which include a suit for unpaid rent, lease charges or damage to the unit, must be brought within 3 years of the act or omission complained of; where the injury could not reasonably have been discovered at the time, the 3 years run from when you discovered it or reasonably should have (RSA 508:4, I). Actions on contracts under seal and on judgments may be brought within 20 years (RSA 508:5), but whether a residential lease counts as under seal is case law this library has not reviewed, so treat 3 years as your deadline. Time while the former tenant is absent from and residing outside New Hampshire is not counted (RSA 508:9). We found no New Hampshire statute saying that a part payment or a written acknowledgment restarts the period; that is case law this library has not reviewed. For a periodic tenancy, sue for each unpaid installment within 3 years of the date it fell due, and once you win, a judgment can be enforced for 20 years (RSA 508:5).

title: Showings Need the Tenant's Consent
bodyText: New Hampshire sets no fixed number of hours' notice for showings, so there is no notice period to waive or shorten. Instead, you may enter only with the tenant's prior consent, except to make emergency repairs or under a court order (RSA 540-A:3, IV and V-d). The tenant in turn may not willfully refuse you access for reasonable and lawful functions of ownership, which include showings, at a reasonable time after notice that is adequate under the circumstances (RSA 540-A:3, V). No statute provides for a separate signed waiver or a no-notice showing agreement, and none limits such an agreement to buyers. If a tenant refuses, you may petition the district court for an order authorizing entry (RSA 540-A:3, V-d(b); RSA 540-A:4). Cautious course: state in the lease the notice you will give for showings (the library's entry clause uses 24 hours), ask for the tenant's consent to each showing or set of showings, and do not enter for a showing over the tenant's objection without a court order; whether a lease clause alone is the 'prior consent' the statute requires is case law this library has not reviewed.

title: Renting to Students in New Hampshire
bodyText: New Hampshire has no student-housing licence, certification or special rent, deposit or termination rule; a student who rents a private apartment or house is an ordinary tenant. The student-housing rules are exclusions from the eviction chapter, not duties. That chapter does not apply to rooms in student dormitories (RSA 540:1-a, IV(c)). It also does not apply to residential units leased by a member of a fraternal or social organization that provides student housing for a postsecondary institution, in a structure the organization owns and operates (RSA 540:1-a, IV(g)). The shared-facility chapter likewise excludes rooms provided ancillary to other primary purposes such as student dormitories (RSA 540-B:1, II(c)). So privately owned student apartments, including buildings leased by the bed near a campus, are covered by the eviction and tenant-protection chapters in full, and you must use the ordinary eviction process. Don't label an ordinary apartment a dormitory to avoid that process.

title: Banning a Non-Tenant from the Property in New Hampshire
bodyText: New Hampshire's criminal trespass law lets you keep a non-tenant out of parking lots, hallways and other common areas. A person commits criminal trespass by entering or remaining in any place knowing he or she is not licensed or privileged to do so (RSA 635:2, I). It is a misdemeanor rather than a violation when the person knowingly enters or remains in defiance of an order to leave or not to enter that was personally communicated by the owner or another authorized person, or in secured premises, meaning premises posted, fenced or enclosed to exclude intruders (RSA 635:2, III(b)(1)-(2), V). Separately, no one who is not a tenant, subtenant or implied tenant may occupy residential property without the permission of the owner, landlord or agent (RSA 540-A:3, IX). So give the person a written no-trespass notice in person, keep a dated copy and a witness, and tell the police. A tenant's invited guest in the tenant's own unit is there with the tenant's permission, so control guests through the lease's guest and conduct terms and the eviction process rather than by a trespass order against the guest.

title: Hunting and Fishing on Rented Land
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute deciding whether you or your tenant holds the hunting and fishing rights on rented land or farmland, so the lease decides. Two rules show that a tenant has a say. Land may be posted against trespass and hunting with signs bearing the name and address of the owner or lessee of the land (RSA 635:4). And no one may discharge a firearm or shoot a bow while hunting within 300 feet of a permanently occupied dwelling without permission of the owner or the occupant of the dwelling, or of the owner of the land the shooter is on (RSA 207:3-a), so your tenant, as occupant, can give or refuse that permission near the home. Entering or remaining on land knowing you are not licensed or privileged to be there is criminal trespass (RSA 635:2, I). If you rent a home with land and want to keep the hunting, fishing and trapping rights or let others use them, say so in the lease, describe where and when you or your guests will hunt, and state whether the tenant may hunt or invite others; if you want the tenant to have those rights, grant them in writing with any limits.

title: Tenant Energy Data: Utility Needs the Tenant's Express Consent
bodyText: New Hampshire has no building energy benchmarking law and no statute that lets a lease clause authorize a utility to release a tenant's energy usage data to you. Its utility privacy law runs the other way: an electric, gas or water utility or other service provider may not share, disclose or make accessible a customer's individual customer data to any third party, including you as landlord, except as the statute allows or upon the express consent of the customer (RSA 363:38, I(a)). Individual customer data includes the customer's name, address, account number and the quantity and characteristics of service used (RSA 363:37, I). A utility may still use aggregate data with identifying information removed for analysis, reporting or program management (RSA 363:38, V(a)). If a unit's utility account is in the tenant's name and you need its usage, for an efficiency program, a lender or a sale, ask the tenant to sign the utility's own consent form; the statute does not say whether a sentence in a lease is enough express consent, so treat a lease clause only as the tenant's promise to sign that form.

title: No Chemical Exposure Warning Rule
bodyText: California's Proposition 65 warning for rental housing has no New Hampshire counterpart. New Hampshire's statutes do not require a landlord to post or give tenants a general warning about exposure to chemicals known to cause cancer or reproductive harm, and they tie no chemical list to rentals. The hazard disclosures New Hampshire does require are specific: methamphetamine production on the property (RSA 477:4-g), the federal lead disclosure for pre-1978 housing with the state's lead-order rules, and the others listed in the library's environmental contamination row (`edu-contamination-disclosures-nh`). Before signing, you must also disclose any public-utility energy-improvement tariff on the premises (RSA 477:4-h). Beyond these, keep the unit safe and code-compliant, and if you know of a hazardous condition, telling the tenant in writing is the cautious course.

title: No Tenant Rights Guide; Fair Housing Notice Posting for Rental Offices
bodyText: New Hampshire does not require you to give a residential tenant a state-published guide to landlord and tenant rights, before signing or at renewal, and requires no signed acknowledgment of one; no statute requires a lease to carry a summary of the landlord-tenant laws. New Hampshire's fair housing law does have a posting duty: every person, real estate agency and rental office subject to the law against discrimination must post in a conspicuous place on the premises a notice prepared or approved by the Human Rights Commission setting out excerpts of the law (RSA 354-A:23). A rental office that refuses to comply commits a violation if it is a natural person, or a misdemeanor if any other person (RSA 354-A:23). If you keep a rental or leasing office, post the Commission's notice there; the statute does not say whether a landlord with no office must post it elsewhere (case law and the Commission's rules not reviewed). The landlord-tenant chapters otherwise require specific notices, such as the written disclosure of any application fee and screening requirement before you collect the fee (RSA 540-A:3, VIII), and the district court provides forms for the demand for rent and eviction notice (RSA 540:5, II).

title: No Government Approval Needed for a New Hampshire Lease
bodyText: New Hampshire has nothing like the territorial communal-land schemes. No New Hampshire statute requires a lease of communal, tribal or native-owned land to be approved by a government officer before it is valid, and New Hampshire has no state reservation or tribal land whose leases state law voids or controls. More broadly, no New Hampshire statute conditions a residential lease's validity on government approval. The only filing rule for leases is recording: a lease for more than 7 years is not valid against anyone but you and your heirs unless acknowledged and recorded (RSA 477:7), and between you and the tenant even that lease binds without recording. Land held in trust by the United States for a tribe is governed by federal and tribal law, outside this library; don't use this lease for it.

title: No Special District Statement Required in a New Hampshire Lease
bodyText: No New Hampshire statute requires a residential lease to state that the property is inside a special district, such as a village district or precinct, or to have the tenant acknowledge district charges, rules or plans. We found no statute that passes district taxes or charges to a tenant; they reach the tenant only if the lease shifts them. The landlord-tenant chapters do let a lease require the tenant to pay all or part of an increase in real estate taxes, and you may then deduct an unpaid share from the deposit with an itemized list (RSA 540-A:7, II). So if you want the tenant to share a district assessment or tax increase, say so plainly in the lease; nothing does it automatically. The one pre-signing disclosure in this area concerns energy-improvement tariffs on utility service, not districts (RSA 477:4-h).

title: Housing for Your Employees
bodyText: New Hampshire has no statute requiring an employer-landlord to give a housed employee a signed disclosure of the conditions for occupying and vacating, or to offer a rental agreement when the job ends. An employee who lives in housing you provide is ordinarily a tenant, so ending the occupancy uses the ordinary eviction process. The one special rule covers caregivers: the eviction chapter does not apply to an occupancy where the occupant is hired to provide care or assistance for a person with disabilities (RSA 540:1-a, IV(h)). In that case the person with disabilities or his or her guardian may order the caregiver to leave without the eviction process, but only if a written agreement says the care arrangement authorizes summary ejection and the caregiver gets written notice to vacate in not less than 72 hours (RSA 540:1-a, IV(h)(1)-(2)). If the agreement pays the caregiver more than free housing, that compensation must be paid before the caregiver vacates (RSA 540:1-a, IV(h)(3)). For any other resident manager, caretaker or farm worker, put the housing terms in a written lease or employment agreement and expect to use the eviction chapter if the job ends and the employee stays.

title: No Senior Housing Staff Card Rule
bodyText: New Hampshire's statutes set no work-card, licensing or background-check requirement for staff who work in 55-and-older or other age-restricted rental housing. New Hampshire's senior-housing rule is a fair housing exemption instead: the familial-status protections do not apply to housing for older persons (RSA 354-A:15, VIII). That means housing provided under a state or federal program designed for elderly persons, housing intended for and solely occupied by people 62 or older, or housing intended and operated for people 55 or older where at least 80 percent of occupied units have at least one person 55 or older, the community publishes and follows policies showing that intent, and it complies with the Human Rights Commission's rules for verifying occupancy by surveys and affidavits (RSA 354-A:15, VIII(a)). Every other protected class, including disability accommodation, still applies. If you operate 55-and-older housing, keep your age-verification surveys and written policies current.

title: Leasing as a Life Tenant (No Usufruct in New Hampshire)
bodyText: Usufruct is a civil-law interest that New Hampshire property law does not use, so the rule about leases granted by a usufructuary does not arise here. The closest New Hampshire interest is a life estate, for example a surviving spouse or a parent who holds the home for life while others own the remainder. No New Hampshire statute says how long a lease signed by a life tenant may run or what happens to it when the life estate ends; that is case law this library has not reviewed. The cautious course if you lease as a life tenant: say so in the lease, keep the term short or month-to-month, and have the remainder owners sign the lease or agree in writing that it continues if your life estate ends first. If the tenant stays after your life estate ends, the remainder owners should not change the locks or otherwise force the tenant out; New Hampshire bars denying a tenant possession other than through judicial process (RSA 540-A:3, II), so the cautious course is the court process.
